Flickering candles lit up Dublin’s O’Connell Street as Ireland’s Nepalese community gathered in grief — and in support — after catastrophic flooding tore through parts of Nepal.

Around 100 people attended a candle lit vigil at the Spire, organised by the Non-Resident Nepali Association of Ireland to honour those who have died and to raise funds for rescue and relief operations.
Avishek Bogati, a vice president of the association, comes from one of the areas struck by the deluge that hit on Wednesday after a glacier collapsed.
He told RTÉ News that “my uncle is also still missing”.
The vigil in Dublin was just one of several events planned around Ireland Mr Bogati said uncertainty is still widespread as families wait for news.
“Nobody knows how many people are missing and how many people have died.
“Maybe after two weeks or after a month they will figure it out.” He said his mother was airlifted by a military helicopter and brought to Kathmandu.
His village, he added, is among several left in ruins.
“There are three villages and 90% of the people are missing, 90% missing,” he said, adding “they still don’t have any information”.
Ireland is home to around 3,000 Nepalese people, most living in the Greater Dublin Area, with others based in counties Galway, Limerick and Cork.
Hundreds are employed on dairy farms, drawing on skills they previously developed while working in Gulf states.
The gathering in Dublin is one of a number of solidarity events planned nationwide.
Prajaya Neupane, a Nepali living in Co Limerick, said a fundraiser will also take place tomorrow night at Hunters Sports Bar in the city, offering food and drinks.
He said all proceeds will be sent to support those affected by the disaster in Nepal.

‘Something unprecedented’ – Nepalese man on flash floods Mahesh Kushwaha originally thought the incident was a monsoon flood Separately, a Nepalese man who recently returned to Dublin from Nepal said that while Kathmandu is already struggling under pressure, the wider response has provided some hope.
Mahesh Kushwaha, a PhD candidate at DCU, said he initially assumed the flooding was linked to the monsoon — an annual threat he described as both regular and worrying.
But as videos began circulating, he said he quickly understood the true magnitude.
“It was massive, it was something unprecedented,” he said.
Authorities said the death toll in Nepal and Tibet from last week’s floods has hit 797 with more than 3,000 missing.
At least 781 people died in Nepal, its disaster authority said, with 2,502 people missing as rescue efforts continue for a fifth day.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead in Tibet and 546 people missing following the disaster, taking the overall toll to 797 dead and 3,048 unaccounted for.
Nepalese man says the situation in Nepal is ‘pretty dire’ Mr Kushwaha said conditions on the ground remain “pretty dire”, with bridges swept away and homes buried by debris.
“It’s really difficult to even get the rescue efforts and teams up in the worst affected areas,” he said.
Even once rain eases and water levels become less dangerous, he warned it will take a “lot of time” to reach those still missing or trapped in the hardest-hit locations.
He said his family are from the southern part of the country — “pretty far” from the flooded areas.
Speaking on RTÉ’s This Week programme, he said: “So, I do not have any of my immediate family or friends directly affected by it.

“But I personally know three to four people who are still missing in the flood from my village, which is quiet far from the affected areas.” He said work patterns tied to the border economy mean people often travel into the regions now impacted — including to drive trucks or take jobs as civil engineers, among other roles.
Mr Kushwaha said the new government responded quickly, and described it as “quiet uplifting to see”.
He said the prime minister and the home minister were “on the ground”, adding “they’re working with the people”.

While some social media posts have framed this as a stunt, he said: “As a whole the government is seen positively right now, especially with regards to the rescue efforts.” Mahesh Kushwaha said the response to the floods ‘has been quite uplifting’ He said hospitals in Kathmandu are receiving both survivors and the dead.
“Kathmandu’s infrastructures are already being overwhelmed … especially by the dead bodies,” he said.
“We don’t have specialised storages for those bodies.” Mr Kushwaha said: “The overwhelming response from the people as well as from the international community has been quite uplifting.
This, he said, is “because we have seen billions of dollars being pulled in for rescue efforts”.
He said the Nepali diaspora has also mobilised to support relief efforts.
“But still, it’s so devastating,” he said.
Mr Mr Kushwaha said Nepal is one of the “smallest contributors in the world when it comes to carbon emissions”.
But he added the nation is “among the most vulnerable countries when it comes to climate change”.
“People are slowly seeing that these events are not just natural disasters out of nowhere it’s being linked to climate change,” he added.

Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School when the school’s accountant rushed in to warn that floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire villages.
Then, a teacher received another warning by phone.
Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home.
Rajendra Dawadi took the decision to clear Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School (AP) The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Mr Dawadi had little time to act.
He rang the school bell and ordered pupils and staff out of the building and to move towards higher ground.
“I immediately decided to stop … school and (get the children out),” he told The Associated Press.
As he followed them to a nearby hill, the floodwaters rose behind him.
From the safety of the hillside, he turned to watch the school where he had once been a pupil – and where he had spent years teaching – disappear beneath a torrent of water, mud, boulders and debris.
Two staff members could not make it, and remain missing.
The death toll in the catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet climbed past 900 on Monday, with more than 4,700 missing.
Mr Dawadi’s decision to evacuate the school saved at least 900 students from last week’s devastating flash floods in Nepal, unleashed after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas.
The disaster killed more than 900 people across Nepal and China, while more than 4,700 remain missing.
As Nepal grapples with the catastrophic natural disaster, Mr Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage.
The Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in the Trishuli Valley of north-central Nepal had 1,643 pupils.
At least 900 were on campus that morning, while some students were still making their way to school.
Mr Dawadi ordered those already there to leave and called bus drivers, telling them to only stop at safer places.
One bus, packed with students, had already reached the school when Mr Dawadi told the driver to turn back, he said.
The bus crossed a newly constructed bridge and, moments later, the old bridge beside it collapsed.
For Mr Dawadi, the scale of the destruction has become personal, as the school had been both his workplace and a large part of his life.
The search for survivors continues (AP) “I have no words.
I got education from that school.
And I gave education at that school,” he said.
The destruction of Mr Dawadi’s school was not an isolated loss.
Across northern Nepal, the floods have left thousands of children without classrooms, disrupted their education and raised fears that the disaster could cost them months of schooling.
Charity group Save the Children said in a statement that at least 69 schools in northern Nepal have been completely destroyed, putting the education of nearly 19,000 students at risk.

September 1, 2026 KATHMANDU – Hours after the Bhotekoshi floods swept away settlements in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts on Wednesday morning, social media platforms were inundated with dramatic clips purporting to show the destruction.
Some depicted genuine disasters, but from other countries or earlier events.
Several appeared to have been created entirely by artificial intelligence.

The scale and speed of misinformation has complicated an already chaotic information environment at a time when families are desperately searching for missing relatives and authorities are struggling to establish the full extent of the disaster.
For social media users chasing views and virality, the flood has also become lucrative content.
At 7:26 am on Saturday, a Facebook page called Dudhauli FM posted a 20-second video claiming to show Home Minister Sudan Gurung inside a tunnel at the disaster site.
“Home Minister Gurung’s unique style: He reaches inside the tunnel at the incident site to join the rescue,” the caption said, praising what it described as the minister’s proactive involvement.
The page later amended the caption.
The video quickly spread across Facebook, TikTok and X.
But it was not from Nepal.
Fact-checkers established that the footage showed a tunnel rescue operation in Uttarakhand, India.
The uniforms worn by the rescuers and the surroundings matched those seen in the original footage, which had been posted by the Fire Service Uttarakhand Police’s Facebook page on August 14.
The false attribution was only one example of misleading content circulating after the disaster.

As rescuers race against time to reach people trapped in tunnels and communities cut off by the devastating flash flood, a torrent of fabricated videos, recycled footage, artificial intelligence-generated imagery and cruel online commentary has bewildered a wider populace.
On August 27, at 7:54 am, an X account named Prakash Kunwar posted a 10-second video showing what appeared to be a catastrophic flood.
“No one imagined this would happen… What can anyone do when nature goes mad!
May all those caught in the disaster be rescued safely,” the caption said.
The video had received more than seven million views, over 4,100 reposts and around 15,000 reactions at the time of reporting.
Yet the dramatic scene was not real.
When analysed using Hive Moderation, an AI detection tool, the video was assessed as 97.2 percent likely to have been generated by artificial intelligence.
X’s community notes also flagged the clip as artificial, while BBC Verify independently debunked it.
Another viral video posted later that day showed a bridge apparently collapsing amid a raging flood.

The user who shared it wrote: “If this video of the Nepal-Tibet flood is true, I have never seen anything like this in my lifetime…” The clip, analysed through Hive Moderation, was assessed as entirely AI-generated.
International fact-checkers have also joined efforts to trace misleading visuals linked to the disaster.
Nepali fact-checking website Nepal Fact Check recently debunked a video that purported to show a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, in Rasuwa.
The clip showed a violent torrent of water and carried the English text: “This is a GLOF.” The footage had no connection to Nepal.
Fact-checkers traced it to a glacial outburst flood at Columbia Glacier in Alaska, United States.
Similarly, a pair of “before and after” photographs claiming to show a picturesque settlement destroyed by the Rasuwa flood went viral on social media.
Both images were fabricated, according to an independent verification by the Australian Associated Press fact-checking unit.
The false videos and manipulated images are only one part of the digital disorder surrounding the disaster.
Graphic footage of bodies, injuries and devastated communities has also spread widely, often shared by personal social media accounts without warnings or consideration for victims and their families.
The Nepal Press Council, the country’s media regulatory body, says it has been monitoring online content related to the disaster.
Over the past four days, it has instructed 72 social media users to remove inappropriate content, most of it posted through personal accounts.
The council has also opened a dedicated portal, titled “Special Complaints on the Bhotekoshi Incident”, through which members of the public can report misinformation and graphic material.
By 5 pm on Saturday, the portal had received 101 complaints, according to Umesh Shrestha, chairman of the Press Council.
“It was found that 67 personal accounts had posted gruesome scenes.
Similarly, complaints have been lodged against some online news portals and their social media pages,” Shrestha said.
He said mainstream media organisations had largely avoided publishing misleading information and excessively graphic visuals.
“This is a positive takeaway,” he said.
For fact-checkers, the Rasuwa disaster illustrates how artificial intelligence has made an old problem more difficult to contain.
Chetana Kunwar, assistant editor at Nepal Fact Check, said misleading visuals connected to the Bhotekoshi flood were increasingly being created with AI.

“AI-generated content and manipulated ‘before and after’ visuals make it significantly easier to create false impressions, which can be extremely difficult for the general public to detect,” she said.
“At the same time, videos from disasters in other countries are deliberately being circulated as if they were from Nepal.” The spread of false information during disasters is not new.
Old photographs and videos have long been recycled after earthquakes, floods and other major emergencies.
But generative AI has added another layer to the problem, allowing convincing images and videos to be created from scratch within minutes.
The result is an information ecosystem in which even genuine footage can become difficult to verify.
The information vacuum Why does misinformation spread so rapidly during disasters?
Shrestha, a former editor of Nepal Fact Check, points to the intense competition for attention that follows major emergencies.
“Some people post such material for views, while others are driven by the desire to go viral,” he said.
“During a crisis, public attention is heavily concentrated on one event, creating a strong emotional response.

People begin liking, commenting on and sharing posts without verifying them.” Deepak Adhikari, an investigative journalist and editor of Nepal Check, says an “information vacuum” often emerges immediately after a major disaster.
When verified information from the ground is delayed, incomplete or contradictory, social media users begin filling the gaps themselves.
“People start crowdsourcing photographs and videos and sharing them without verification, which makes the problem worse,” Adhikari told the Post.
At the same time, he said, social media influencers and content creators face constant pressure to publish material that attracts attention.
“As a result, they share visually striking graphics and videos without properly verifying where they were recorded,” he said.

The dynamic is particularly dangerous during a fast-moving disaster, when official information can take time to emerge and the public is searching urgently for news about relatives, roads, rescue operations and possible further threats.
Kunwar said people were particularly vulnerable to misinformation during such periods.
“When there is an information vacuum, people often do not stop to assess what is right or wrong.
They tend to believe whatever information reaches them first,” she said.
Social media algorithms can amplify the problem, she added.
Once users engage with disaster-related content, platforms often recommend more of the same, regardless of whether it is accurate.
The consequences can extend beyond confusion.

Shrestha warned that circulating old or fabricated footage as current events could create unnecessary fear and panic, not only among the public but also among rescue and relief workers operating in difficult conditions.
Adhikari said misinformation could directly interfere with emergency operations.
“Someone may already have been rescued and moved to a safe place, but people might continue sharing an old video showing that person trapped somewhere,” he said.

“The primary focus should be rescue and relief, but many people appear more concerned about promoting themselves and posting photographs and videos.” For survivors and families of the missing, false information can repeatedly reopen trauma.
Rumours suggesting another flood is imminent, or that the disaster is about to repeat, can further frighten people who have already lost homes, relatives or livelihoods, Kunwar said.
Government agencies are now attempting to respond.

The government’s Social Media Regulation and Management Committee, which has been tasked with addressing graphic content, AI-generated misinformation, fake QR codes and other forms of online deception, has begun discussions with social media platforms.
But controlling misinformation after it has gone viral remains a formidable challenge.
A crisis of empathy The information crisis surrounding the Rasuwa flood has also revealed something more troubling: a striking absence of empathy.
A video showing a woman tearfully appealing to the government to speed up the search for her husband, who is missing inside a tunnel, has drawn a stream of cruel and abusive comments.
The woman, visibly distressed, pleads for authorities to rescue her husband.
Instead of offering sympathy, some users mocked her grief.
Others criticised her for speaking only about her husband or attacked her for blaming the government.
The cruelty was often casual and anonymous, delivered from behind screens to someone facing the possibility of losing a loved one.
Comments questioning why her husband had taken the job and suggesting that she was secretly happy about his disappearance turned an expression of grief into another spectacle for online consumption.

Such reactions have become an unsettling feature of Nepal’s social media culture during the disaster, where genuine suffering is sometimes treated as entertainment, political ammunition or an opportunity for engagement.
For journalists and fact-checkers, the combination of misinformation and insensitivity presents a broader challenge than simply identifying fake videos.
Disasters create an extraordinary demand for information.
They also create a market for attention.
The faster the information circulates, the less time users may spend asking whether it is authentic.
And when a video provokes fear, outrage or shock, the incentive to share can overwhelm the instinct to verify.
That is why responsibility cannot rest solely with authorities, technology companies or fact-checkers, Kunwar said.

Five days after a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-Tibet border and unleashed a flood that has killed more than 900 people, rescue teams from three countries are focused on one of the most operationally complex high-altitude tunnel rescue efforts in recent Himalayan history: reaching an estimated 500 workers who may still be alive inside the same hydropower tunnels that were designed — and built robustly enough — to survive the disaster around them.
The Nepal flood death toll has reached 903 in Nepal and 16 in Tibet, with hydropower workers trapped in tunnels at 12 affected projects in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

The engineering situation is described precisely by Arnold Dix, an Australian geologist and former ITA president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, who played a leading role in saving 41 workers from the 2023 Uttarakhand tunnel collapse in India and is now advising the Nepal operation remotely from Melbourne.
"Normally, they collapse and I'm trying to get people out," Dix told CNN on August 30.

"This time, they haven't collapsed, but everything around them has, and I'm trying to get in." That distinction — tunnel structurally intact; tunnel entrance buried under meters of Himalayan debris — is the defining challenge of an ongoing rescue effort across at least 11 hydropower projects in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

The Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal, or IPPAN, which represents private power developers, reported that approximately 900 workers remained unaccounted for across 12 projects as of Monday morning, with its president, Mohan Kumar Dangi, estimating that 500 workers believed in tunnels.
Nepal's government disaster agency, NDRRMA, put its NDRRMA missing hydropower worker count at 933.

How a Mountain Fell and Sealed the Tunnels The flood began before dawn Nepal Standard Time on August 26, when a mass of glacier ice and bedrock detached from the northern slope of Langtang Lirung — a 7,234-meter (23,734-foot) peak on the Nepal-Tibet border — and plunged roughly 1,200 meters (3,940 feet) into the valley below.

Geological Survey, which initially detected the event as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake, re-examined seismic waveform data and satellite imagery and USGS reclassified the glacial collapse: no earthquake had occurred.
The seismic signal was generated by the collapse itself, reclassified as a magnitude 5.2 glacial landslide.
The falling ice and rock temporarily dammed the Lhende Khola, a river draining toward the Nepal-China border crossing at Gyirong Port.
When that debris dam failed, a surge of water, rock, and liquefied sediment tore southward through Nepal's Trishuli River system.
At one monitoring point, the river rose 9 meters in minutes — nearly 30 feet in 30 minutes.
The flood carried some victims 240 kilometers (150 miles) downstream into northern India.
By Monday, 903 dead and 4,247 missing had been confirmed in Nepal and 16 dead in Tibet's Gyirong County, with 546 more missing in China.
The dead span citizens of at least 39 countries; 590 foreign nationals still missing, according to Nepal's foreign ministry.

Why the Tunnels May Have Saved Hundreds — and Why That Complicates Everything Nepal's hydropower industry relies on large-bore tunnels bored directly through Himalayan rock to divert and carry water from river intakes to turbine chambers.

These tunnels are engineering accomplishments built to exacting specifications for one reason: Himalayan rivers carry sediment, boulders, and seasonal floods that would destroy above-ground structures.

The Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project — the site where the largest number of workers, roughly 300, are believed trapped — has a 9,490-meter headrace tunnel breakthrough 2025, with a 7.5-meter (25-foot) horseshoe cross-section, constructed by POWERCHINA through difficult geological conditions and completed in late 2025.

The tunnels at other affected projects are similarly sized — large enough, as Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria, noted, "to drive trucks through." That structural robustness is now both the source of hope and the source of difficulty.
If the tunnels themselves survived the flood — as Dix believes is likely — then workers who were inside them when the surge hit may have had protection from the worst of the debris flow.
But the portal entrances of those tunnels, which open onto the valley floor, were buried under the same debris that destroyed surface infrastructure across the flooded corridor.

To reach anyone inside, rescuers must first clear those portals, which can involve moving tens of meters of packed boulders, mud, and rock under live monsoon conditions with active barrier lake secondary flood risk from two barrier lakes that formed upstream.
At the Trishuli-3A powerhouse in Nuwakot District, the tunnel portal was completely buried.
Heavy excavation equipment had to be disassembled and airlifted in by helicopter to reach the site.
On August 29, a controlled blast broke into tunnel in the upper section, allowing rescuers to pump in fresh air and lower a camera — a moment of cautious relief.

Dix, advising from Melbourne with access to technical drawings, satellite images, and aerial video, warned that once inside the portal, rescuers still faced an unknown: "We don't know how much of that tunnel is full of mud or water," he told CNN.

"So, we might only have to dig 10 meters [33 feet], or we might have to dig 100 meters [330 feet]." He also flagged a separate turbine room emergency shutdown risk: if the plant's emergency shutdown systems failed when the flood hit, the turbine rooms themselves could have flooded, potentially drowning any workers sheltering there.
At the Upper Trishuli-1 site in Rasuwa District, the numbers are larger and the status less clear.
IPPAN's Dangi said as many as 576 workers were unaccounted for at that project, with an estimated 300 workers believed in tunnel.

By Monday morning, 208 workers had been rescued from a third Trishuli project on August 29 alone — 43 of them foreign nationals, including 38 Chinese and 5 Indian workers — and a combined total of approximately 361 workers accounted for August 31 through rescue or self-evacuation across all affected sites.
Raja Ram Basnet, was direct about the Nepal Army's challenge opening tunnels.
"A large amount of debris has been deposited, and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels," he told Reuters on Monday.

"Our main focus is on opening the tunnels." What a Teacher's Decision Tells You About the Warning Gap While the tunnel rescue dominates Monday's rescue effort, what happened at a secondary school in Nuwakot District illuminates how little warning time communities had.

Rajendra Dawadi, headmaster of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, ordered the school evacuation 10 minutes before flood — evacuating more than 900 students approximately 10 minutes before the flood reached the school.
By any measure, that decision saved hundreds of lives.
By any engineering measure, 10 minutes is not a warning system — it is a headmaster's judgment call.
The absence of a structured warning has been documented before in this same watershed.
In July 2025, a glacially triggered flood swept away the Nepal-China border bridge at Gyirong, killing at least nine people.
After that event, Nepal and China verbally agreed to establish a cross-border data-sharing system for river levels and glacial flood risks.
As of August 26, 2026, that cross-border data agreement never signed — it had never been formalized.
Survivors Speak Among the workers who escaped, Ram Chandra's six-hour tunnel escape has become emblematic of what those inside faced.
He grabbed hold of a rung bolted into the ceiling as water churned around him.
"The water was rising and it was difficult to move my legs," he said.

"If I had let go from that rung I would have fallen." He and five colleagues spent six hours making their way toward the portal, passing a sheet of tin between them as an improvised foothold, emerging without the clothing the floodwater had torn from them.
The Madan Singh Budha flood account was starker.
He had finished a night shift when the water came.
He looked out and ran uphill.
"Those who weren't able to climb up were swept away," he said.
Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, were buried in shallow graves as decomposition accelerated in Nepal's late-monsoon humidity.
Relatives gathered at mass burial sites in Chitwan, some searching faces for their missing, others in grief over those already recovered.
Three Nations Dig Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who initially declined broader foreign assistance, Nepal reversed foreign assistance decision as the scale became clear.
By Monday, approximately 21,000 security personnel were deployed across affected districts.
China mobilized more than 2,100 rescue workers and disbursed 220 million yuan in relief funds — approximately $33 million USD.
Chinese teams deployed thermal cameras and acoustic detection equipment specifically designed to locate signs of life in enclosed underground spaces.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, speaking from Bishkek, Kazakhstan, on Monday, Xi confirmed Beijing's search efforts for both Chinese and foreign nationals.
India sent tunnel rescue specialists — 18 army officers trained in tunnel operations — alongside six forensic teams equipped for DNA-based identification of flood victims.

India also supplied prefabricated Bailey bridges to reconnect communities severed from the road network when the flood washed out crossings, and delivered four tranches of humanitarian aid including generators, water purification tablets, tents, and medicine.
International support has also arrived from the United Nations, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Australia, South Korea, and the United States.
The Red Cross estimated that more than 90,000 people had been affected by the disaster.
Secondary Flood Threat Hangs over the Rescue The disaster has not stabilized.
Two large barrier lakes formed from debris deposited by the initial flood in the upper Lhende watershed.
The lower lake subsequently drained through natural outflow; the upper barrier lake half drained, according to China's water ministry.

But Nitesh Khadka, a Nepali physical geographer who specializes in glacial floods, warned that a sudden failure of the remaining upper lake could send a surge directly into the active tunnel excavation sites — into the same spaces where rescue workers are operating.
Chinese state media additionally warned that glaciers near the original collapse site on Langtang Lirung could be further destabilized, raising the possibility of a second collapse event.
On Sunday night, monsoon rain temporarily flooded excavation sites across several tunnel locations, halting work before conditions eased.

A Nepal Army statement confirmed that teams had army resumed drilling and excavation using "drilling machines, excavators, hydraulic cutters and other equipment." Warming World, More Workers at Risk The Langtang region was devastated by an ice-and-rock avalanche during the 2015 Nepal earthquakes.
Glacially triggered floods struck the same corridor in 2025.
A comparable glacier-flood event destroyed the Upper Bhote Koshi Hydropower Plant in 2016.
Analogous disasters struck Chamoli, India, in 2021 and Blatten, Switzerland, in 2025.
Scientists are explicit about the limits of attribution: no single event can be directly linked to climate change without specific causation evidence.

What the broader record does show is that the Himalayan region is warming considerably faster than the global average, and as it warms, the permafrost that once stabilized mountain slopes thaws, glacier tongues thin and retreat, and the mechanical foundations of peaks that have stood for millennia begin to fail.
The ICIMOD glacier ice loss doubled since 2000, according to the organization's March 2026 glacier assessment of the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.
"Rising temperatures are changing the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and melting glaciers," said Saswat Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD.
"We have to be cautious and not draw a connection yet.

However, the chances of such disasters increase." That cautious climate change attribution statement reflects the scientific consensus: individual events resist direct attribution; the accelerating pattern does not.
The pattern matters for what Nepal has built.

Academic research has documented for years that hydropower projects across High Mountain Asia face compounding, climate-driven hazards: glacial detachments, rock-ice avalanches, permafrost-triggered landslides, and the outburst floods of glacially and landslide-dammed lakes.
The 2026 Nepal disaster has brought those risk assessments to catastrophic life.
As researchers at The Conversation noted this week: as countries build more infrastructure in these places, the hazard risk rises because more people and assets are exposed.

What the disaster has also revealed is that Nepal's tunnel-heavy hydropower construction model — built for a mountain environment — created an unintended and undesigned form of worker protection against glacial flooding.

But no protocol existed for warning workers inside them to evacuate, because no early-warning system exists for the category of glacial hazard that triggered this flood, and no systematic evacuation plan has been required for tunnel workforces in Nepal's hydropower licensing framework.
What Comes Next Nepal's energy sector faces a difficult reckoning.
The 27 hydropower plants damaged or destroyed represent a severe blow to a national grid already struggling to meet demand.
As Prime Minister Shah acknowledged, a full damage assessment remains impossible while active rescue operations and secondary flood threats continue.
For now, everything depends on the tunnels.

Whether the emergency shutoffs functioned, whether the workers inside have air and dry space, and whether the portals can be cleared before monsoon weather closes in again are questions whose answers will determine not only the fate of hundreds of individuals but the political reckoning that Nepal's hydropower development strategy will face in the months ahead.
"Just to find the tunnel is a miracle," Dix told ABC News Australia on Monday.
The search for what lies inside it — and who — continues around the clock.

Frequently Asked Questions How many workers are trapped in Nepal's hydropower tunnels, and are they likely still alive?

As of Monday, August 31, approximately 500 of the 900-plus hydropower workers still missing are believed to be inside tunnels at 11 to 12 affected projects in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, according to Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of IPPAN, the private sector hydropower industry association.
The IPPAN estimate of 500 trapped comes with significant uncertainty.

Survival depends on whether the tunnels' emergency shutdown systems operated correctly when the flood hit — if they did, the turbine halls may be dry; if they did not, flooding inside could have been fatal.
Australian geologist Arnold Dix, advising the operation remotely, noted that the tunnels' structural integrity is likely intact — the critical unknown is what is inside them.
After six days, the urgent concerns are oxygen availability, dehydration, and the physical condition of anyone who survived the initial flood surge.
Dix's assessment that Dix advised on tunnel survivability offers measured hope: the structures built to withstand Himalayan floods may have done exactly that for those inside.
Why couldn't rescuers reach the tunnel entrances sooner, and what is making it so difficult?
The portals — the entrances to the tunnels — were buried by the same debris cone that destroyed everything else on the valley floor.
At the Trishuli-3A site, the portal completely buried by debris required dismantling heavy excavation equipment and airlifting it to the location by helicopter.
A controlled blast on August 29 broke through to the upper section of the tunnel.
But after entry, rescuers still face an unknown length of potentially mud-filled tunnel before reaching the powerhouse area where workers may be sheltering.
Rain and secondary flood risk from an upstream barrier lake have repeatedly paused work.
The engineering paradox, as Dix put it, is that structures built to survive a Himalayan flood did survive — and are now the hardest thing in the valley to reach.
What is the risk of a second flood while rescue teams are inside the tunnels?
Two barrier lakes formed from debris deposited by the August 26 flood.
The lower lake has since drained naturally; the upper lake more than half drained, according to China's water ministry.

But Nitesh Khadka, a Nepali glacial flood specialist, has warned that a sudden failure of the remaining upper lake could send a surge directly into the excavation sites and — potentially — into the tunnels themselves.
Rain on Sunday night temporarily flooded excavation areas, a demonstration of how quickly conditions can change.
Rescue teams are monitoring river levels continuously and have suspended operations multiple times this week due to rising water and weather.
Why weren't the workers warned before the flood arrived?
No early-warning system exists for the specific category of hazard that caused this disaster.
Himalayan monitoring infrastructure is built around glacial lake outburst floods — events that originate from pre-existing lakes that can be watched with water-level sensors and satellite imagery.

The August 26 event was a rock-ice avalanche from a steep glacier face, which requires a fundamentally different monitoring approach: satellite-based radar measurement of glacier surface velocity, seismic detection of mass movements, and cross-border river gauge data from the Tibetan portion of the Lhende watershed.
Nepal's Flood Forecasting Division received no advance warning from China in either the 2025 or 2026 flood events on the same river system.
A cross-border data sharing never finalized — an agreement was promised after the 2025 flood, but it has never been signed.
What does the disaster mean for Nepal's hydropower sector?
Nepal poured billions into hydropower as its primary development and export strategy, harnessing Himalayan rivers to address chronic domestic power shortages and sell electricity to India.
The 2026 disaster struck 27 of those plants — damaging or destroying them and knocking a significant share of national generating capacity offline.

Beyond the physical damage, the disaster has exposed a structural vulnerability in Nepal's development model: the same tunnel engineering that made hydropower possible in a Himalayan environment created an unplanned and undesigned form of worker exposure during precisely the glacial hazard events that climate scientists have been warning about for years.
No evacuation protocol existed for tunnel workers facing a glacial flood.
No GLOF warning system covered the type of event that occurred.

The political and regulatory reckoning over Nepal's hydropower strategy — and the safety standards required for workers inside mountain tunnels — is likely to define the sector's governance for years ahead.

A bomb dropping on a dam, glitchy flood waters destroying an entire village street, and an elephant rescuing a man are some of the fake images circulating online.
The cause of the floods was a glacier collapse triggered by a vast flow of icy debris, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).
But if you're scrolling on social media, you might've instead seen the narrative that it was caused by a bomb being dropped on a dam.
The fake AI-generated clip was actually published in May 2026, with early copies of the video labelled with an AI watermark.
Associate Professor at the Queensland University of Technology Paula Dootson told SBS Examines AI labels can easily be missed, causing people to share posts before they realise it's fake.
"For any more obvious visual content labels, it's quite possible it's AI accounts or bots that are sharing these rather than human accounts.
And we know there's a lot of those." Dootson said mislabeled content is the most common type of problematic visual that response agencies deal with.
"How that visual gets there is not always clear," she told SBS Examines.
"Sometimes it could be because maybe you and I, we search 'landslide' or 'flood' and an old video pops up, and we don't check the metadata and we just share it.
And then of course it gets momentum.
The algorithm picks it up as being the first search response.
"But it could also be because the synthetic content is labelled, but content from a past event isn't.
So it's harder to distinguish what you are sharing," Dootson added.

Implications for understanding disaster Fake and mislabeled content can impact how people understand the scale of an event, such as the damage to infrastructure and how many people and communities are affected.

Dootson said misleading visuals can be used to push political or organisational agendas and to shift public conversations, by "aiming to really confuse the public and create uncertainty." She added that financial incentives could be driving the spread of such content.

And we can use tools like reverse image lookup for that," she said.

The Government of Nepal has laid down a nine-step procedure for handing over mortal remains of foreign nationals, including documentation, recording photographs and details, post-mortem examination, verification of the cause of death and formal identification, the embassy said in a press release.

The process also includes collection of fingerprints, DNA and other forensic samples, verification of the deceased’s passport or identity documents, completion of embassy or consular coordination, and issuance of a handover or release memo and receipt, it said.

A first-degree relative is a biological family member who is exactly one step away in the family tree.
This category includes parents (biological mother and father), full siblings (brothers and sisters who share both biological parents), and children (biological sons and daughters).
In cases where identification is not possible, or the remains have been temporarily interred, Nepal will facilitate DNA matching, it said.
Nepali authorities are collecting DNA samples from the mortal remains to create their DNA profiles.
First-degree relatives of the deceased can send their DNA profiles through email or provide blood samples along with preliminary information required by the Nepali authorities, the embassy said.

AP Photo/Dar Yasin What caused the Nepal flood?

On 26 August, a sudden flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district after a massive chunk of glacial ice and rock broke off from an altitude of about 5,200 metres and plunged roughly 1,200 metres into the valley below.

Inter-governmental body the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), based in Kathmandu, has concluded that the flood was most likely triggered by an ice-rock avalanche, rather than a glacial lake outburst flood.

It’s important to remember that attribution studies take months and researchers are still examining the precise sequence of events and whether long-term changes such as permafrost degradation and rock-slope instability played a role.
Glacier at heart of disaster had been retreating for decades It has emerged that the glacier that collapsed in Nepal had been in retreat for decades, like many glaciers across Europe.

“The failed glacier retreated by approximately 450m between 1990 and 2020, potentially reducing the mechanical support provided by the glacier to the underlying rock slope,” says Professor Maria Shahgedanova, a climate scientist researching climate impacts on mountain glaciers at the University of Reading in the UK.
It has been known for decades that climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.
Scientists say the Himalayas, the world’s highest mountain range, are warming at an unprecedented rate and losing ice faster than the global average.

Nepal has lost almost a third of its ice volume in 30 years, with glaciers melting 65 per cent faster in the last decade than in the previous one, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
Rising temperatures induced by climate change are quite literally melting the glue (permafrost) that holds the mountains together.

Kyoko Yokosuka UNDP Resident Representative for Nepal "Rising temperatures induced by climate change are quite literally melting the glue (permafrost) that holds the mountains together," Kyoko Yokosuka, UNDP Resident Representative for Nepal, tells Euronews Earth.

"As temperatures rise and glaciers retreat, these frozen ice sheets that stabilise mountain slopes loosen, triggering catastrophic landslides and floods downstream." This, Yokosuka explains, is creating "a dangerous chain reaction: small, isolated pockets of meltwater on top of glaciers are growing, merging into massive lakes, and putting immense pressure on the moraine" – the collection of rocks, soil and sediment left behind by a moving glacier – which can trigger "catastrophic glacial lake outburst flooding".
"When these dams burst, millions of lives downstream are put in immediate peril," she adds.

Shahgedanova says the recent disaster demonstrates how climate-driven changes in the cryosphere can change conditions that make hazards in high-mountain regions even more risky for people in the area.
"Such events cannot be prevented, but their impacts can be reduced through systematic hazard assessment and monitoring,” she says.
Would early warnings have helped in Nepal?
It may be of some comfort to families and friends of the victims that experts believe that it would have been “very difficult” to predict the disaster.
But better preparedness could have helped.
“This was an unprecedented and unexpected disaster.
There was simply no detection and no time to issue a warning.
The event was a sudden-onset hazard that could not be captured by conventional warning systems,” explains Dr Farooq Azam, senior cryosphere specialist and intervention manager at ICIMOD.

“In such rock-ice avalanches, establishing a warning system is very difficult to ascertain the place of the breakpoints, which can sometimes be below the bedrock or glaciers and not easily visible with satellite or eyes.” Still, UNDP says that continuous monitoring of glaciers, lake volumes and moraine dam stability using satellite and sensor technologies is critical to assess future risks.
"Governments need the systems and coordination mechanisms to anticipate rapidly evolving risks," Yokosuka adds.

"Communities in downstream areas need warnings they can act on – clear evacuation routes, identified safe areas, and regular exercises." European countries may be able to assist by bringing "technology solutions, such as precise engineering and avalanche-mitigation technologies used in the Alps directly to the Himalayas," as well as by scaling-up financing for risk prevention and early warning systems, says Yokosuka.
What does Nepal need to do to be more prepared for disasters?
ICIMOD says there are three immediate priorities to improve the region’s preparedness for global warming-related disasters.
Firstly, make sure clear policies are in place that determine what land can be used for, particularly in areas close to rivers, slopes and mountains.

Secondly, assess how the environment can impact infrastructure using Environmental Impact Assessments before it is built, as well as assessing how environmental conditions could affect infrastructure over its lifetime.
Thirdly, bring Indigenous knowledge back into risk planning.
Historically, communities often lived on higher ground and away from river channels, while newer development has increasingly moved closer to riverbanks and, in some cases, onto riverbeds.
Indigenous knowledge should inform contemporary disaster-risk and land-use planning, ICIMOD says.
UNDP says interventions like physically managing high-risk lakes and strengthening vulnerable slopes could be considered but require careful assessment.

“If this heartbreaking tragedy can help countries realise the need for a shared approach – for building adaptation and resilience, early warning signals, and transboundary monitoring – that will be a step ahead for humanity in the fractured world order we are living in today,” says Khosla.

Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while another 590 from 39 countries remain missing following the Aug.

On Thursday, the Australian government said it would send a team of drone operators to Nepal within days to assist search and rescue efforts.
Sunil Sharma, a spokesperson for the Nepal Tourism Board, said at least five other tourists who were previously reported missing had contacted authorities by email or telephone in recent days.
It is thought the disaster happened when a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
The surge entered rivers flowing through Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly.
Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges, carrying mud and rocks downstream.

Mukunda Rijal said his cousins and their daughters had not been found, prompting the family to perform a symbolic funeral for them.

They were extracting sand, as they had done before, when the river suddenly rose to consume them.

Some 45 miles north, high in the Himalayas along the Nepal-Tibet border, a large section of a glacier had collapsed, sending a torrent of water, sediments, and boulders and swallowing downstream settlements.
It took the flood barely 30 minutes to reach Tamang’s village in Nuwakot district, hitting with the terrible speed of a tsunami.
Tamang survived by holding on to a patch of weed.
But it swept away his wife, his two brothers and their wives, and his elder sister.
The body of one of his brothers has been retrieved, while the five other family members remain missing.
Tamang was ferried to Kathmandu for treatment two days later.
“I’ve lost everything,” he said from a hospital bed.
“We didn’t receive any warning and weren’t expecting the water to rise that high.
One moment I was hanging by the weeds, and the next moment when I looked, none of my family members were there.

I now have a hole in my leg and my heart.” A crowd of people standing on a muddy slope watching rescuers, with a fallen concrete pole in the midground and a rescue worker in a yellow helmet and bright orange vest in the foreground.
26 flood has obliterated parts of three districts—Rasuwa, Dhading, and Nuwakot—in north and central Nepal, but the shock has reverberated throughout the country.

The death toll from the flood has climbed to more than 1,000, with nearly 4,000 people still missing, of which nearly 600 are foreign nationals, many of them pilgrims to Tibet’s Mount Kailash, revered by both Hindus and Buddhists.
As quickly as disaster hit, such cataclysmic events have been decades in the making.
Carbon emissions have steadily warmed the Himalayas and destabilized its glaciers.
A February study shows that the temperatures in Nepal’s glacier collapse area have increased 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit since 1940, twice the average global warming rate.
Low-income countries in the Hindu Kush—which stretches roughly 2,100 miles across eight countries, including Nepal—are paying a grim price for a climate crisis they did little to create.
Floods and landslides have become routine and largely normalized despite significant loss of life and economic damage, but a disaster on this scale poses harder questions.

“The ecosystem and landscapes have evolved over geological time, but carbon emissions are changing them so quickly that they’re adapting on a human-dominated time scale,” Simon Cook, a geoscientist and senior lecturer at Scotland’s University of Dundee, told Foreign Policy.
High-angle landscape view showing severe soil erosion, steep mudbanks, and a wide river flowing through a mountain valley near a small settlement.

Almost a week after the event, scientists, including three Foreign Policy spoke with, have determined what caused the Aug.
26 disaster: a rock-ice avalanche.
The glacial collapse and landslide occurred on the northern face of the Langtang Lirung peak—the 99th highest peak in the world—on the Nepali side bordering Tibet at around 8:37 a.m.
Satellite images show that a 2,000-foot-wide mass of rock and ice fell from an elevation of 17,000 feet to around 4,000 feet in the valley below.

Basanta Raj Adhikari, director at the Centre for Disaster Studies at Kathmandu’s Institute of Engineering, told Foreign Policy that his estimates show it took about nine minutes for the water and debris from the landslide to reach the Rasuwa border checkpoint, about 12.5 miles from the site of the glacier collapse.

That is where waves—potentially as high as 1,500 feet in some places—crashed into the border buildings, hotels, and houses in Gyirong Port on the Chinese side and Rasuwa, crushing people running for their lives—all captured in unsettling CCTV footage.
“The rock is holding the ice, and when it fell both the rock and ice mass broke off, triggering a rock-ice avalanche,” Adhikari said.
“Its mass could be over 300 million cubic meters—the size of nearly 120,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools—from our estimate.
The energy it created is more than the atom bomb that fell in Hiroshima.” The thud was so immense that it created a 5.2 magnitude tremor—which the U.S.

Geological Survey initially believed to be a 4.4 magnitude earthquake—with the debris blocking the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, flowing through villages such as Timure and Syabrubesi, before merging into the Trishuli river system.
When it burst, an enormous volume of water was released, roaring past the trading posts and villages, which Adhikari said could have been flowing at about 100 miles per hour downstream.

Cook said the potential energy stored in the substantial block of ice gets converted into kinetic energy when it falls, with “all that material being pulverized and broken into smaller pieces of ice slush and water.” “There were possibly dead and decaying glaciers, too, downstream, which could have been pulverized into the flowing mix of ice, rock, boulders, and so on,” he said.
“Some sort of snowmelt or water within the glaciers we didn’t see—it’s common for glaciers to contain pockets of water—could also have resulted in the water flow.

Also, the narrow constriction created a funneling effect, resulting in huge waves enveloping buildings.” An elderly woman covered in mud sitting in the metal bucket of an excavator, being assisted by two men, one wearing an orange life jacket and another in a blue uniform.
By the time the ferocious waves reached downstream districts, they had turned into a muddy slush, swallowing person after person and house after house.
Bhakta Bhandari from Devighat in Nuwakot—one of the worst-hit communities—was working on his farm that morning when a neighbor sounded the alarm.
He had just started running when the waves violently tossed him into the air before he landed in neck-deep muddy water, injuring his back.
I visited him at a Kathmandu hospital, while his wife lay in a bed beside him with severe arm and neck wounds.
One of his relatives, he suspects, is missing, with another one dead.
“In all my lifetime, I’ve never seen anything like this,” he told Foreign Policy.
“We didn’t even imagine the flood would be this intense.
We thought it would be like the previous year.

But it was like a tsunami, just like in other countries.” A damaged concrete bridge ending abruptly over a wide, muddy riverbed, with a motorcyclist parked near the broken edge and onlookers standing along the sides.

Studies have shown links between climate change and extreme weather events, with a Carbon Brief analysis from March showing that 71 percent of 504 such episodes globally were “found to be made more likely or more severe by human-caused climate change.” Nepal has also been at the forefront of such events, with erratic and intense monsoon rains triggering flash floods and landslides almost every year.
Last year, an outburst of a supraglacial lake on the Purugu Glacier in Tibet caused widespread devastation in the same area as last week’s disaster.
In 2024, the Kathmandu Valley suffered one of the country’s most severe urban floodings ever, and the 2021 flooding of Melamchi River inundated the Melamchi Bazaar.
Other mountain countries are facing similar disasters.

From the 2023 glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim, India, to the 2025 rock-ice avalanche that flattened the Swiss village of Blatten, thousands of people have been killed in such disasters, with economic losses mounting in the billions of dollars just over the past few years.

Miriam Jackson, a research scientist at Norway’s hydrology department who has worked extensively in Nepal and Bhutan, told Foreign Policy that the recent incident in Nepal has similarities to the 2021 Chamoli disaster in India’s Uttarakhand state, where a hanging glacier broke off, releasing energy approximately equal to 15 times the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.
She added that the powerful 2015 earthquake also destabilized mountain slopes across Nepal, increasing the risk of landslides and rockfalls.
“Some 25 years ago, you barely heard about glaciers detaching, but there have [been] a few similar incidents in the past two decades,” Jackson said.
“Before they were unusual, and now we’re seeing more and more of them—perhaps we’re becoming better at attributing them through satellite images and advanced technology.

But these events are huge, and they come suddenly and are hard to predict.” Back view of a person carrying a young child on their shoulder while standing in a crowd of people looking at photos posted on a closed shop shutter.
On the ground, thousands of people are still waiting to hear if their relatives or friends survived.
Outside Kathmandu’s Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, a steady stream of people stops by every day.
Their desperate eyes scan the wall where photos of the dead bodies, many of them muddy and naked, are plastered.
Dev Bahadur Rana has been visiting one hospital after another, hoping to trace his nephew, Dil Bahadur Magar, a police officer stationed in Rasuwa.
Another man, Risan Tamang, looked away from the photos and called family with no answers.
Two of his in-laws, both truck drivers, are missing.
“Once the videos of the floods surfaced, we have been calling, but the phone is now switched off,” Risan said.
“We haven’t been able to eat.
Their mother and wives have fainted multiple times.” Close-up of two women crying and embracing each other on a street, with one covering her face with her hand and wearing a black face mask.
Nearby, Rabin Lama, who was checking updates on his phone, said that his niece, nephew, and brother-in-law are missing, along with 25 others from his village of Gatlang in Rasuwa.
“I’m sending photos because not everyone can come to Kathmandu, so we want to send them to others with missing family members and relatives for identification,” he said.
A few miles away at the National Trauma Center, people gathered at a temporary information booth set up by the Nepal Police, where Devi Sapkota came looking for his cousin Laxman’s whereabouts.
Laxman worked for a Chinese road construction firm on the Syabrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road stretch along the border.
The family does not even know the company’s name.
“He had gone on leave three days before the flood and was coming home on Thursday (the day after the disaster),” Sapkota said.
“He was going to Timure on Wednesday and taking a bus for Sindhuli.
He has been out of contact since then.
His wife and 5-year-old son are waiting.” Families of more than 600 people who are trapped inside the tunnels of as many as 11 hydropower stations are also waiting.
They are angry and urging the government to expedite the search for people who may be buried in remote areas near the Chinese border.
Nepal Army personnel have been seen navigating waist-deep muddy slush inside the tunnels, while India and Chinese tunnel rescue workers have also joined the search since Saturday.
But many are already questioning the government’s initial reluctance to accept foreign help before accepting “specialized” support only on the third day.
Two people viewed from behind standing on a rocky riverbank, looking out over a wide, turbulent river under a dark sky with sun rays breaking through clouds.
Nepal ranks sixth globally among countries most affected by climate change, according to development organization Germanwatch’s 2026 Climate Risk Index.
As the intensity of such extreme weather events rises, the country is inadequately prepared to face them.

Adhikari, the disaster risk reduction expert, said that Nepal has a disaster strategy, but it’s highly focused on rescue and response, calling for more investment in preparedness and risk assessment, including mapping, monitoring, and early-warning systems.

“There should be risk-sensitive landscape planning that would identify suitable areas for settlements and infrastructure construction, as well as identify risk areas, which Nepal hasn’t done yet,” he said.

Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said during a press conference Saturday that the country is “one of the major victims of climate change and its impacts,” despite its negligible contribution to carbon emissions responsible for global warming.
Amid growing calls for transboundary collaborations on an early-warning system, he said Nepal and China have been “actively working” to establish such mechanisms.

“Since this disaster, we are in very close coordination, cooperation, and communication with the Chinese authority, and they have been very forthcoming with sharing information and data,” Khanal added.
But climate activists and policy analysts say that narratives around disasters should go beyond devastation to address climate justice.

Sneha Pandey, a climate diplomacy and policy analyst at Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, told Foreign Policy that the cost incurred by emissions from the richest nations must not overburden poor countries and communities on the front lines.

She added that the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage—a global climate finance mechanism—financing “must be scaled up substantially to meet the scale of climate-imposed disasters.” “At COP31, pressure must be built at the high level to mobilize more finance for loss and damage and adaptation and resilience-building, and to reduce global emissions in line with the Paris Agreement,” Pandey said, referring to the 2026 U.N.
Climate Change Conference being held in Turkey later this year.

“Nepal must continue to push for dedicated negotiations space for mountain-related concerns so that cryospheric risks are more firmly anchored in the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change process.” Nepal has fallen, risen, and rebuilt only to be shaken again over the past decades.
The end of the decade-long Maoist insurgency in 2006 brought a push for new development, which was shattered by the devastating 2015 earthquake.
And as Nepal rebuilt again, the 2025 Gen Z uprising shook the country, leaving behind widespread arson, destruction, and economic losses.
But just as a young government took office in March, the floods have now washed away hopes of a fresh start for many.
And once again, those with the least are likely to pay the highest price.

Survivors like Bhandari and Subash Tamang, who relied on marginal and climate-sensitive industries like agriculture and sand extraction, respectively, survived the floods, but they feel living with the uncertainty that comes next could be worse.
“We don’t know what sort of help we’ll get from the government, and we don’t know if we are going to be displaced from our home,” Bhandari said.
We only have a pair of clothes now.
Everything is gone.” “After being discharged, I have nowhere else to go,” Tamang added.
“I don’t know what to do.”

One week after a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-Tibet border and sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through Himalayan valleys, this is what grief looks like when there is no body to bring home.

The United Nations has described the event as Nepal's worst natural catastrophe since the April 2015 earthquake, which killed approximately 9,000 people.

An army team accompanied by engineers and a drone unit entered the 111-megawatt facility's tunnel system, advanced to its innermost section and flew a drone through the full interior.

Vertical drilling — boring down from the mountain's summit to pierce the top of the powerhouse — remains under examination where frontal access stays blocked.

Six days after the disaster, survival conditions inside sealed shafts are increasingly in doubt.

His brother-in-law remained among the missing — his pregnant wife waiting at home.
What began as a rescue operation is, at most sites, now being managed as a recovery mission in all but official terminology.

Hundreds of graves were prepared along trails that until recently served as morning walking paths.

The avalanche of ice and rock reached the Gyirong Port complex within six to seven minutes of the initial collapse — catching pilgrims, traders and hydropower workers simultaneously in their most exposed positions along the valley.

The high-mountain zone above 4,000 meters is warming significantly faster than the global average.
Permafrost that once bound rock, ice and glacial mass together for millennia is weakening, increasing the likelihood of sudden, catastrophic detachments.
Nepal's Prime Minister stated publicly there is no doubt climate change contributed to the disaster.

Yet, out of the 38 glaciers ICIMOD monitored, only seven met the global benchmark, and many in the region remained largely unmonitored.
But Prakash Pokhrel said the same satellite images are far less useful for anticipating a glacier collapse.
We can’t know from the images how fractures have developed or if weathering has occurred,” he said.

When “Clean & Green” development deepens risks For Thakkar, the responsibility is also on the investors of the 13 hydropower plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts that were damaged by the floods, disconnecting roughly 431MW, a tenth of its total power, from the national grid.

The Asian Development Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and International Finance Corporation were among the major financiers of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, while China’s state-owned Exim Bank funded the Upper Trishuli 3A project.
The projects also included financing from British International Investment, Korea Development Bank, and Exim Bank of Korea, as well as the Netherlands FMO, OPEC Fund and Canadian Climate Fund.

The Asian Development Bank’s panel of independent experts overseeing the Upper Trishuli-1 project had recommended strengthening the warning system and emergency plan, coordinating alerts with hydropower projects upstream and downstream, and putting evacuation protocols in place for dangerous floods.
“But they don’t do it.
There is no accountability in South Asian countries,” said Thakkar.

“They [funders] know nobody is going to be held accountable so they just get away with it.” Thakkar said that hydropower projects can aggravate disaster risks by creating additional vulnerabilities in already fragile Himalayan landscapes through deforestation, tunnelling, blasting, excavation and muck dumping.
Dams can also worsen downstream flooding, while reservoirs accumulate silt that can create additional risks.
When multiple hydropower projects are built in a cascade, he said, these impacts accumulate and multiply.
Climate change is adding another layer of risk through more intense rainfall, warmer winters, melting glaciers and thawing permafrost.

“Our dishonest EIAs, lack of accountability in governance and non-implementation of basic monitoring, forecasting and implementable disaster management plans is worsening the disaster impacts in river valleys with multiple hydropower projects,” said Thakkar.

“By not doing independent post-disaster impact assessments, we have shut the doors for learning any lessons for the future.” Nepal’s Trishuli river basin alone, which originates in Rasuwa, has 36 hydropower projects in various stages of construction and planning.
In Tamang’s village in Hakubesi, he said about eighty percent of the population worked at the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant, and the rest of them were children or the elderly.
“We have no choice but to go to Kathmandu or to the Dhunche [headquarters of Rasuwa] for work.
But with the hydropower people stayed back.
Now all of them are trapped in it, the hydropower is gone, we have nothing,” he said.
The government’s latest data shows 639 people remained trapped in Upper Trishuli-1 and Trishuli 3A.

Saswata Sanyal, who is a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD, people need to understand the changing realities of living in the Hindu Kush region, where the risks we were familiar with yesterday are no longer the same today.
The Rasuwa flood was a testament to the complex interactions of hazards.
“Something triggered an ice avalanche that led to flash floods, debris, sediments and boulders,” he said.
Relief efforts since the disaster have also been affected by monsoon rains and flood alerts.
“The risks can be further exacerbated by earthquakes or climate change, so we need to understand the complex nature of hazards in the mountains,” he added.

Flood sensors, even if some of them were washed away in the flash floods in the Trishuli river in Galchchi, continued to be critical in monitoring the drastic increase in water levels and warning people.
Sanyal suggested that it’s imperative for Nepal to increase those sensors upstream, not just in its own territory, but other countries in the Hindu Kush region should collaborate to do the same.
Pokhrel, the former chief executive of NDRRMA, added that Nepal needs to set up multiple sensors in diverse locations.

Even for floods, he suggested, it’s not enough to install sensors in the bridges, and recommended setting them up on top of hills that can detect seismic waves or the rumble of boulders and floods to alert people using sirens.
Sanyal says people need to comprehend the scale of the Hindu Kush region.
“It has around 54,000 glaciers and more than 2000 glacier lakes, and permafrost covering an even larger area,” he said.

While it is not possible to track every inch of the region, he suggested prioritizing the monitoring of areas with settlements downstream, with the countries not only sharing data but also working closely with each other.

Similarly, to identify risks in remote mountain areas that are difficult for scientists and government officials to routinely access, Anoop Nautiyal, climate advocate based in Dehradun, Uttarakhand, recommended training local communities on basic glaciology and hazard monitoring.

“They are on the frontline dealing with the climate crisis and need to play a central role in prevention and disaster risk reduction.” But monitoring cannot stop at national borders when the hazards themselves do not.
Many disasters across the Hindu Kush Himalaya are transboundary, making regional cooperation critical.

Climate activists, scientists, as well as researchers emphasised the importance of tripartite agreements between Nepal, China, and India, as well as bilateral agreements that go beyond non-binding commitments and include mandatory protocols and action plans for timely communication and response.
“Every sensor, siren, drill is ultimately to ensure next time more people get a chance to reach safety,” said Sanyal.
Meanwhile, Tamang is worried about his grandparents back at home in Hakubesi.
He said they are staying on higher grounds right now, but is concerned that they will soon run out of the limited food they have.
“Rescue, relief, everything reaches very late in our village.
There are still 100 to 200 people waiting with no rescue,” he said, showing his mobile phone, which showed that he received the warning text message at 9:42 AM.
“I wish they would take them to Dhunche, because I hear there will be another massive flood; perhaps the water won’t reach as high.”

Photo credit: Reuters The problem is bigger than the burial grounds Nepal is a Hindu-majority country where cremation is the customary final rite for most Hindus.
Yet after the devastating floods that swept through parts of the country, authorities have been burying unidentified bodies instead of cremating them.
The reason is not a change in religious practice.

It is a response to the large number of bodies being recovered, limited morgue space and the fact that many victims cannot yet be identified.Authorities are treating the burials as a temporary arrangement.

Before a body is placed in the ground, officials are collecting DNA samples and recording identifying details so that families may still be able to locate and claim the remains later.According to The Statesman and various media reports, unidentified flood victims are being buried in Chitwan district after authorities collect DNA samples, assign identification codes and record the exact locations of their graves.The scale of the disastrous floods has put Nepal's mortuaries under severe pressure.

Bodies recovered from the floods were also beginning to decompose, making prolonged storage increasingly difficult.According to media reports, authorities were dealing with unidentified bodies at hospitals while freezing facilities were unable to accommodate all the remains.

With the bodies decomposing, temporary burial became necessary.Morgues and mortuaries were overwhelmed by the number of bodies being brought in, leaving authorities with the difficult task of managing and preserving unidentified remains.
The burials therefore do not mean that the victims' identities have been abandoned.
Instead, authorities are trying to preserve enough information to identify them later.The bodies are not simply being placed in an anonymous mass grave.
Authorities are creating records for the individual remains.
According to The Statesman, each unidentified victim is assigned a unique identification code, while the burial location is recorded so the remains can be traced later.
This creates a link between the remains and the records kept by the authorities.
The burial sites are also being documented.
Photographs and other records are being maintained, while GPS coordinates are being recorded for the graves.
That means authorities can potentially locate a particular grave even after the burial has taken place.DNA samples are being collected from unidentified bodies before burial.
At the same time, relatives of people reported missing can provide their own DNA samples.
The samples can then be compared with DNA taken from the recovered remains.

DNA records are being preserved specifically to allow future identification if relatives come forward.The process is important because some bodies have been recovered far from where people went missing, while others are too badly decomposed or damaged to be identified through appearance alone.Officials are recording more than genetic material.
According to various media, photographs, clothing, jewellery, tattoos and other identifying marks are also being documented.

Nepal Police has also published details of some unidentified victims in an effort to help families searching for missing relatives.The burial arrangement is designed with future identification in mind.
Burial pits are being dug around 1.5 metres deep, with about 40 cm of space left between bodies.
The arrangement is intended to reduce the risk of DNA contamination and make future identification and exhumation possible.Identification does not end with the burial.
If DNA testing establishes that a buried victim is the missing member of a family, officials can use the identification number and burial records to locate the remains.
According to media reports, the remains can be handed over to the family once the victim has been identified.
The family can then perform the funeral rites according to its traditions.
This is why the burials are being handled differently from a conventional mass burial.

Authorities are attempting to preserve the identity of every victim even when the person cannot be named immediately.The decision to bury the unidentified bodies comes as Nepal continues to deal with a large number of missing people.
