A border post, a customs yard, hydropower stations, and enough of the grid to take a tenth of Nepal’s generating capacity offline.
That is a partial inventory of what the water removed from the Trishuli valley on the morning of August 26, 2026.
Somewhere inside that inventory, at Nuwakot, a small mint-green house did not move.
Footage from that morning shows a family on its upper balcony with nowhere left to go, surrounded by mud.
Debris hit the walls and moved past.
Structures beside it were damaged or swept away.
The house stayed, and the people inside it lived.
The clip found an audience within hours, and with it came the obvious question: why that one?
It is a better question than it first appears.
Answered carelessly, it becomes a parable about concrete.
Answered honestly, it opens onto something larger, because in most disasters what stands and what does not was settled long before the hazard arrived, by people holding site plans and budgets.
What the green house can and cannot tell us Begin with what is established.

On August 26, a rapid slope failure involving a glacier in Langtang National Park, near the China border, released a debris avalanche that the United States Geological Survey estimates generated energy equivalent to a magnitude-5.2 earthquake.
The flow ran roughly 100 kilometres down the Lhende and Trishuli systems.
By the morning of September 2, Nepal’s disaster authority put the death toll at 1,114, with about 4,500 people unaccounted for across both sides of the border.
The United Nations has called it Nepal’s deadliest disaster since the 2015 earthquake .
About the green house, far less is established.
No engineering body or public authority has published a structural assessment.

One analysis circulating after the video went viral credited a reinforced-concrete frame, a compact plan that allowed the flow to divide around it, and a position slightly off the main channel on higher ground.
None has been verified on site.
A fact-check also found that the claim that it was the only structure left standing was exaggerated.
So the honest formulation is narrower.
The evidence establishes that the structure remained standing.
It does not establish that any one design feature caused that survival.
The survival is visible; the engineering is not.
That asymmetry is the problem in miniature.

The Himalayan warning was already visible India’s Himalayan states and territories — Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh — sit in the same geological neighbourhood, where seismicity, slope instability, extreme rainfall and a changing cryosphere overlap.
Two Indian cases are worth more than a catalogue.
On October 3, 2023, roughly 14.7 million cubic metres of frozen lateral moraine collapsed into South Lhonak Lake in north Sikkim.
The impact wave breached the moraine and drained about 50 million cubic metres of water into a flood that ran 385 kilometres down the Teesta.
Research in the journal Science records more than 25,900 buildings damaged or destroyed and 31 major bridges lost.
The 1,200 MW Teesta-III dam at Chungthang failed.
None of it was unforeseen.

Sikkim’s own post-disaster needs assessment records that the lake’s growth had been tracked since the 1990s, that siphons were installed in 2016 to lower it, and that an experimental water-level sensor was destroyed within six months.

Two years earlier, at Chamoli in Uttarakhand, about 27 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice fell from Ronti Peak , wrecking two hydropower projects and killing or leaving missing more than 200 people, most of them workers.
Later satellite analysis found that the collapse block had already moved more than 10 metres in the preceding five years .
The pattern is not that these hazards are invisible.
It is that they are legible only to those looking, and legible in time to matter only if someone is authorised to act.
When infrastructure fails, the bill is larger than repair A road, a bridge or a powerhouse is capital with a yield, and Nepal is now learning what that means.

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle told the news agency Reuters that rebuilding may cost $4-5 billion, close to a tenth of national output, and that damaged power projects account for more than 12 per cent of generating capacity.
The bridge and road tally above was the latest count available when this was written, and it was still climbing.
The clearest number is at the border.
The Rasuwagadhi crossing carried 4.72 per cent of Nepal’s merchandise imports in 2024-25.
After an earlier flood shut it for six months from July 2025, that share fell to 2.18 per cent.
It has now been destroyed twice in 13 months.
The repair bill was never the main cost; the forgone trade was.
The World Bank’s Lifelines study makes the same point globally.

Direct hazard damage to power and transport assets in low- and middle-income countries runs to roughly $18 billion a year, while the disruption caused to households and firms costs at least $390 billion.
Its headline finding — $4 of benefit for every $1 invested — is a system-level average rather than a promise for any one project.
But the direction holds: the expensive part of failure is the activity the asset can no longer support.
That makes what gets counted consequential.
Sikkim’s assessment put damages and losses at Rs 1,480 crore across eight sectors.
Power is not among them, so the largest single asset lost sits outside the state’s headline figure.
Losses that go uncounted are rarely priced, and losses that go unpriced rarely reach a design brief.
India is not short of science.

Roughly 7,500 glacial lakes in the Indian Himalaya have been inventoried, and the National Disaster Management Authority’s GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme , funded at Rs 150 crore for four states, has prioritised high-risk lakes for early warning and lake-lowering.
After Teesta-III, the Central Water Commission decided to review the design flood of every dam vulnerable to glacial lake outburst floods.
A hazard is becoming a design variable, if belatedly.
There is a habit worth naming here.
The green house was one structure, at one point in one channel, meeting one flow.
Nothing about a single outcome tells us what to require of the next ten thousand buildings.
That is why design codes deal in distributions rather than anecdotes.
India spent the past year arguing about precisely that.
The hazards differ, but the policy problem is the same: whether new risk information is allowed to change what gets built, where it gets built and what it costs.
Pricing risk before the next disaster The harder question is what happens when that knowledge carries a price.
In November 2025, the Bureau of Indian Standards notified a revised earthquake code, IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025, built on probabilistic hazard assessment.
It created a Zone VI covering the Himalayan arc and placed about 61 per cent of India’s land area in moderate-to-high hazard zones.

In March 2026, after the housing ministry and infrastructure agencies raised concerns about consultation and costs, estimated at 10-15 per cent for buildings in the highest zones, the notification was withdrawn and the 2016 code restored.
Two readings are defensible: that a major standard was issued without adequate consultation with the ministries that must build it, and that the seismicity did not change on March 3.
What is not in dispute is where the decision turned: not on the seismology, but on the capital cost.
Tectonic strain does not respond to temperature.
The hazard the 2025 code tried to capture is broadly the hazard that was there in 2016, and the case for pricing it in was already on the table.
A design flood is a statistical statement about the past, and where the cryosphere is changing, the past is a weakening guide.
If a standard for a hazard that is holding still was judged too costly, the harder tests are the ones where the baseline is moving.
Sikkim’s assessment holds one further finding worth carrying.
Seventy-nine per cent of the housing destroyed or damaged in 2023 was well-built reinforced concrete, and many frames came through the water load with only their lower floors affected.
What failed was rarely the frame.
It was the decision to build metres from the riverbed, where building bye-laws were not mandatory at all.
That is the distinction the green house obscures.
A structure that stands is one kind of resilience.
A network that keeps working — roads open, bridges intact, power flowing — is another.
A hospital that survives is worth little when the only road to it lies under 10 metres of debris.
The question worth carrying from Nuwakot is not why one house stood.
It is what share of India’s Himalayan asset base should be expected to remain standing and working when the next documented hazard arrives, and whether that expectation ever reached an estimate.
Survival is currently something explained after the event.
In a risk-informed system, it would be a specification fixed before it, priced and attributed.
A disaster is sudden only for the people watching it.
For those who chose the site, sealed the drawings and cleared the budget, it was years in preparation.
What was never settled was who would pay to design for it.

The latest incident of flash floods in Nepal has drawn the attention of the world towards the geologically fragile Himalayan region, which has been warming rapidly, experiencing glacier retreat, snowmelt and degradation of permafrost, which can remove the cement covering on the mountain slopes.
In the 26 August 2026 incident, the evidence available so far points to a glacier/rock collapse and massive debris avalanche, rather than an ordinary monsoon flood.
The glacier/rock mass destabilisation led to an ice-rock avalanche which in turn caused a temporary blockage/surge in the Bhote Koshi river.
With the enormous debris flowing along the Bhote Koshi/Trishuli river, there was large-scale destruction in the lower reaches.
The avalanche, which occurred in the high Himalaya near the Nepal-Tibet frontier, travelled downwards at the rate of 50 metres per second.
Nepal is today sitting on a geological precipice.
The Himalayas are among the youngest and most tectonically active major mountain systems on Earth.

Nepal sits directly on the collision zone between the Indian and Eurasian plates which produces four overlapping vulnerabilities - Active tectonics, very steep topography, monsoon rainfall and rapidly changing glaciers.

Active tectonics is a constant feature based on the push northward by the Indian plate beneath Eurasia, thus producing earthquakes, fractured rocks, fault zones, extremely steep slopes and frequent landslides and rockfalls.
The 2015 earthquake in Nepal demonstrated the interaction dramatically.

Research following the 2015 earthquake found that earthquake-triggered landslides were the principal mechanism damaging hydropower infrastructure, and estimated that about 25% of existing, constructed and planned Himalayan hydropower projects had high probabilities of moderate-to-severe earthquake damage.
This brings into question the viability of various projects, including hydro projects being undertaken in the region with the help of Chinese companies.

The Rasuwa border region is marked by the presence of large number of Chinese construction companies which are involved in numerous projects turning the green belt into a maze of white rock and cement feature, without any consideration for the surrounding flora and fauna and the geological damage these can cause.
Moreover, the extremely steep topography in the region has led to enormous elevation differences over very short horizontal distances.
A river can descend thousands of metres through a narrow valley, and once a large volume of water, ice and rock enters such a valley, it becomes an extremely efficient natural chute.
There are several river pathways in the region, that pass through very high mountain walls that are virtually hugging each other.
Any glacial outburst in the region can thus lead to a massive rush of mud, ice and stones causing severe destruction to nature and any physical features on the way.

The heavy monsoon rainfall further saturates already-fractured slopes and weakens the soil at certain locations thereby enhancing the threat level of landslides and downward flow of water, rocks and soil.
Therefore, Nepals landslides identify a combination of steep slopes, geological weakness, intense rainfall, river erosion and land-use changes as major drivers.
The rapidly changing glaciers is the new and increasingly important variable.
Glaciers are retreating and the high-altitude environment is becoming less stable.
Nepal has thousands of glacial lakes, some of which have the potential to produce catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF).
A tracking of the incidents of glacial outbursts and flash floods in the region indicates that the August 26 incident should not be a surprise.
On the contrary, more such instances could be anticipated in the coming times.

A look at the number of such incidents that have taken place indicates that their frequency has gone up several folds in recent times as climate change and heating of the high mountains increasingly become a regular feature.
There have actually been more than 100 documented flood-related events in Nepal since 1954, according to a reconstruction of Nepal's flood history published recently.
These include GLOFs, cloudbursts, landslides and major river floods.
Geologists have warned about the vulnerability of the Rasuwa/Bhote Koshi access since the 2025 floods in the region.
They had accordingly suggested that enough preparations need to be made to deal with any such eventualities.
The region has also seen large-scale construction by Chinese companies.

As one drives towards the Rasuwa crossing on the Nepali side, one can see a change in the landscape from the lush green forest and pine trees to a wide patch of rocks and quarries with heavy construction equipment spread across.
Most of these construction projects are undertaken by Chinese companies who operate freely in the area using Chinese heavy vehicles without registration plates.

The local offices of these Chinese companies are clearly marked on the rock walls alongside the road and one can see Chinese engineers and senior company officials moving about in their facilities 5 to 10 kms inside Nepal.

While construction of bridges, roads , tunnels and hydro projects is a necessity, at the same time construction of any kind in these areas leads to cutting mountain slopes, removing vegetation, blasting rock, excavating tunnels, dumping spoil, altering drainage and narrowing river corridors besides creating large concrete structures in the valleys.
Research on Nepal has found that construction related cut slopes account for a substantial proportion of landslides, and that poorly planned roads can dramatically increase landslide risk.
China has been constructing several projects in Tibet which would cause significant change in the geological matrix of the Tibetan plateau.

Some of the projects which are along the Nepal-China border in the high Himalayas, which could cause serious damage to nature and the geological features are : --Girong-Rasuwagadi corridor - on the Chinese side, the project involves logistics and highway infrastructure, while on the Nepal side the project is marked by the Syaphrubeshi-Rasiwagadi highway and Timure border facilities; --Zhangmu-Tatopani project - the traditional China- Nepal highway project connecting Kathmandu to Tatopani and includes port facilities; -- Korala-Mustang project - border infrastructure along Lomangthang/Burang which aims to open western Nepal to Tibet; -- Burang - Hilsa road and border facilities - This involves Burang border facilities on the Chinese side and Hilsa-Simikot road and Hilsa bridge on the Nepal side.

The project aims to open western Nepal to Tibet; --Kerung/Rasuwa- Kathmandu project - involves construction of highway and logistic network connecting Nepal with Tibet and involves significant tunnelling, such as the Tokha-Chhahre tunnel; --Kamathanka project - a network of road structure on the Tibetan side which will form the Kimathanka-Khandbari/Koshi corridor aiming to connect Eastern Nepal with Tibet -- Power connectivity - Several power connectivity projects being considered including the Ratmate-Rasuwagadhi-Kerung 400-kv transmission proposal; -- Railway - Shigatse-Gyirong railway project under development Natures challenges being confronted and hence moving slow.

-- Gyirong - Kathmandu railway project this is a proposed China- Nepal cross border railway with the aim of having a direct Tibet-Kathmandu connection; Besides the above projects, which have a direct cross border connect between Tibet and Nepal and involve mass scale construction work causing serious ecological damages in the high Himalayas, China is also undertaking several projects along the Tibetan lower plateau which would have an impact on the mountain ranges with a ripple effect on Nepal over a period of time.

Some of these projects are : Yarling tsangpo/Medog hydropower, Sichuan- Tibet railway project, Xinjiang Tibet Railway project, G 219 Western highway, G 318 and associated Himalayan tunnels, Medog-Zayu connectivity, Yadong/Sikkim connectivity and the Chinese border settlements along Arunachal Pradesh, Bhutan and Sikkim.

All of these projects require cutting into mountains, blasting, removing vegetation, dumping excavation rock, alerting natural drainage, constructing bridges and retaining structures, drilling through unstable geological formations etc.
A major landslide high above in the mountains can cause landslides and river blockage.
This in turn will cause temporary lake formations at very high altitudes, which when breached can cause flash floods.

Chinas massive railway and highway projects have increasingly caused serious damage to nature in the mountains, especially due to the long kilometres of tunnelling which cause intersecting geological faults, change ground water movement, destabilise rock masses, drain or redirect underground water and weaken slopes above tunnel portals.

On the Tibet-Nepal axis, the scale and importance of the Gyirong (Tibet) - Rasuwagadhi (Nepal) corridor is the most consequential, and its scale of importance became particularly obvious during the August 2026 disaster as the flood devastated the Gyirong/Rasuwagadhi corridor and temporarily cut the principal ChinaNepal land connection.

The GyirongRasuwagadhi corridor is particularly ecologically sensitive, not because the road automatically causes floods or glacier collapses, but because construction takes place in an exceptionally steep, seismically active and hydrologically unstable Himalayan environment.

There is already a strong warning from Nepal's Langtang National Park management plan that the SyaphrubesiRasuwagadhi road passes along the Bhote Koshi within the park, and the plan specifically identifies risks of habitat fragmentation and impacts during construction.

Animal conservationists mention of rare animals such as the red panda, Himalayan black bear, snow leopard, Assamese macaque and other forest and high altitude species being endangered as a result of these projects.
One of the major potential ecological interventions by China in Tibet is the Yarlung Tsangpo mega project.
China has already started the construction process in the great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo in Medog.

The site is marked by an extraordinarily deep gorge, enormous elevation gradient, active tectonic environment, very steep slopes, glaciers and unstable rocks and having exceptionally heavy rainfall in the region.
The geological concerns are particularly serious as the area is seismically active.

While climate change is bound to destabilise high altitude rock and ice and increase the potential for floods, landslides and avalanches, construction of tunnels, roads, dams, hydro projects, settlements only act as risk multipliers.
Another important issue is that of hydropower projects which are potentially more consequential than the roads.
Nepal is undergoing an enormous hydropower build-out.
Chinese capital as well as Nepali investment are involved.

The problem is that hydropower development as well as construction of roads and tunnels naturally tends to take away the crucial space meant for nature in its own surroundings, and further narrows down the path of water flow making the impact piercing and damaging.
Infrastructures in narrow valleys, steep slopes and along major rivers are indeed geological fault zones.
That is almost the perfect combination for cascading disaster.

While these projects would have to be implemented looking at the larger issue of energy generation and potential for Nepal to emerge as a major energy producer and supplier, there is need for a combined effort by the international community to assess the prevailing challenges that the Himalayas face.

This would require mandatory cumulative environmental-impact assessments for entire river basins, geological assessment before road/tunnel construction, much stricter controls on mountain - slope cutting, comprehensive glacier and permafrost monitoring.
There should also be real-time GLOF warning systems in place and cross border sharing of satellite, hydrological and seismic information.
There is also need to ensure that there is no major infrastructure in identified avalanche/debris - flow corridors and independent safety audits of existing hydropower projects should be carried out.
Nepal should take the lead in assessing the projects in a cumulative manner to examine their viability at a particular location given the fragile play of nature.

The Kathmandu based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) could be involved in setting up an advanced Himalayan disaster-warning mechanism, while India can work closely with Nepal in this sphere considering India lies downstream from all these Himalayan rivers and would inevitably get affected by the ecological disasters that occur in these mountains.

The world cannot let Nepal deal with these challenges alone and this has been brought out clearly by the Prime Minister of Nepal Balendra Shah, who declared on 2 September 2026 that climate change is the worlds shared responsibility, and that Nepal must forcefully campaign for climate justice and international financial compensation rather than simple post-disaster aid.

During his address to the House of Representatives, he linked the recent catastrophic flash floods in Rasuwa directly to warming climate, framing it as a warning for the entire Himalayan region and global civilisation.

“I saw people running and being washed away by the waters.
There were screams all over the place, and houses and buildings collapsed,” said Guru.
The 42-year-old had stood frozen in panic for a few seconds before turning to run uphill toward his house.
“I did not take out my mobile [phone] to film or stop for a second.
I have never seen something so dangerous so closely.
I saw death so close.” It took less than two minutes for the waters to sweep everything away, including several of the area’s schools and hospitals, he recalled.
Not everyone was caught off-guard.
At one school in the area, a principal heeded the warning and evacuated 900 children minutes before the floods buried the school in mud, water, boulders, and debris.
Guru struggled to compare the flood to anything he’d lived through, including COVID-19.
The pandemic, he said, at least gave people warning once they knew they were infected, time to isolate and protect themselves.
This disaster came with such short notice and swept away so many lives in a single pass.

The deadly flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border were caused when a massive section of rock and glacier ice near Langtang Lirung peak in the Himalayas collapsed into the valley below, gathering rock and debris as it fell.

The impact registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event, according to the US Geological Survey, which initially read the signal as a small earthquake before concluding it had come from the landslide itself.

The resulting debris flow surged more than 62 miles down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, tearing through the border towns of Timure and Syapru Besi in Rasuwa district, part of the mountainous stretch of northern Nepal that borders China’s Tibet Autonomous Region.
Wider flooding continued downstream through Nuwakot, Dhading, and beyond.
As of September 2, the confirmed death toll is 1,114 people with more than 3,900 people still missing, according to Nepal’s disaster agency.
Nearly 12,000 people have been rescued.
The day after the flood hit, Guru set out to check on his friend, pastor Bed Bahadur Khadka, who lived in Betrawati, one of the worst-hit towns about eight miles from Guru’s house.
Khadka pastored Punaruthan Ecclesia, a small church with 65 weekly attendees.
When Guru arrived at Betrawati, he found that the church had “completely disappeared,” along with the town’s houses and buildings.
Khadka and many of the people living in the area—including the church members—were missing.
“Those who are missing are probably dead,” Guru said, still visibly shaken.

“On one hand I feel I am blessed to have built my house at this height where the waves could not touch it, but then on the other I feel so sad that I have lost so many people.” He grappled with how to tell Khadka’s wife, who is living in Kathmandu with their two children, that her husband was missing.
Meanwhile, Balkrishna Shrestha, pastor of Himalayan Christian Church, said their church plant in Timure near the Tibet border lost at least six members to the flood.
Their bodies have not been recovered.
The churchgoers, who were working at the local bazaar that morning, were swept away along with some of their family members, including children ages 2 and 3.

The fellowship’s leader survived: That morning as he headed down the hillside to work as a barber at the bazaar, he stopped for 10 minutes to speak with a friend, and because of that delay, he narrowly escaped the waters.
“It moved swiftly, like a hooded cobra, snapping up people and structures in its path,” Shrestha told CT, recounting what eyewitnesses had described to him.
Shrestha said he had “barely escaped” the catastrophe himself.
He’d left his home in Chilime, a village in Rasuwa district, for Kathmandu before the flood hit.
Yet his wife, Kumari, who runs a boarding school less than three miles from the river, had stayed behind.
When he heard about the flood through Facebook posts, “I quickly called my wife and found that she was safe but stuck in Chilime with 150 children,” Shrestha said.
He continued messaging Kumari for the next two days until the cell towers and electricity in the area went down.
Since August 31, he has heard nothing about her or the students.
When they last spoke, Kumari had rations to feed herself and the children for four more days.
“After that, there is no food or water.
There is no market to resupply from,” he said.
“Everything has been wiped out.” He described a landscape stripped bare: no trees left standing, only rock on either side of what used to be the village.
Shrestha said the flood destroyed 4 out of the 42 churches in his district and killed roughly 400 believers.
About 700 houses, including 100 Christian homes, were destroyed in Rasuwa alone, he said.

Two days after the flood, a barrier lake that had formed from debris left by the collapse broke its banks upstream, sending a second surge of water down the valley, briefly halting rescue operations in both Nepal and China due to fears of further flooding.
The danger, Shrestha said, still hasn’t passed: The area remains under an active flood warning, which is obstructing help.
Helicopters that could otherwise fly in and pull survivors out, he said, are being held back due to the flood warning.
What rescue work does get through is focused on the dead, the injured, and pregnant women.
Timothy Dangal, director of the relief group Himalayan Youth Transformation, said trucks loaded with rice have lined up on whatever roads remain open, waiting for a way through.
After losing his job as a music teacher during COVID-19, Dangal started cooking and distributing food to the hungry in Kathmandu.
That effort led to the creation of Himalayan Youth Transformation, which he now directs.
From his experience with disaster relief in the past five years, he knows how the next few months will likely play out.
“Everyone will rush to do relief at once,” Dangal said.

“After a while, maybe after some weeks, everything will be normal, and everyone will forget about that, and no more relief organization will be there to help.” His organization is deliberately holding back from the immediate all-out push and will be gathering data on who still needs help once the initial wave of attention fades.
He expects recovery to take three to five years.
Dangal added that the relief they provide isn’t just reserved for Christians.
“We focus on everyone because this is the time to show the love of Christ to everyone,” he noted.

Currently, Nepali authorities require churches, nonprofits, and private donors to funnel relief through the government rather than distribute it independently in the hardest-hit areas, as many towns are restricted due to ongoing flood risk.
“The most critical need I have seen is food,” Dangal said.
Yet he also sees the need to care for the trauma that entire communities have experienced.
“They have lost their family in front of their eyes.
They have lost their friends.
They have lost everything they built over years.” Counseling, therapy and spiritual care, he added, must come alongside food, water, sanitation, and medicine.

Himalayan Youth Transformation has about 25 staffers and volunteers working across Nepal and partners with groups including the Singapore Red Cross and a UK-based trust, but it still needs more funding to meet the immense needs of this disaster.

His own informal tally—which he cautioned was incomplete, as large parts of the affected region remain unreachable—put losses at roughly a dozen churches damaged or destroyed and 200 to 300 Christian families still missing in Nuwakot district.
“What we have lost, it will take years to build up again,” Dangal said.
“But the lives that have been lost, no one can compensate for that.”

citizens to monitor weather updates, follow instructions from local authorities and avoid independently entering disaster zones that could interfere with ongoing rescue and recovery operations.

Patna (Bihar) [India], September 3 (ANI): Water levels in several rivers in Bihar, including the Ganga, Kosi and Gandak, have risen rapidly following flash floods in Nepal, forcing residents of low-lying Diara areas to evacuate their homes and move to safer locations.
Residents of Nakta Diara and other riverine areas said floodwaters have entered their homes, roads have been submerged, and livestock are struggling for food and shelter.
They also alleged that relief materials and essential facilities have not reached them.

Affected residents have also alleged that relief camps lack adequate arrangements, with shortages of food, drinking water and fodder for livestock forcing families to make their own arrangements to meet basic needs.

With the flood situation worsening, affected residents have urged the administration to intensify relief and rescue operations and ensure timely supply of food, drinking water, fodder and other essential items for both people and livestock.
A local resident from the affected area said the Ganga water level was continuing to rise and had crossed the danger mark.
'The water level continues to rise.
It has crossed the danger mark, and water has inundated everything.
Water has also entered our homes.
We are crossing over by boats.
I appeal to the government to arrange fodder for the animals and food and drinking water for the people as soon as possible,' the resident told ANI.
The resident said families had been forced to leave their homes two to three days ago and alleged that no relief supplies had reached them.
No relief supplies have reached us so far,' he said.
Another resident, Nirala Kumar, said the situation in Nakta Diara was 'very bad' as water had entered houses and people were facing shortages of food and drinking water.
'Water has entered all the houses.
There is a severe shortage of food supplies.
People have no food to eat or water to drink, and all walking paths and roads are blocked,' Kumar said.
He said more than half the residents had already left their homes and urged the government to arrange food, water and facilities for livestock.
'The government should arrange food and water for us and make arrangements for the cattle.
They should set up community kitchens or arrange food relief,' he said.
Kumar said residents face the same hardship every year during the floods and sought relief arrangements for the three months when the area remains affected.
Another resident, Umesh Kumar Yadav, said families were fleeing with their cattle and children as floodwaters entered their homes.
'Yes, that's why we are fleeing with our cattle and our children.
We are bringing all our cattle along,' Yadav said.
He alleged that residents of Diara areas were not receiving adequate government support.
Only the market town people get relief.
People from Diara receive nothing,' he alleged.
Yadav said residents were being forced to arrange food and fodder for their livestock with their own money.
'We will feed them with our own money,' he said, adding that the damage across the panchayat was extensive.
Meanwhile, a local shopkeeper at a cremation ground said the rising Ganga water level was making it increasingly difficult to conduct last rites.
'The water level of the Ganga is continuously rising.
If it rises by another foot or so, it will reach the road, and cremations will have to be done on the road itself,' shopkeeper Santosh Kumar told ANI.
He urged the administration to take measures to prevent soil erosion and place sandbags along the riverbank.
BJP MLA from Digha, Sanjeev Chaurasia, said the administration was monitoring the situation and taking steps to provide shelter and fodder to affected residents and livestock.
'We are continuously conducting ground inspections along the Ganga and monitoring the water levels.
You can see how rapidly the water level of the Ganga has surged.
Consequently, a large number of cattle are arriving from the Nakta Diara panchayat area,' Chaurasia said.
He said the Circle Officer had been called and temporary shelters and fodder arrangements were being made.
'Tents and temporary shelters have been erected immediately, and more are being set up.
Fodder arrangements for the cattle are also being made here,' the MLA said.
Chaurasia said he had coordinated with the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and would visit Nakta Diara and Bind Toli to assess the situation.
'In coordination with the administration, all necessary flood relief facilities provided by the government will certainly be delivered.
There will be no shortage of relief; everyone will receive aid,' he said.
Appealing to residents to remain assured, Chaurasia said the government was taking measures to provide shelter, fodder and food through community kitchens.
'The government is taking swift, proactive measures on all fronts.
We are ensuring that no one faces hardships-whether it is arranging fodder for livestock, setting up shelter homes for flood victims, or running community relief kitchens,' he said.
He said Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary had reviewed the situation following the deluge in Nepal and asserted that the state government was prepared to deal with the flood situation.
The situation in Bihar comes amid devastating floods in neighbouring Nepal.
According to an official update by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), the death toll from the flash floods has reached 1,204.

The crisis began after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26, sending a powerful surge of water, sediment and boulders through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems and causing widespread destruction.
As water levels continue to rise in Bihar, residents of vulnerable riverine areas have sought immediate relief, including food, drinking water, shelter and fodder for livestock.

Kathmandu [Nepal], September 3 (ANI): As disaster relief operations kick into full swing in Nepal following the devastating August 26 Bhote Koshi floods, the United States has sent additional humanitarian and disaster response assistance to the Himalayan nation.

Gor said that the assistance responds directly to requests from the Government of Nepal and comes in addition to the $3.6 million in U.S.
assistance already announced for the flood response.
Countries from across the world have stepped up as rescue and rehabilitation efforts kick in in Nepal.

Singapore will send humanitarian supplies and deploy a specialist team of police officers to Nepal following deadly flash floods along the Nepal-China border, Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday.

KATHMANDU: The United Nations warned on Thursday (Sep 3) of the immense challenge of reaching Nepal flood survivors, with destroyed roads forcing aid workers to consider using cargo drones and porters to reach isolated Himalayan communities.

More than 1,200 people have been killed, and some 5,600 are missing on both sides of the China-Nepal border since the catastrophic glacial mountain collapse on Aug 26, according to tolls by both nations on Thursday.
"It is just incredible - the magnitude of the disaster, the magnitude of the destruction," UN Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia told reporters in Kathmandu.
More than 800 foreigners from at least 34 countries are among those missing, including tourists and pilgrims, in both Nepal and Tibet in China.
In Kathmandu, families of some of the missing foreigners said they were combing hospitals and morgues for any information.

In China, photographs of missing people are being shared on social media by relatives hoping for news.
"Hurry up and come back, your parents miss you a lot, we need you," one woman wrote on a popular platform, posting an image of her relative, a police officer, and his wife.
Beijing keeps tight control over media access and information, and foreign journalists are restricted from reporting in Tibet.

Conrad Kathmandu [Nepal], September3 (ANI): The latest incident of flash floods in Nepal has drawn the attention of the world towards the geologically fragile Himalayan region, which has been warming rapidly, experiencing glacier retreat, snowmelt and degradation of permafrost, which can remove the cement covering on the mountain slopes.
In the 26 August 2026 incident, the evidence available so far points to a glacier/rock collapse and massive debris avalanche, rather than an ordinary monsoon flood.
The glacier/rock mass destabilisation led to an ice-rock avalanche which in turn caused a temporary blockage/surge in the Bhote Koshi river.
With the enormous debris flowing along the Bhote Koshi/Trishuli river, there was large-scale destruction in the lower reaches.
The avalanche, which occurred in the high Himalaya near the Nepal-Tibet frontier, travelled downwards at the rate of 50 metres per second.
Nepal is today sitting on a "geological precipice".
The Himalayas are among the youngest and most tectonically active major mountain systems on Earth.

Nepal sits directly on the collision zone between the Indian and Eurasian plates which produces four overlapping vulnerabilities - Active tectonics, very steep topography, monsoon rainfall and rapidly changing glaciers.

Active tectonics is a constant feature based on the push northward by the Indian plate beneath Eurasia, thus producing earthquakes, fractured rocks, fault zones, extremely steep slopes and frequent landslides and rockfalls.
The 2015 earthquake in Nepal demonstrated the interaction dramatically.

Research following the 2015 earthquake found that earthquake-triggered landslides were the principal mechanism damaging hydropower infrastructure, and estimated that about 25% of existing, constructed and planned Himalayan hydropower projects had high probabilities of moderate-to-severe earthquake damage.
This brings into question the viability of various projects, including hydro projects being undertaken in the region with the help of Chinese companies.

The Rasuwa border region is marked by the presence of large number of Chinese construction companies which are involved in numerous projects turning the green belt into a maze of white rock and cement feature, without any consideration for the surrounding flora and fauna and the geological damage these can cause.
Moreover, the extremely steep topography in the region has led to enormous elevation differences over very short horizontal distances.
A river can descend thousands of metres through a narrow valley, and once a large volume of water, ice and rock enters such a valley, it becomes an extremely efficient natural chute.
There are several river pathways in the region, that pass through very high mountain walls that are virtually hugging each other.
Any glacial outburst in the region can thus lead to a massive rush of mud, ice and stones causing severe destruction to nature and any physical features on the way.

The heavy monsoon rainfall further saturates already-fractured slopes and weakens the soil at certain locations thereby enhancing the threat level of landslides and downward flow of water, rocks and soil.
Therefore, Nepal's landslides identify a combination of steep slopes, geological weakness, intense rainfall, river erosion and land-use changes as major drivers.
The rapidly changing glaciers is the new and increasingly important variable.
Glaciers are retreating and the high-altitude environment is becoming less stable.
Nepal has thousands of glacial lakes, some of which have the potential to produce catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF).
A tracking of the incidents of glacial outbursts and flash floods in the region indicates that the August 26 incident should not be a surprise.
On the contrary, more such instances could be anticipated in the coming times.

A look at the number of such incidents that have taken place indicates that their frequency has gone up several folds in recent times as climate change and heating of the high mountains increasingly become a regular feature.
There have actually been more than 100 documented flood-related events in Nepal since 1954, according to a reconstruction of Nepal's flood history published recently.
These include GLOFs, cloudbursts, landslides and major river floods.
Geologists have warned about the vulnerability of the Rasuwa/Bhote Koshi access since the 2025 floods in the region.
They had accordingly suggested that enough preparations need to be made to deal with any such eventualities.
The region has also seen large-scale construction by Chinese companies.

As one drives towards the Rasuwa crossing on the Nepali side, one can see a change in the landscape from the lush green forest and pine trees to a wide patch of rocks and quarries with heavy construction equipment spread across.
Most of these construction projects are undertaken by Chinese companies who operate freely in the area using Chinese heavy vehicles without registration plates.

The local offices of these Chinese companies are clearly marked on the rock walls alongside the road and one can see Chinese engineers and senior company officials moving about in their facilities 5 to 10 kms inside Nepal.

While construction of bridges, roads , tunnels and hydro projects is a necessity, at the same time construction of any kind in these areas leads to cutting mountain slopes, removing vegetation, blasting rock, excavating tunnels, dumping spoil, altering drainage and narrowing river corridors besides creating large concrete structures in the valleys.
Research on Nepal has found that construction related cut slopes account for a substantial proportion of landslides, and that poorly planned roads can dramatically increase landslide risk.
China has been constructing several projects in Tibet which would cause significant change in the geological matrix of the Tibetan plateau.

Some of the projects which are along the Nepal-China border in the high Himalayas, which could cause serious damage to nature and the geological features are : --Girong-Rasuwagadi corridor - on the Chinese side, the project involves logistics and highway infrastructure, while on the Nepal side the project is marked by the Syaphrubeshi-Rasiwagadi highway and Timure border facilities; --Zhangmu-Tatopani project - the traditional China- Nepal highway project connecting Kathmandu to Tatopani and includes port facilities; -- Korala-Mustang project - border infrastructure along Lomangthang/Burang which aims to open western Nepal to Tibet; -- Burang - Hilsa road and border facilities - This involves Burang border facilities on the Chinese side and Hilsa-Simikot road and Hilsa bridge on the Nepal side.

The project aims to open western Nepal to Tibet; --Kerung/Rasuwa- Kathmandu project - involves construction of highway and logistic network connecting Nepal with Tibet and involves significant tunnelling, such as the Tokha-Chhahre tunnel; --Kamathanka project - a network of road structure on the Tibetan side which will form the Kimathanka-Khandbari/Koshi corridor aiming to connect Eastern Nepal with Tibet -- Power connectivity - Several power connectivity projects being considered including the Ratmate-Rasuwagadhi-Kerung 400-kv transmission proposal; -- Railway - Shigatse-Gyirong railway project under development - Nature's challenges being confronted and hence moving slow.

-- Gyirong - Kathmandu railway project - this is a proposed China- Nepal cross border railway with the aim of having a direct Tibet-Kathmandu connection; Besides the above projects, which have a direct cross border connect between Tibet and Nepal and involve mass scale construction work causing serious ecological damages in the high Himalayas, China is also undertaking several projects along the Tibetan lower plateau which would have an impact on the mountain ranges with a ripple effect on Nepal over a period of time.

Some of these projects are : Yarling tsangpo/Medog hydropower, Sichuan- Tibet railway project, Xinjiang - Tibet Railway project, G 219 Western highway, G 318 and associated Himalayan tunnels, Medog-Zayu connectivity, Yadong/Sikkim connectivity and the Chinese border settlements along Arunachal Pradesh, Bhutan and Sikkim.

All of these projects require cutting into mountains, blasting, removing vegetation, dumping excavation rock, alerting natural drainage, constructing bridges and retaining structures, drilling through unstable geological formations etc.
A major landslide high above in the mountains can cause landslides and river blockage.
This in turn will cause temporary lake formations at very high altitudes, which when breached can cause flash floods.

China's massive railway and highway projects have increasingly caused serious damage to nature in the mountains, especially due to the long kilometres of tunnelling which cause intersecting geological faults, change ground water movement, destabilise rock masses, drain or redirect underground water and weaken slopes above tunnel portals.

On the Tibet-Nepal axis, the scale and importance of the Gyirong (Tibet) - Rasuwagadhi (Nepal) corridor is the most consequential, and its scale of importance became particularly obvious during the August 2026 disaster as the flood devastated the Gyirong/Rasuwagadhi corridor and temporarily cut the principal China-Nepal land connection.

The Gyirong-Rasuwagadhi corridor is particularly ecologically sensitive, not because the road automatically causes floods or glacier collapses, but because construction takes place in an exceptionally steep, seismically active and hydrologically unstable Himalayan environment.

There is already a strong warning from Nepal's Langtang National Park management plan that the Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi road passes along the Bhote Koshi within the park, and the plan specifically identifies risks of habitat fragmentation and impacts during construction.

Animal conservationists mention of rare animals such as the red panda, Himalayan black bear, snow leopard, Assamese macaque and other forest and high altitude species being endangered as a result of these projects.
One of the major potential ecological interventions by China in Tibet is the Yarlung Tsangpo mega project.
China has already started the construction process in the great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo in Medog.

The site is marked by an extraordinarily deep gorge, enormous elevation gradient, active tectonic environment, very steep slopes, glaciers and unstable rocks and having exceptionally heavy rainfall in the region.
The geological concerns are particularly serious as the area is seismically active.

While climate change is bound to destabilise high altitude rock and ice and increase the potential for floods, landslides and avalanches, construction of tunnels, roads, dams, hydro projects, settlements only act as risk multipliers.
Another important issue is that of hydropower projects which are potentially more consequential than the roads.
Nepal is undergoing an enormous hydropower build-out.
Chinese capital as well as Nepali investment are involved.

The problem is that hydropower development as well as construction of roads and tunnels naturally tends to take away the crucial space meant for nature in its own surroundings, and further narrows down the path of water flow making the impact piercing and damaging.
Infrastructures in narrow valleys, steep slopes and along major rivers are indeed geological fault zones.
That is almost the perfect combination for cascading disaster.

While these projects would have to be implemented looking at the larger issue of energy generation and potential for Nepal to emerge as a major energy producer and supplier, there is need for a combined effort by the international community to assess the prevailing challenges that the Himalayas face.

This would require mandatory cumulative environmental-impact assessments for entire river basins, geological assessment before road/tunnel construction, much stricter controls on mountain - slope cutting, comprehensive glacier and permafrost monitoring.
There should also be real-time GLOF warning systems in place and cross border sharing of satellite, hydrological and seismic information.
There is also need to ensure that there is no major infrastructure in identified avalanche/debris - flow corridors and independent safety audits of existing hydropower projects should be carried out.
Nepal should take the lead in assessing the projects in a cumulative manner to examine their viability at a particular location given the fragile play of nature.

The Kathmandu based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) could be involved in setting up an advanced Himalayan disaster-warning mechanism, while India can work closely with Nepal in this sphere considering India lies downstream from all these Himalayan rivers and would inevitably get affected by the ecological disasters that occur in these mountains.

The world cannot let Nepal deal with these challenges alone and this has been brought out clearly by the Prime Minister of Nepal Balendra Shah, who declared on 2 September 2026 that "climate change is the world's shared responsibility, and that Nepal must forcefully campaign for climate justice and international financial compensation rather than simple post-disaster aid".

During his address to the House of Representatives, he linked the recent catastrophic flash floods in Rasuwa directly to warming climate, framing it as a warning for the entire Himalayan region and global civilisation.

"The collapse of bridges, the poor road access - all of these elements will be making it difficult for people to travel quickly," Ms Batch said.

At Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu, families gathered Wednesday to perform a ritual that Nepali Hindu tradition reserves for those whose bodies cannot be recovered.
They cremated effigies woven from kush grass — surrogate bodies representing the souls of the missing — and performed the rites of death for people they cannot confirm are dead.
One week after a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-Tibet border and sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through Himalayan valleys, this is what grief looks like when there is no body to bring home.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority confirmed Wednesday that the death toll from the August 26 disaster has risen to at least 1,252 on the Nepali side alone, with the combined toll across Nepal and China surpassing 1,270.
Some 4,216 people remain missing across both countries, while nearly 12,000 have been rescued.
The United Nations has described the event as Nepal's worst natural catastrophe since the April 2015 earthquake, which killed approximately 9,000 people.

The NDRRMA called it "not just a flood — a Himalayan climate disaster that came without warning." The kush grass effigies — dressed, garlanded and carried to the river steps — served as proxies for a goodbye that the flood had denied thousands of Nepali families.
Among those mourned Wednesday was Bishi Pandey, 48, whose body remains missing; his relatives wept through the smoke at Pashupatinath as the effigy burned in his place.
The ceremonies continued through the morning as helicopters carried more bodies from Rasuwa district to Kathmandu, and morgues already past capacity struggled to hold what the river kept returning.

The most consequential development from Wednesday's operations was the conclusion of search work at the Rasuwagadhi hydropower facility in Rasuwa district — the last of eleven sites where active searches had been under way.
An army team accompanied by engineers and a drone unit entered the 111-megawatt facility's tunnel system, advanced to its innermost section and flew a drone through the full interior.
The prime minister's secretariat confirmed no one was found inside.
Approximately 897 workers across all eleven projects remain out of contact, with roughly 500 believed to have been inside tunnel systems when the surge struck.
At the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project alone, at least 576 people are missing, with approximately 300 believed trapped inside the tunnel.
Rescue crews have used controlled explosives to clear boulders while simultaneously pumping water from the shafts.
Vertical drilling — boring down from the mountain's summit to pierce the top of the powerhouse — remains under examination where frontal access stays blocked.
The tunnel at Trishuli 3A runs more than four kilometers; Indian and Chinese tunnel specialists continue working alongside Nepali army engineers at the most critical remaining sites.
Six days after the disaster, survival conditions inside sealed shafts are increasingly in doubt.
The head of the Independent Power Producers' Association said publicly that some workers may have suffocated.
One survivor estimated roughly 1,000 people had been working across nearby projects the morning the flood struck, with only about 100 making it out.
Another described gripping ceiling rungs for six hours as water rose in the darkness, passing a tin sheet between colleagues as the group inched toward the exit.
By the time they emerged, the flood had claimed their clothing.
His brother-in-law remained among the missing — his pregnant wife waiting at home.
What began as a rescue operation is, at most sites, now being managed as a recovery mission in all but official terminology.
In Chitwan district, nearly 200 kilometers downstream from the disaster's origin, mass burials continued in the Devghat forest area of Bharatpur Metropolitan City.
Hundreds of graves were prepared along trails that until recently served as morning walking paths.
Before each burial, DNA samples, photographs and fingerprints were collected, and precise location coordinates were recorded so remains could be matched and exhumed if families came forward.
A forensic team from India is assisting in the identification process.
In Chitwan alone, 233 bodies had been recovered from riverbanks in the initial days, with only four identified before mass burial preparations began.
Nepal's foreign minister said refrigerated storage for decomposed remains was urgently needed and had been formally requested from foreign governments without confirmed commitment.
Across the disaster zone, survivors are improvising in conditions that relief workers describe as among the most logistically complex they have encountered.

At Devighat in Nuwakot district, hundreds of displaced residents gathered at a temporary relief camp Wednesday to receive utility supplies — the modest inventory of tarpaulins, rice sacks and clothing laid out on blue sheets in an open field representing, for many, everything they now own.

Elsewhere in Nuwakot, flood survivors grip a makeshift cable above the swollen Trishuli river as Nepali soldiers and residents pull them hand over hand to the opposite bank — a zip line strung between the ruins of what was once a bridge.

In Trishuli Center, the turquoise house that locals have taken to calling the "miracle house" stands almost intact amid a landscape of gray sludge, the only structure in its immediate surroundings that the flood left whole.
The family inside survived as the water destroyed everything around them.
The China-Nepal border crossing at Gyirong — the primary land route between the two countries, handling roughly a third of bilateral trade — was destroyed entirely in the initial surge.
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported Wednesday that the road to the border has been largely reopened after excavators carved a new route along the riverbank.
Chinese rescue teams continue searching for survivors on the Tibetan side, where at least 16 people have died and 546 remain missing.

The avalanche of ice and rock reached the Gyirong Port complex within six to seven minutes of the initial collapse — catching pilgrims, traders and hydropower workers simultaneously in their most exposed positions along the valley.

The August 26 collapse struck at the peak of the pilgrimage season on the Kailash Mansarovar route, which draws tens of thousands of travelers through Rasuwa district and across the Gyirong crossing each year.
Among the missing are approximately 583 foreign nationals on the Nepali side alone.
Australia confirmed Wednesday that five previously listed nationals have been found safe, reducing its missing count from 43 to 38.
Approximately 80 Americans, 53 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 33 British nationals and 32 Canadians remain unaccounted for.
Three American families have described searching publicly for parents on a Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage who have not made contact since the morning of August 26.
Malaysia's prime minister pledged a rescue team and $1 million in aid.
Singapore dispatched a police rescue team alongside humanitarian supplies.
The United Nations estimates 65,000 people require urgent emergency water, sanitation and hygiene support.
More than 22,000 children have been identified as requiring protection services.

Nepal has deployed approximately 30,000 security personnel across relief operations, and the UNDP estimates the disaster generated more than 2.4 million tons of debris across five affected districts — Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan.

A rapid hazard assessment by an international scientific consortium raised serious questions about whether the disaster could have been anticipated — and whether workers could have been evacuated in time.
Analysis of pre-event satellite imagery revealed visible signs of instability in the days before the collapse, including brown meltwater discharge and cracks forming in surrounding bedrock.
Researchers noted that water within the affected glacier appeared to accelerate measurably before the final collapse.

The findings call for improved early warning systems and cross-border data sharing between Nepal and China, as well as risk protocols extending beyond the immediate perimeter of infrastructure project boundaries.
That the same river corridor had flooded catastrophically just fourteen months earlier, killing nine people, makes the absence of enhanced monitoring especially difficult to defend in retrospect.
The glacier responsible sits within a system that has been deteriorating for decades.
The Langtang Valley has lost more than 40 percent of its glacier volume since 1815, with the pace of loss accelerating sharply in recent years.
The high-mountain zone above 4,000 meters is warming significantly faster than the global average.
Permafrost that once bound rock, ice and glacial mass together for millennia is weakening, increasing the likelihood of sudden, catastrophic detachments.
Nepal's Prime Minister stated publicly there is no doubt climate change contributed to the disaster.

In a region where hydropower investment has expanded rapidly over the past two decades precisely because meltwater resources appeared abundant and predictable, the August 26 collapse now tests the foundational assumptions of that development model.

China's Ministry of Water Resources has warned that glaciers surrounding the impact crater may still be unstable, and a barrier lake of approximately 14,000 square meters upstream remains under active monitoring.
With Nepal's monsoon season continuing through September, compounding risk to already-saturated riverbanks remains a live concern.

At Pashupatinath, the smoke from the kush grass pyres drifted over the Bagmati river as more families arrived through the afternoon — each carrying an effigy for someone the flood had taken without leaving a body behind.

Two more Australians have been found safe in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, but grave concerns remain for the 36 still missing.
The two Australians, who had been uncontactable, have confirmed they are safe and do not require consular assistance.
It brings the number of Australians found since the catastrophic floods began on August 26 to seven, after five were confirmed safe on Wednesday.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the update would bring relief to their families, but the federal government remains concerned for those still missing.
“That would be a huge relief to the loved ones of these two Australians who have been located,” Dr Chalmers said on ABC News Breakfast on Friday.

“But we still have very serious concerns for the 36 Australians that we haven’t been able to locate yet.” More than 1200 people have died since a glacier collapse near Nepal’s border with Tibet triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.
The three dozen Australians still missing are among more than 5000 people unaccounted for, according to the latest count from Nepali authorities.
The federal government has sent 19 officials and disaster response specialists to the region, with another 23 to be deployed within days.
On Thursday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed local authorities would conduct searches in areas where many Australians were believed to have been staying.
Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to search those target areas identified by Australia on foot, with helicopter and drone support.

“I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others,” Senator Wong told reporters.
Australian drone operators and incident management specialists would be sent to the region along as part of a broader on-the-ground support team.

The 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team will use advanced drone technology for real-time imagery and geospatial information and mapping of affected regions, where transport routes and critical infrastructure remain severely damaged.
The technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify trapped victims through heat sources.
DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.
Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.
“We continue to work around the clock to ascertain as much information as we can and provide it to the families of missing Australians,” Senator Wong said.
“We all hold on to hope, and we’ve got to hold on to hope.” Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.

It comes after Australian authorities on Friday confirmed two citizens had made contact overnight, bringing the number of missing Australians to 36.
As the search for the remaining survivors continues, Australian Red Cross head of migration Nicole Batch said infrastructure damage was posing a major challenge.
The missing Australians are among more than 5000 people unaccounted for after the deadly floods.
(EPA PHOTO) Interruptions to mobile networks, intermittent power and collapsed bridges and roads meant fewer opportunities to make contact, added to a surge in demand.
"The collapse of bridges, the poor road access - all of these elements will be making it difficult for people to travel quickly," Ms Batch said.

"The scale of the disaster and the number of people that are trying to make contact - that is one challenge in itself." Ms Batch, who specialises in locating missing people following disasters, said reaching loved ones was almost always the first thing survivors tried to do.
But many likely lost their phones during the floods or else were limited in their ability to use them due to power or mobile network blackouts.
State-owned provider Nepal Telecom announced on Thursday services had been fully restored to disaster-hit regions, after being progressively brought back online.
But it followed days of coverage challenges and ongoing capacity strain, added to more immediate infrastructure roadblocks.
It comes as rescue efforts continue for the hundreds of workers feared trapped in underground power stations damaged or obscured by the floods.
Melbourne-based engineer and geologist Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepalese authorities on the rescues, said there was no test case for their work.

"It's like solving a puzzle you can't see." He is advising on the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where rescuers reportedly pulled two workers alive from a tunnel on Friday, nine days after the floods began.
Melbourne-based engineer Arnold Dix is advising Nepalese authorities on the rescues.
(James Ross/AAP PHOTOS) The rescues have been reported on local television news channels and by Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane on Facebook, AP reported.
Speaking hours before the reports surfaced, Mr Dix told AAP he had received word members of the Nepali army had heard voices inside the tunnel.
"When you're exhausted, sometimes your mind plays trick on you ...
but once rescuers hear there might be someone alive ...
this spurs you on," he said.
More than 1200 people have died and 5000 are missing since a glacier collapse brought flash flooding to towns and valleys along the border region.
The federal government has sent 19 officials and disaster response specialists to the region, with another 23 to be deployed within days.
Penny Wong says the government is holding on to hope, despite grave concerns for those missing.
(Michael Errey/AAP PHOTOS) Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke with his Nepalese counterpart on Friday, offering Australia's deepest condolences.
"The loss of life and destruction is devastating, and we will keep doing everything we can to find the Australians still unaccounted for," he wrote on X.
On Thursday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed local authorities would conduct searches in areas where many Australians were believed to have been staying.
Rescue teams from the Nepali army were expected to search those target areas identified by Australia on foot, with helicopter and drone support.
DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and to contact next of kin where appropriate.
Disaster response specialists will use drone technology in the search for missing Australians.
(HANDOUT/Fire Rescue NSW) Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.
More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.
Australians have donated more than $4 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support recovery efforts.
The federal government will provide a further $3 million to match public donations, bringing the ongoing humanitarian support package to a total of $11 million.

New Delhi: To facilitate the identification of mortal remains of Nepal flood victims, the Centre will make available the services of central and state-level forensic labs for DNA profiling of their first-degree biological relatives in India, the MEA said on Thursday, September 3.
First-degree biological relatives residing in India, i.e.

father, mother, son, daughter or sibling, may have their biological samples collected and DNA profiles prepared at Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs); State Forensic Science Laboratories (SFSLs); laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU); and NABL-accredited laboratories having DNA profiling capability, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said in a statement.
The death toll from last week’s flash floods in Nepal has risen to at least 1,259 after rescue workers recovered more bodies from affected areas, according to Nepalese authorities.
While emergency teams have rescued more than 12,000 people, roughly 5,000 remain missing as search and rescue operations continue.

Also Read Death toll rises to 1,252 in Nepal amid threats of fresh floods In a press statement on Tuesday, the Embassy of India in Kathmandu outlined the information available regarding the procedures for identification of mortal remains of the August 26 flash flood victims, the MEA said.
The MEA also shared a list of government forensic science laboratories having DNA profiling facilities.
“As advised by the Nepal Police, Autosomal STR DNA profiling may be undertaken for the purpose of identification, subject to the technical requirements communicated by the Nepali authorities.
The helpline number in this regard is: +977 9841 6160 95,” it said.

Once prepared, the DNA profiles, along with the preliminary information required by the Nepali authorities, may be sent by email — dnacodis@nepalpolice.gov.np — for comparison with DNA profiles obtained from unidentified mortal remains, the statement said.
For facilitation and coordination by the Embassy of India, Kathmandu, a copy of the DNA profile may also be sent to eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com, it said.
The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, leaving a trail of destruction.

Two hydropower workers were pulled from a tunnel buried by debris in Nepal on Friday, a rare ray of hope on the 10th day of rescue efforts after catastrophic Himalayan flooding.
Rescuers cheered as one man was pulled from a muddy opening, video released by the energy ministry showed.
He was helped to his feet by rescuers, and later carried on the backs of the emergency workers, raising his hand as they took him towards a helicopter.
A photograph showed the second man caked in mud, his hands pressed together in prayer, as rescuers carried him away on an orange stretcher.
“As long as there is breath, there is hope!” Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said in a statement.

Kathmandu, Sep 4 (IANS) Laxmi Kumari Sah, wife of Sanjaya Sah, who was rescued from the tunnel of Nepal’s flood-hit Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project, is over the moon after her husband was rescued alive on Friday morning.
Sah was one of two people rescued by a joint team of the Nepal Army and Armed Police Force from deep inside the tunnel, which was damaged by last week’s deadly floods.
Sanjaya Sah, 30, a foreman employed at the project, hails from the southern district of Saptari.
Along with him, Kabir Maharjan, 45, a supervisor in the Hydropower Automation section of the project, was also rescued alive.
“I am very happy about the rescue of my husband, and it has brought happiness to all my family members,” Laxmi told IANS in a brief conversation.
“I was at home when I heard about his rescue at around 8:30 a.m.
It has brought immense joy to our family.” She said she was heading to Kathmandu to meet her husband following his rescue.
She said the last 10 days were very painful for her and her family.
Earlier, the Nepali Army said the two men were rescued following sustained efforts to reach those believed to be trapped inside the tunnel, which was affected by the deadly floods last week.
The disaster has so far claimed 1,259 lives, while 5,053 people remained out of contact as of Thursday evening, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
“After 10 days of darkness, life has seen the light again.
Two people have been rescued alive from inside the hydropower project tunnel at Trishuli-3A,” the Nepali Army said earlier in a social media post.

“The rescue operation is underway.” The successful rescue of the two men alive has revived hope that others believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several flood-affected hydropower projects could also be rescued alive.

The Independent Power Producers’ Association, an association of private-sector power developers, said on Thursday evening that as many as 945 people working in 11 hydropower projects affected by the floods remained out of contact.

Nepal flash floods aftermath LIVE: Two trapped workers rescued alive from a tunnel in Nepal First-degree biological relatives residing in India — father, mother, son, daughter or sibling — may have their biological samples collected and DNA profiles prepared at Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs); State Forensic Science Laboratories (SFSLs); laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU); and NABL-accredited laboratories having DNA profiling capability, the ministry said in a statement.
The death toll from last week's flash floods in Nepal has risen to at least 1,259 after rescue workers recovered more bodies from affected areas, according to Nepalese authorities.
While emergency teams have rescued more than 12,000 people, roughly 5,000 remain missing as search and rescue operations continue.

In a press statement on Tuesday (September 1, 2026), the Embassy of India in Kathmandu outlined the information available regarding the procedures for identification of mortal remains of the August 26 flash flood victims, the MEA said.

In this backdrop, and as an additional measure to facilitate the ongoing identification process, the Union Ministry of Home Affairs has decided to make available the services of CFSLs, SFSLs and NFSU laboratories in India for "DNA profiling of first-degree biological relatives of persons who remain missing following the flash flood in Nepal", it said.
The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) also shared a list of government forensic science laboratories having DNA profiling facilities.
"As advised by the Nepal Police, Autosomal STR DNA profiling may be undertaken for the purpose of identification, subject to the technical requirements communicated by the Nepali authorities.
The helpline number in this regard is: +977 9841 6160 95," it said.

Once prepared, the DNA profiles, along with the preliminary information required by the Nepali authorities, may be sent by email — dnacodis@nepalpolice.gov.np — for comparison with DNA profiles obtained from unidentified mortal remains, the statement said.
For facilitation and coordination by the Embassy of India, Kathmandu, a copy of the DNA profile may also be sent to eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com, it said.

Some families have also held symbolic funerals for loved ones whose remains may never be found.

This material devastation is compounded by psychological trauma.
Thousands of survivors escaped the initial surge by scrambling up the steep valley sides into the surrounding mountains.
Helicopter drops of rice, lentils, and tarpaulins have reached some locations, but the scale of need far outstrips what has been delivered.
Medicine, clean water, and blankets are critically short, with night temperatures dropping and monsoon rains continuing; exposure and illness are mounting threats.
At present, rescue operations are focused on the ruins of hydropower projects, where hundreds of workers are trapped.
For more than a week, rescue teams have been drilling, cutting, and pumping to reach these spaces, but progress is slow and dangerous, with the risk of secondary collapses and renewed surges.
Every hour that passes reduces the chances of finding anyone alive.
The disaster has laid bare the bankruptcy of Nepal’s early warning system (EWS).
An article published in the Kathmandu Post on September 2 said although Nepal invested in sensors and SMS alert infrastructure over the past decade, the system collapsed when it was most needed.
Automated gauging stations in upper Bhote Koshi stopped functioning at 8:40 a.m.
on August 26, just as the flood crossed the border from Tibet.
The first SMS warnings to downstream communities were sent only after the surge was already racing through Rasuwa.
By the time the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology posted a public update that the upstream blockage had not fully drained, five hours had elapsed, and the worst destruction was already done.
A robust, multi-hazard EWS covering glacial lake outbursts, landslide-dammed lakes, and trans-boundary floods is entirely feasible with existing technology.
But it requires sustained investment, cross-border data sharing, and a state that prioritizes the lives of workers and peasants over debt servicing and elite enrichment.

The Post cited research by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), which has identified 21 potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Nepal across the Gandaki, Koshi, and Karnali river basins, and mapped 2,070 glacial lakes in total.
As temperatures rise, both the number and size of glacial lakes are increasing.

The same technological arsenal deployed for destruction—satellite imagery, drone swarms, thermal sensors, AI-driven surveillance systems, and rapid-deployment engineering units—could within hours locate survivors trapped under rubble, map real-time landslide risks, and deliver food and medicine to villages cut off by floods.

Halting the destruction of the environment is inseparable from the fight against the capitalist system that is destroying it.
