Nepal's government has announced a special relief package for businesses hit by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, offering concessions, loan restructuring and cheaper credit, as authorities began work on relocating settlements destroyed by the disaster.

The measures came as the government stepped up recovery efforts following the devastating floods, which swept away homes, roads and bridges in Nepal on August 26, leaving hundreds dead and thousands missing, with several settlements along the Trishuli riverbanks destroyed.
The Nepal Cabinet on Thursday described the business-related measures as the first phase of its recovery package, The Kathmandu Post newspaper reported.

Businesses whose commercial vehicles, transport equipment, plants, machinery, tools or other equipment were destroyed beyond repair or swept away will be allowed to import replacements without paying customs duties, the report said.
The concession will also apply to goods on which customs duties had already been paid but which were destroyed before reaching their destination.
Replacement goods will have to be imported through any customs office within six months, it said.

Provincial and local governments will also be asked to provide temporary concessions on property and business taxes, building permit fees and other local charges for affected businesses and properties, the report added.
The government has directed Nepal Rastra Bank, the country's central bank, to facilitate restructuring or rescheduling of loans taken by flood-affected borrowers, it said.
The Insurance Authority has separately been asked to speed up claims by allowing insurers to deploy surveyors through simplified procedures.
Insurers will be required to provide advance payments of up to 50 per cent of estimated losses based on preliminary assessments.
The relief measures come as authorities prepare a longer-term plan for communities whose homes and settlements were swept away.
The August 26 flood destroyed around 15 settlements across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, The Kathmandu Post reported.
The National Planning Commission (NPC) has begun work on a master plan to rebuild infrastructure, develop safer settlements and address longer-term development needs.

NPC vice-chair Gunakar Bhatta said the commission was also preparing a post-disaster needs assessment, which will examine damage and losses across infrastructure, productive sectors, services, the environment and the wider economy.

A preliminary assessment by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) found that around 1.6 million people across 15 local units were directly affected, while 8,317 houses were destroyed, the report said.
The Ministry of Infrastructure Development will first focus on restoring roads and bridges connecting the affected areas before planning new settlements.
Ministry Secretary Gopal Prasad Sigdel said the long-term plan would be to relocate people away from flood-risk areas.
“The long-term plan will be to establish settlements in areas outside the flood-risk zones,” he was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post.
Authorities are mapping settlements that are no longer habitable while continuing rescue, relief and temporary shelter operations.
Around 3,948 people rescued by the government were staying at holding centres in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Dhading and Kathmandu, the report said.
NDRRMA chief executive Dharmaraj Upreti said teams were identifying safer locations for displaced communities.
“People cannot return to settlements that have been swept away by the flood.
The government has formed teams to identify safer locations and is working on a plan to relocate them,” he was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post.
Officials are considering moving some communities to other districts or finding safer vacant land within the affected districts.
The government has previous experience of relocating disaster-hit communities, including after the 1993 floods and the 2015 earthquake.
Experts have also urged authorities to consider livelihoods, social ties and future disaster risks while choosing new locations, the report said.

“There is a serious risk of major disasters in the Himalayan region from Taplejung to Darchula in the coming years,” former prime minister Baburam Bhattarai was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post.
“Safer areas should be identified nearby, such as small valleys in the mountains and higher ground in the hills, where at-risk settlements can be relocated,” Bhattarai said.
Meanwhile, Nepal's government has also announced support for personnel engaged in the rescue effort.

Government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel said the Cabinet decided on Thursday to provide risk allowances and meal expenses to security personnel and government employees deployed for search and rescue operations following the Bhotekoshi flooding, Onlinekhabar news portal reported.
Those injured during the operations will receive free medical treatment, while families of personnel who die during rescue operations will receive NRs 1 million in relief, according to the report.

New Delhi, Sep 4 (IANS) Continuing with its humanitarian assistance to Nepal, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Friday said that India has so far sent around 95 tonnes of relief material on seven aircraft, along with 54 personnel to support rescue and relief efforts following the devastating flash floods in the Himalayan nation.

Addressing a bi-weekly press briefing in New Delhi on Friday, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India would continue to extend assistance based on the requirements communicated by the Nepalese government, with plans to send additional forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other requested materials in the coming days.
"We will continue to provide assistance as per the requirements of the Nepal government.
In the coming days, we plan to send more forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other materials that are requested by the Nepal government.
Yesterday, we had two Indian aircraft flying to Kathmandu along with 21 tonnes of relief material.
Till now, we have supplied around 95 tonnes of relief materials on seven aircraft.
In addition to the relief material, we've also sent 54 personnel to support relief and rescue efforts in Nepal.
This comprises 30 tunnel rescue experts, 19 forensic experts, and a five-member medical team.

Our rescue and forensic teams are deployed on the ground, and they are working closely with the Nepalese authorities," said Jaiswal Jaiswal further said that 275 Indian nationals are currently unaccounted for, while 1,907 Indian nationals have so far crossed safely into Nepal from China.
He added that, according to official sources in China, no Indian travellers are currently stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region.
“As per our current information, 275 Indian nationals remain missing.
We continue to be in close touch with the Nepali government, with the Ministry of Home Affairs here and the concerned state governments in India.
We have been regularly releasing the names of Indians who have been rescued.
We deeply appreciate the efforts of the Nepal authorities in this regard.
So far, 166 Indian nationals have been rescued in Nepal.
So far, 1,907 Indian nationals have safely crossed into Nepal from China.
And as per official sources in China, there are no Indian travellers who are stranded in the Tibet Autonomous Region,” the MEA spokesperson mentioned.

The death toll from the flood disaster in Nepal had reached 1,252 by Thursday noon, with 4,216 people remaining out of contact, according to the latest data released by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
The massive flood that struck Nepal's Rasuwa originated in the Tibetan region of China on August 26.
It swept through the transboundary Bhote Koshi River, leaving over a thousand dead, including foreign nationals, and caused widespread destruction in the Himalayan nation.
For nearly 20 members of a family in Trishuli, one room has become home after devastating floods destroyed homes, cut roads and left several families without basic amenities.

A week on, Indian volunteers are travelling up to 10 hours through damaged mountain roads and bridges to take food, bedding and household essentials to such communities, while some areas of Rasuwa remain accessible only by helicopter.

The relief effort is increasingly shifting from accessible flood-hit areas to isolated settlements, where families have lost homes, livestock, belongings and livelihoods, but the terrain and damaged infrastructure make reaching them difficult.

“Almost a week after the floods, some of the more accessible areas are slowly seeing relief reach them, but our biggest concern now is reaching the families who have been most severely affected and remain isolated,” Manohar Naidu, a Khalsa Aid volunteer, told The Hindu from Nepal.
In Trishuli, Tupche and other remote communities, volunteers have found several families living together with little shelter or basic household equipment.
Some, they said, have effectively lost everything.

The volunteers also described mass burials being carried out as mortuaries run out of space, with forest land being cleared to accommodate bodies as the death toll rises and many remain unidentified.
“Our immediate support is focused on essential relief such as food, clothing, bedding and basic household requirements.
At the same time, we are assessing and documenting what each community will need for longer-term recovery,” Mr.
Reaching the affected communities has become a major logistical challenge.
Some journeys from Kathmandu to areas such as Trishuli take nine to 10 hours, with damaged or completely washed-out roads and bridges forcing volunteers to take longer routes.
Teams are travelling in trucks carrying supplies, while demand for 4x4 vehicles has surged, making them difficult to arrange and prompting suppliers to raise prices.
The problem is more acute in Rasuwa, where some affected areas have no road connectivity and helicopters are the only practical option.
Each trip can cost around $2,000, significantly increasing the cost of delivering relief.
“So the challenge is not simply having relief material available.
The biggest challenge is getting that aid to the families who need it most,” Mr.
The organisation is procuring supplies locally, but demand is outstripping availability for mattresses, solar lights and other household items.
“People need much more than food.
They are asking how they are going to rebuild their lives,” Mr.

The next phase will require shelter, clean water and sanitation and getting children back into education, followed by restoring livelihoods and rebuilding homes, roads, bridges and community infrastructure.
Khalsa Aid had earlier proposed adopting inaccessible villages for longer-term support.

The proposal is being assessed on the extent of damage, families affected, livelihood losses and infrastructure needs, with the aim of concentrating resources in severely affected communities rather than spreading assistance thinly.
The organisation is also considering temporary holding centres with mattresses, portable washroom facilities and cooking arrangements for families living together without basic amenities.
Ten Indian volunteers are currently involved in logistics, assessments, packing and distribution.

Many have prior disaster-response experience, including during the recent Assam floods, but Nepal has posed added challenges of mountainous terrain, long journeys and limited electricity and internet connectivity.
The organisation has also sought official permission to clear debris in local areas to restore connectivity and ease access to affected communities.

TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The death toll from devastating flash floods along the Nepal-China border has risen to 1,280, while more than 5,600 people remain missing as search and rescue operations enter their second week.
As reported by Anadolu, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reported 1,259 deaths and 5,083 people still missing as of Thursday, September 3.
The missing include 583 foreign nationals.
More than 21,400 security personnel have been deployed to affected areas as authorities continue searching for victims and delivering emergency assistance.
With many missing people presumed dead, some families in Nepal have begun holding symbolic funeral ceremonies for relatives whose bodies have not been recovered.

Families Hold Funerals for Missing Relatives In Rasuwa, one of the areas hardest hit by the floods, families have created symbolic funeral effigies using kaas-kush, a type of sacred grass, to perform rituals intended to help release the souls of missing relatives.
The ceremonies were held as families increasingly lost hope of recovering the bodies of loved ones swept away by the floods, The Kathmandu Post reported.
On Wednesday, September 2, dozens of the effigies were cremated in a mass funeral ceremony at Pashupati Aryaghat, a cremation site on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu.
The rituals reflect the growing humanitarian and emotional toll of the disaster, with many families still unable to locate relatives more than a week after the floods.
In Chitwan, another badly affected district, authorities have cremated unidentified bodies after collecting DNA samples in an effort to preserve the possibility of future identification.
The scale of the disaster has made identifying and storing bodies increasingly difficult.
In some districts, floodwaters swept away homes as well as family members, leaving survivors without suitable places to conduct funeral rites.
Families who have lost their homes and traveled to Kathmandu in search of shelter have also struggled to find adequate public facilities for traditional funeral ceremonies.
Search and Rescue Operations Continue Meanwhile, military and police personnel continue search and rescue operations across flood-hit areas.
Their efforts have been hampered by damaged or severed roads, power outages and disruptions to communication networks.
Rescue teams are also working to deliver humanitarian supplies and maintain sanitation at temporary shelters to reduce the risk of infectious diseases.
Anadolu also report that in neighboring China, authorities reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing, including 261 foreign nationals.
Together, the reported figures from Nepal and China bring the death toll to 1,280 and the number of missing people to 5,624.
The flash floods struck the Nepal-China border on August 26 after a glacier at an elevation of about 5,200 meters broke away from Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal.
The collapse triggered a massive flow of ice, rocks and debris that swept through valleys along the border.
The resulting flash floods and mudslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts before reaching the Kathmandu Valley.
On the Chinese side, debris also buried the Gyirong border crossing in the southwestern part of the Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
Search teams remain deployed as authorities race to locate survivors, recover victims and provide assistance to communities whose homes and infrastructure were swept away by the disaster.

Credit: Sunita Neupane/IPS KATHMANDU, September 4 (IPS) - That day, Subash Tamang was mining sand along the banks of the Trishuli River near the Trishuli Hydropower Project, working alongside his wife, brother, sister-in-law, and two other family members.
Suddenly, he noticed water gushing down from above the hydropower site.
His first thought was that the dam had burst.
In an instant, everything changed.
He and his family dropped everything and ran toward the river, desperate to save their lives.
But then he saw something even more terrifying—huge waves of water were surging from the other side too, carrying clouds of dust and thick black mud.
“I couldn’t make sense of what was happening,” he recalls.
“It looked like a monster coming at us.” He was holding his wife’s hand, trying to run toward the hill, when the flood swept him away—carrying him nearly 500 metres downstream.
Helplessly, he watched as the same raging waters took his wife, his brother, his sister-in-law, and three other family members right before his eyes.
“I was holding her hand, and then the flood pulled her away,” he recalls.
His leg was broken in the disaster.
An army helicopter later rescued him and brought him to Kathmandu, where he is now receiving treatment at the Trauma Center.
“Our village has been reduced to ruins,” he says.

“I don’t know where to go after this.” Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, a professor at Kathmandu University, says the August 26 disaster started when a massive chunk of glacier and surrounding rock gave way at altitudes of about 5,200 to 1,200 metres above the Lhande River in Tibet, just across the border.
The falling ice and rock turned into a powerful slurry, sending a massive cascade of water, ice, and debris into the Lhande River in Tibet.
That surge triggered a devastating flood that raced downstream through the Bhotekoshi River, causing immense destruction.
The death toll from the disaster in Nepal has climbed to 1,114, with 3,996 people still unaccounted for, according to recent government figures.
Among the missing are Nepali Hindu pilgrims travelling to the sacred Kailash Mansarovar site in Tibet, as well as tourists from at least 39 countries.
Authorities have recovered bodies swept away by the floods from Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahun, Nawalparasi East, and Nawalparasi West districts.
Dr Bijay Jaisi, Director General of the Department of Roads, said initial assessments show flood damage to roads and bridges alone exceeds 30 billion rupees.
Around 80 km of roads have been washed away and another 40 km destroyed, while 35 concrete bridges have been damaged and 53 suspension bridges swept away.

The disaster has wreaked havoc on the region’s hydropower infrastructure: the Rasuwagadhi and Chilime projects have been destroyed, and at least 13 other hydropower projects under construction in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have sustained significant damage.
The Rasuwagadhi hydropower project was completely washed away by the flood.
Most Devastating Flood “This is one of the deadliest disasters in Nepal’s modern history,” said Dharmaraj Upreti, executive director of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
“We have never faced a flood this devastating and widespread before.” Such floods are not unique to Nepal.
In 2015, a similar disaster is believed to have killed around 200 people.

More recently, on July 8, 2025, a sudden outburst from a large glacial lake in Tibet sent a surge of water down the Lende River, sweeping away the Maitri Bridge at Rasuwagadhi and killing at least nine people.

Just three weeks later, on July 30, the Bhotekoshi flooded again, damaging roads and other infrastructure along the same corridor, according to Binod Parajuli, a senior divisional hydrologist at Nepal’s Flood Forecasting Division.
Arun Bhakta Shrestha, an expert on climate change and Himalayan glaciers, describes it as a “mountain tsunami”.
Kayastha explains that the disaster was first thought to have been triggered by a glacial lake bursting.
But satellite images showed something different: a large chunk of glacier on the Nepal side broke off and slid down.
Below it lay what experts call a “debris-covered glacier”—a mix of ice and gravel.
When that mass collapsed, the ice and its contents began to melt, releasing a surge of water from the glacial lake.
Because the terrain below is extremely steep, the mixture raced downhill at high speed, scouring the land next to the river and quickly turning into a devastating flood.

According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), research over 50 years of monitoring reveals that 89% of recorded years experienced a negative glacier mass balance.
Crucially, the rate of glacier ice loss doubled post-2000 compared to the preceding decades.

Between 1990 and 2020, Hindu Kush Himalaya glaciers lost roughly 12% of their total area and 9% of their estimated ice volume, amounting to a cumulative loss of up to 27 metres of ice thickness since 1975.
Arun Bhakta Shrestha explained that rising temperatures are melting the glacier’s surface, allowing meltwater to infiltrate the ice.
As this water percolates downward, it enlarges existing cracks and forms new fractures called crevasses.
“Crevasses are multiplying rapidly, and as more water pours into them, they grow both wider and deeper,” Sherstha said.
“Meltwater moving through the glacier can reach the bedrock below, undermining large ice masses until they collapse.
This is precisely the process we are witnessing now.
Rising temperatures are hastening the expansion of these fissures.” Kayastha said the crevasses on the glacier, which had persisted for several months, may have widened.
He added that analysing satellite imagery could have helped minimise the damage, but the images were not reviewed.

Climate Change Reshaping Nepal’s High Mountains Glaciologist Mohan Bahadur Chand warns that climate change is reshaping Nepal’s high mountains in ways that make new kinds of natural disasters more likely.
In recent years, he said, the landscape has become increasingly unstable.
Snow once accumulated gently and settled low on the slopes.
But as temperatures rise and glaciers retreat upslope, bare ground is becoming exposed.
Sections of rock and ice are now left “hanging” precariously on mountain faces.
“It will fall one day or another,” Chand said.

“We will see more such processes in the coming days.” Three days after the flood, Ekat Bahadur Thapa stood at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, pinning photographs of his son and nephew to the missing-persons board.
His son, 28-year-old Subindra Thapa, and his nephew, 33-year-old Resham Bahadur Thapa, were driving along the China–Nepal border that day.
Thapa said they called to tell him they were ready to transport people from Nepal into China and that they would return home soon.
When news of the flood broke, Thapa tried calling his son, but the call wouldn’t connect.
He told himself they must have found shelter on the Chinese side.
Still, by evening, there had been no word from either of them.
But as three days passed after the flood with no word from them, that hope began to fade.
He rushed from hospital to hospital across Kathmandu, desperately searching for survivors, but they were not there.
He went to the rivers where bodies had been recovered, hoping against hope.
“When they could not be found there either, he returned to his village with a heavy heart,” said Thapa, 58.
On Wednesday, eight days after they vanished, Thapa performed funeral rites according to Hindu tradition, believing the remains to be theirs.
Tears streamed down his face.
“How hard it must have been for them,” he said, his voice breaking.

“How many times they must have tried to escape.” He said, “May their souls rest in peace, wherever they are.” “The early warning system was delayed because we couldn’t detect the flood in time,” says Binod Parajuli, Senior Hydrologist at the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
“We were only able to act 15 minutes after the flood entered Nepal.
By then, damage had already occurred in Rasuwa.
When we finally sent out early warning messages to everyone, people assumed it wouldn’t be much worse than previous floods.
But the damage ended up being far greater.” Parajuli continued, “We couldn’t detect the flood early because it began outside our monitoring area.
By the time it reached Nepal, we had very little time to respond.

Our system sends SMS alerts when it detects rainfall, but this event did not begin with the kind of rain we normally monitor, making it difficult to issue timely warnings.” He added that this represents a distinct form of cascading, compounding debris flow, and that early-warning systems for such events have not yet been developed.
Kayastha said that last year, when the flood struck, the area was considered highly vulnerable.
The Nepal government was also advised to install an early warning system, which would not have been very expensive.
The plan included installing two water-level sensors, a monitoring station and cameras in the field so that people could receive flood information more quickly.
“We couldn’t save the people in the upper reaches, but we were able to save those downstream,” says Rajendra Mishra, Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment.
“This flood taught us that simply sending out a message is not the same as an early warning.” He said that it was important to understand exactly who and what was at risk.
Only then can we build a system that observes hazards in real time, communicates alerts effectively, and prepares communities for emergencies.

This flood was a warning: bigger floods could come again.” “Many people also failed to take the early warning seriously,” said Professor Dr Ranjan Kumar Dahal, an engineering geologist and geohazard expert.

“Warnings should be communicated in clear, simple language that everyone can understand.” Disaster Awareness Should Start Young He added that disaster awareness should also be included in school curricula from an early age so that people understand the risks and know how to respond.
The process of risk communication must be better understood.
Manish Raj Pandey, head of climate change at the National Trust for Nature Conservation, said the region’s topography is a key factor.

On August 26, 2026, a massive volume of bedrock and glacial ice broke loose 5,200 meters above sea level on the north side of Nepal’s Langtang range, triggering a “rock-ice avalanche” that crashed into the Lhende River on the Nepal-China border fueling the deadliest extreme flow disaster on record in the country.
This cascade barreled downstream at an average of ~160 kilometers per hour downstream toward the Nepal-China border.

It slammed into and overwhelmed Chinese border facilities at Rasuwagadhi just 7.5 minutes after the mountain gave way, then tore across the border and down the Bhotekoshi/Trishuli River corridor into Nepal, swallowing towns and causing extensive damage over 100 kilometers from its source.
As of 2:00pm ET on September 3rd a total of 1,259 people are confirmed dead and over 5,000 people are still reported missing.

These numbers include Nepalis living and working along the river corridor, hundreds of foreign tourists visiting the Langtang region and pilgrims crossing to Mount Kailash, and hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in tunnels.

The border town of Timure and the market hub of Syaphrubesi were essentially wiped away; 19 bridges and 40 kilometers of highway are gone, and more than 430 megawatts of hydropower capacity, representing more than 10% of Nepal’s national supply, is offline.
Cropped from Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response, Situation Response #3, Issued September 3, 2026.

Source: National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority (NDRRMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Nepal The residents of Nepal’s Rasuwa district, which includes a large Tamang population, have lived with disaster risk (e.g.
floods, landslides, earthquakes, and avalanches) for centuries and they have adapted to and managed these risks.
But the risks are changing fast, and the level of exposure communities face today is unprecedented.

I say this, having spent nearly 14 years conducting research in this river basin (in all of the affected settlements in Rasuwa), having led post-disaster relief activities in many of these towns after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, and having personally survived a massive glacier avalanche on the other side of the very same mountain, which led to years of research and direct engagement.
None of this is abstract to me, and my heart breaks for Rasuwa again.
A Cascade, Not a Rainfall Disaster This catastrophic event happened on a clear day.
Unlike many of Nepal’s recent disasters, it wasn’t triggered by extreme rainfall or an earthquake, and surprisingly, given the volume of water, there wasn’t a lake involved.

Post-event analysis points to an unexpected culprit: the sheer force of the rock-ice avalanche that became more flood-like as it gathered water, rock, and sediment and funneled through the Trishuli’s tight canyons, arriving downstream as a fast-moving wall of concrete.
This was a single, continuous, cascading extreme flow event.

Figure 1: Map of the impacted areas with timestamps for flood propagation (Source: CLaSH, Accessed September 2, 2026) Scientists are still working to establish whether climate change played a role in destabilizing the source area, and formal processes of evaluating attribution are now underway.
But the frequency of extreme flow events in recent years suggests that climate change is destabilizing the mountain cryosphere across the Himalayan region.
Simply put, warming and climatic volatility can impact glaciers, weaken permafrost, and drive rapid or unseasonal changes in snowpack.
In Nepal, climate-related risks interact with monsoon dynamics and seismic risk to compound danger in ways that existing monitoring frameworks aren’t built to see.

This event joins a grim and growing list of Himalayan cascading disasters — the 2021 Chamoli flood, the 2021 Melamchi disaster, the 2023 South Lhonak GLOF (Glacial Lake Outburst Flow), and the 2025 Blatten collapse in Switzerland.

Notably, a smaller glacial flood struck this exact watershed in July 2025, destroying the same border bridge and killing 19 people — a warning sign that didn’t translate into readiness for what came next.
Of Blind Spots and Needles in Haystacks It would be wrong to read this as a failure of Nepal’s early warning systems.

The source area sits in a genuine gap — a narrow sliver of unpopulated Nepali territory that drains north into China, falling between the scientific attention long focused on the south side of the Langtang range and the Chinese monitoring effort that intensified after last year’s flood.
Nepal’s gauge and station networks were built to catch monsoon floods and glacial lake outbursts, not a catastrophic flow that outran any possible alert.
But generating alerts for an event like this isn’t just a problem of data scarcity or blind spots, it’s also a problem of speed and scale.
The Himalaya has more slopes capable of failing this catastrophically, across more vertical relief, than anywhere else on Earth.

Scientists can and have highlighted a variety of high-risk areas and landforms, but finding subtle changes in a timely fashion requires skillfully separating signal from noise as risk changes across the Himalaya.
The overall point is that experts need a signal to effectively direct their tools and attention – and finding these signals can often feel like finding needles in Himalaya haystacks.
Of roughly a dozen extreme flow events in the region over the past decade, only one — the 2023 South Lhonak outburst — struck a site already flagged as risky.
Every other event originated from somewhere no one was watching, including this one.
Learning from Disasters Like This Each event offers lessons and insights that allow us to return with greater precision and a new understanding of where similar hazard chains might be stacking up.

For example, the 2024 Thame (GLOF) taught researchers that small glacial lakes can grow dangerously fast; last year’s transboundary flood event along the same Lhende River into Rasuwa showed that supraglacial lakes — lakes on top of glaciers — can expand and drain catastrophically.

Last week’s event highlights the increasing prevalence of another kind of risk: showing how an ice-rock avalanche can trigger a massive flood-like event and impact communities more than 100 kilometers downstream.

Tools are rapidly developing, but no single instrument will catch everything, so the approach has to be layered — weather stations and river gauges as a foundation, satellite monitoring to track remote terrain, seismic networks to triangulate a failure within seconds, and, critically, local observers such as herders, mountaineers, and fishers who can flag a crack or a filling lake long before a sensor does.
Even a few minutes of warning can be the difference between an evacuation and a recovery operation.

What the Stimson Nepal Early Warning Team is Doing In the wake of this event, on the Stimson Center’s Early Warning for Cascading Disasters in Nepal project team, working in Nepal and Washington, rapidly mobilized to assess the event, gather information, and share expert analysis with Government of Nepal institutions such as the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and government hydrologists and meteorologists.
Using Sentinel-1, Landsat, and Planet Labs imagery, we identified the avalanche’s source, ruled out a supraglacial lake we had assessed last year, and confirmed the landslide-dam mechanism.
We also tasked commercial radar/SAR imagery from ICEYE US over the source and blockage sites and delivered pre- and post-event comparisons to NDRRMA and Nepal’s Home Ministry within hours.

After two new lakes formed in the avalanche flowpath — one along the Lhende River, another high in the upper catchment — we worked with the NDRRMA to assess changing conditions, analyze breach scenarios, and provide scientific analysis of the flood pulses that came when the lake began to finally drain on August 30th.

Members of our team also contributed to the HIRISK rapid assessment, prepared by an international group of Chinese, Nepali, American, Austrian, Swiss, and Dutch scientists, which was published on August 28.

Lingering Risks and Uncertainties, in Both Nepal and China Risks remain throughout the region, and heavy rain could still reactivate destabilized slopes or remobilize other landforms within the impacted area.
Critically, the monsoon season is not yet over.
There are risks that we know of, such as risks from specific glacial lakes in China.
But we can’t discount the risks we are not yet aware of from other potential cascading hazards.
Monitoring these risks often requires both focused efforts on high-risk areas and triaging between uncertainties.
In this wake of this devastating event, we are already seeing better transboundary coordination between Nepal and China.
High-priority information is being shared and new channels of communication opened between Chinese and Nepali authorities — a promising, if overdue, shift.
A variety of people have called for greater formal coordination and the establishment of transboundary monitoring networks.
To be clear, no one — not Nepal, not China, not the international scientific community — could have identified the subtle changes and specific risks that triggered this disaster.

Forensic analysis is yielding new insights that we can use to search for similar risks in the future, but this event began with a sudden mass movement that turned into an extreme flow far too fast for a true alert to be shared.
The hope is that this disaster will catalyze the kind of sustained, cross-border monitoring and cooperation the region has needed for years.

Newswise — A water scientist at the University of Rhode Island, Soni Pradhanang is balancing the professional and the personal, watching her home country of Nepal make news after the recent glacial collapse and flooding there.

As a hydrologist with expertise in environmental science and water quality, flooding, and hazard communication, the events in her home nation are the subject she has made her career in since she left Nepal in 2001.

Pradhanang, in URI’s College of the Environment and Life Sciences, conducts research in runoff, flood, drought, and water quality modeling, and has served as a point of contact in URI’s prior work with Nepal.

In 2022, during her Fulbright tenure, she served as an instructor for a hydrological modeling training program in Kathmandu, part of a project on “Modeling Hydrological Response to Changes in Climate and Glacier in a Data-Scarce Glacierized Region in Nepal Himalaya.” The training covered core concepts in hydrology, climate change, and cold-region hydrology, providing early-career professionals with the tools to study these issues.
“This tragedy highlights the urgent relevance of this research,” she said.

Raised in Kathmandu, approximately 40 miles aerial distance from the affected area in Rasuwa/Langtang National Park, she shares insight into recent events, while keeping tabs on family members and loved ones there.
“For me, this is not an abstract scientific event,” Pradhanang said.

“It is a human tragedy affecting communities, families, livelihoods, and landscapes in my home country.” What were the contributing factors for the recent events in Nepal and has anything like this happened there before?

Based on the best available satellite imagery, seismic observations, and preliminary field interpretation, the disaster in northern Nepal appears to have begun with a rapid failure of a glacierized mountain slope in Langtang National Park near the Nepal–China border.
A very large mass of ice, rock, and debris descended into the valley, likely obstructing the Lhende Khola River temporarily.
When that unstable blockage failed or was overtopped, it released a powerful debris-laden flood that traveled downstream through the Lhende and Trishuli river valleys.
It is important to be careful about the cause.
The collapse itself generated seismic energy comparable to a magnitude 5.2 event; it should not automatically be described as an earthquake-triggered disaster.
Scientists worldwide are still determining the relative roles of steep terrain, fractured bedrock, glacier geometry, meltwater, rainfall or snowmelt conditions, and thawing permafrost.
Climate warming is a highly relevant background factor because it causes glacier retreat and can thaw the frozen ground that helps stabilize high-mountain rock and ice.
But attributing this particular collapse to one single factor would be premature.
Nepal has experienced destructive glacier- and landslide-related floods before, although every event has its own sequence of triggers.
Nepal has recorded 26 glacial lake outburst floods since 1977, including events originating both within Nepal and beyond its borders.
The Langtang region also has a history of serious mountain hazards, including earthquake-triggered avalanches in 2015 and recent floods and ice-rock avalanches in nearby valleys.

This event is especially notable because it appears to involve a rapid ice-and-rock avalanche and a temporary river-dam failure, rather than a conventional moraine-dammed glacial lake suddenly bursting.
A similar devastating event occurred in India in 2021, involving a rock-ice avalanche.
More recently, in 2024, a cascading glacial lake outburst flood event in Nepal's Thame Valley, triggered by a rock avalanche and a chain reaction of lake breaches, caused widespread destruction.
These past disasters highlight the growing danger.
Is there any technology that could provide a warning for an event like this?

No system can predict the exact moment when every slope or glacier will fail, or when a rock-ice avalanche will occur; that would defeat essentially every operational flood warning system in the world.
However, technology can provide critical warning—especially once a collapse, blockage, or sudden rise in river level begins.
A strong system would combine satellite monitoring with ground-based instruments.
Satellites can detect changes in glacier extent, new or expanding lakes, ground deformation, slope movement, and post-event flood extent.
On the ground, river-stage and rainfall gauges, time-lapse cameras, geophones or seismic sensors, and automated alarms can detect rapidly developing hazards.
Warnings then need to be distributed immediately via sirens, cell broadcasts, radio, local responders, and community networks.
In narrow, steep valleys, a debris flood may reach downstream settlements in minutes.
Therefore, the system must be automated, resilient to damage, powered and connected with backups, and linked to practiced evacuation plans.
Monitoring alone does not save lives unless people receive, understand, trust, and can act on the warning.
What can be done to lessen impact in events like this in the future?
We cannot eliminate all high-mountain hazards, particularly in a country with steep terrain, active geology, and rapidly changing glaciers.
But we can substantially reduce loss of life and damage.

While predicting these sudden events is incredibly difficult, especially when no immediate rainfall precedes them to trigger traditional flood warnings, several measures can be taken to mitigate the risks and protect vulnerable communities.

The most important actions are to identify hazardous slopes, glaciers, and glacial lakes; map the downstream pathways that floodwaters and debris would follow; install robust monitoring and warning systems; and ensure that communities, schools, hydropower operators, road agencies, and border facilities know exactly how to respond to an alert.
Risk reduction should include four inter-connected elements: Regular satellite and field monitoring of glacierized slopes, glacial lakes, landslide-prone areas, and thawing permafrost, if any.
Multi-hazard early-warning systems using river-level sensors, cameras, weather stations, seismic instruments, satellite data, and redundant communications.
Community preparedness: alarms, evacuation routes, safe assembly areas, drills, and warning messages that are understandable and accessible to everyone.
Critical facilities such as bridges, hydropower stations, roads, schools, and settlements should, when alternatives exist, be avoided in the highest-hazard flood corridors.
Where exposure already exists, structures and evacuation systems should be designed for rapid-onset debris floods, not only ordinary monsoon flooding.

For selected high-risk glacial lakes, direct interventions can also help—for example, carefully lowering lake levels, reinforcing or modifying unstable moraine dams, and coupling those interventions with locally managed warning systems.
Nepal has already implemented lake-lowering and community early-warning measures at Imja Tsho in the Everest region, demonstrating that targeted mitigation is possible.
Was the glacier that triggered the event considered vulnerable and how do researchers assess glaciers?
At this early stage, it is more accurate to say that the glacierized slope was demonstrably hazardous than to imply that the precise failure was fully predictable.

Researchers assess vulnerability by examining satellite imagery and aerial data, glacier retreat and surface changes, slope angles, fractures and crevasses, rock and ice volumes, evidence of permafrost thaw, nearby lakes, drainage pathways, and the likely consequences for people and infrastructure downstream.
Researchers assess the vulnerability of glaciers and glacial lakes, using satellite imagery to map their size, evolution, and growth over time.
This helps identify which lakes are expanding rapidly and are therefore potentially dangerous.
Pratik Singh Thakuri, a Ph.D.

student in my lab also from Nepal, has been actively acquiring and analyzing satellite imagery to better understand both the physical processes that drove this event and the extent of resulting damages.
Trained as a water resources engineer, he focuses his research on modeling floods and other extreme hydrologic events.
His work provides an important connection between remote-sensing observations of this disaster and the broader effort to understand, model, and reduce flood risks.
Pratik’s comparison of satellite-based images, from Aug.
26, 2026, look at the two scenes over the same geographic area, comparing the glaciers, surrounding slopes, avalanche pathways, valley floods, and downstream river corridors.

By comparing different time periods, scientists can piece together the development of an event and ascertain whether there were any visual changes in the glacier or adjacent region prior to the event.
Although this does not identify the cause of the event, it represents an important starting point for analyzing it.
When possible, teams conduct on-the-ground surveys to study glacial conditions, measure lake depth, assess the stability of moraine dams, and gather data for computer models.
Scientists integrate data on lake size, surrounding topography, and downstream population and infrastructure to assess risk.
A lake might be deemed "high risk" if a potential outburst could impact a populated area.
We use computer models to simulate what would happen if a lake were to breach, predicting the path, speed, and volume of a flood wave.
The key question is not only ‘Could a glacier or lake fail?’ but also ‘Who and what lies in the potential flow path?’ There are other sites of concern in Nepal and across the Hindu Kush Himalaya.

A 2020 assessment, by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development / United Nations Development Programme, identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes across the Koshi, Gandaki, and Karnali basins spanning Nepal, Tibet, and India—21 in Nepal, 25 in Tibet, and one in India.
These inventories are vital but need to be updated because glaciers, lakes, slopes, and downstream exposure are changing rapidly.
Could this kind of an event happen elsewhere and are there other areas that might be vulnerable or at-risk?

Similar cascading hazards can occur wherever steep, glacierized mountains contain unstable ice, thawing permafrost, fractured rock, glacial lakes, and communities or infrastructure in narrow downstream valleys.
The Hindu Kush Himalaya is a major concern, but the underlying processes also occur in the Andes, Alaska, western Canada, the European Alps, Iceland, and parts of Central Asia.

In a paper I co-authored in 2023, we discussed cascading hazards becoming more prevalent in the central Himalayas and how the need for an integrated modeling framework means more reliable prediction, with early warning systems essential for reducing impacts.
The specific hazard may differ by place.

In some valleys, the major concern is a glacial-lake outburst flood; elsewhere, it may be an ice avalanche, a rock-and-ice avalanche, a landslide-dammed lake, a rain-on-snow flood, or a compound event involving several of these processes.
Warming does not make every individual collapse directly attributable to climate change, but it is altering the conditions that affect glacier and permafrost stability in many mountain regions.

“I thought the water would only rise along the banks,” said Gokul Chitrakar, a farmer who lost everything.
He is now left with a 30 lakh bank loan taken just a few years back to build a house.
He was seen trying to pull clothes and other belongings from the wreckage.

“The smell is from bodies,” says Ramji Prasad Gojurel (70).
“There are human bodies and animal carcasses beneath the mud.

Garuda Aerospace Deploys Drones for Flood Relief Operations in Nepal IPO-bound Garuda Aerospace, one of India’s leading drone manufacturers, deploys drones in Nepal to support ongoing flood relief and emergency response operations in Rasuwa district, where severe flooding has caused widespread infrastructure damage and disrupted road connectivity, telecommunications networks and critical supply chains.

The deployment is aimed at strengthening relief efforts in affected areas by enabling rapid aerial assessment, supporting emergency response teams and improving access to regions where conventional rescue and relief operations remain challenging.

As part of the relief effort, Garuda Aerospace is deploying its Sanjeevani logistics drones, capable of carrying up to 25 kg, to enable point-to-point delivery of essential supplies, including food, medicines and water, to flood-affected and isolated communities.

To support sustained relief operations in the challenging mountainous terrain, the company is also providing battery systems, communication and ground-support equipment, along with certified drone pilots based on operational requirements, enabling relief teams to respond more efficiently and reach areas that remain difficult to access through conventional modes of transport.

Agnishwar Jayaprakash, Founder and CEO, Garuda Aerospace, said, “At Garuda Aerospace, we have always stepped forward to support communities during times of crisis and have been at the forefront of disaster relief efforts.
We are honoured to support Nepal and contribute to the ongoing relief efforts.
In difficult times, every effort counts, and we hope our drones and teams can help ensure essential supplies reach people in need, especially in areas that are difficult to access.

Our commitment is to stand alongside relief teams and communities and do everything we can to support the recovery efforts.” Garuda Aerospace has extensive experience in using drone technology for disaster response, emergency operations and humanitarian relief across India.

The company has supported ISRO-linked emergency medical supply operations using its White Knight drones, as well as relief efforts during the Chamoli glacier burst in Uttarakhand, floods in Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Chennai, locust-control operations in Rajasthan, and with the Indian Army in Jammu and Kashmir.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Garuda pilots and drones were airlifted on a chartered Air India aircraft to provide essential emergency services across India.

Garuda has also deployed logistics drones for medicine and food deliveries at ISRO’s Sriharikota facility, alongside loudspeaker-equipped surveillance drones to support rescue operations across the country.

In 2024, Garuda drones delivered food, water and medicines to rain-affected, inaccessible areas in Chennai, while in 2025, its consumer drone Droni supported the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) during the Srisailam Left Bank Canal (SLBC) tunnel collapse in Telangana, providing real-time mapping and video feeds to assist rescue teams in locating trapped workers.
The deployment in Nepal further reinforces Garuda Aerospace’s commitment to supporting rapid disaster response in challenging and hard-to-reach environments.

Photo: Suryams Upreti/AAP PHOTOS Australia is throwing more resources at search and rescue efforts in flood-devastated Nepal, with drone operators and victim identification experts joining the operation.
Australian rescue teams have landed in Nepal to join the search for those still missing after catastrophic floods swamped the country in August.

A 15-person Disaster Assistance Response Team arrived in Kathmandu late on Friday while additional support, including victim identification specialists, is also on the way upon the request of Nepali authorities.
A glacier collapse near Nepal's border with Tibet on August 26 triggered horrific flooding across towns and valleys.
The death toll in Nepal has passed 1300, while 4800 people are still missing including 601 foreign nationals, according to official figures released on Friday.
At least 36 Australians remain among the missing.
The death toll rose to 31 on the Tibetan side of the border on Friday, and Reuters reports some 531 people have been reported missing in the region.
A disaster assistance response team is in Kathmandu to provide aid and support.
(HANDOUT/DFAT) Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed on Thursday that local authorities would conduct searches in areas where many Australians were believed to have been when the floods hit.

"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Senator Wong told reporters.
The Disaster Assistance Response Team consists of specialists from the Queensland Fire Department and Fire and Rescue NSW.
Fire and Rescue NSW Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell farewelled six remotely piloted drone operators and four incident management specialists as they travelled to Nepal on Friday.
"I was proud to farewell our team this morning as they began their journey to Nepal to support communities impacted by this disaster," Mr Fewtrell said.
"Their drones will give search and rescue teams critical information about areas that may be inaccessible or too dangerous to reach from the ground.
"They have an important job ahead of them.
I wish them a safe deployment and, most importantly, a safe return home." Members of the Disaster Assistance Response Team have a tough task ahead.
(Suryams Upreti/AAP PHOTOS) The drone technology they will use has AI capabilities that can help locate victims, including thermal imaging that can be used to identify anyone trapped.
The Foreign Affairs Department is continuing to work with local authorities to establish the whereabouts of Australians affected by the disaster and contact next of kin where necessary.
This includes giving Nepali authorities telecommunication data to help establish the last known location of missing Australians.
The federal government confirmed on Friday that two more Australians had been found safe, bringing to seven the total number of Australians found since the floods.
Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane arrived in Kathmandu earlier in the week including more than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers.

US military provides humanitarian aid to Nepal flash flood victims Washington: The US military has joined humanitarian operations in Nepal after devastating flash floods killed more than 1,300 people, destroyed critical infrastructure and left thousands missing, including dozens of American citizens.
US forces are helping deliver urgent lifesaving supplies and equipment to affected areas, according to information released on the response.
At least 65,000 people were affected after floods struck several districts along Nepal’s border with China on August 26.
The rapid deployment underscored Washington’s commitment to Nepal and the partnership between the two countries, the material said.
The military response came as 30 members of the US Congress urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio to deploy additional American capabilities to support search-and-rescue operations.

“We write to urge the State Department to use every available resource to support ongoing search-and-rescue efforts following the catastrophic flash floods in Nepal and to ensure the safety and recovery of American citizens and others affected by this disaster,” the lawmakers said in a letter dated September 4.
The signatories included Indian American Representatives Ro Khanna, Raja Krishnamoorthi, Suhas Subramanyam, Pramila Jayapal and Shri Thanedar.
The lawmakers asked the State Department to provide daily updates to families and Congress, adequately staff consular hotlines and support repatriation services.
They also sought the deployment of a Disaster Assistance Response Team to assist with search, rescue, logistics and medical services.
The lawmakers called for high-altitude equipment, thermal and infrared drones, phone location data and satellite imagery to help locate people in difficult terrain.
They said the State Department should work with the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, other Defence Department agencies and commercial satellite companies.
“The scale of the catastrophe requires DART deployment as soon as possible,” the letter said.
The disaster was triggered by a glacial collapse and landslide in the Himalayas, which sent water, mud and debris through the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river corridors.
Roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure were destroyed.
The US has announced $500,000 through a global award with Catholic Relief Services and another $3.6 million in humanitarian assistance.
India has sent temporary shelters, blankets and medicine, while Britain, South Korea, China, the World Bank, the United Nations and humanitarian organisations have also offered assistance.

Highlighting the speed of India's response following the August 26 flash floods, Ambassador Srivastava noted that India has mobilised five relief flights packed with emergency supplies, and direct outreach with top Nepalese leadership began immediately.

The devastating flood that struck Nepal’s Lhende-Bhotekoshi corridor in Rasuwa District on August 26,, 2026, was not simply another flood in the Himalayan region.
Rather, it was a chain reaction of multiple events.
The event began with a high-altitude glacier disturbance and rapidly developed into a destructive flood and debris-flow event downstream.

The immediate cause of the event is still being investigated, and scientists are examining the roles of an ice-rock avalanche and the subsequent blockage and release of water in the Lhende river system.
However, the larger significance of the disaster goes beyond the question of what exactly triggered the flood.
The event highlights a broader problem in understanding Himalayan climate risk.
A hazard that begins several kilometres upstream can rapidly change the behaviour of a river and affect communities, infrastructure and livelihoods far at the downstream.

The disaster therefore needs to be understood as a cascading hazard, where different physical processes can interact and where the consequences of one event can create further risks to the downstream region.
This is not a completely new phenomenon in the Himalayan region.
The region has experienced several disasters in which one hazard has triggered another.
What is changing is the combination of a changing mountain environment with increasing human exposure in mountain valleys.
The 2026 Nepal disaster gave another example of why risk assessment in the Himalaya needs to move beyond looking at individual hazards separately and to multi-hazard assessments.
The history of Himalayan disasters has given important lessons in this regard, for example: one of the most well-known examples is the Dig Tsho glacial lake outburst flood in Nepal in 1985.

On August 4, 1985, the moraine-dammed Dig Tsho lake suddenly released a large volume of water, and this water travelled downstream and caused extensive damage, including the destruction of the nearly completed Namche Small Hydroelectric Project.
The event became an important example of the potential damage that a glacial lake outburst flood can cause to downstream infrastructure.
The August 2, 2014, Jure landslide in Nepal demonstrated a different type of cascading hazard.
A large landslide blocked the Sunkoshi River and created a temporary lake behind the landslide dam.
This created the possibility of a much larger flood if the blockage failed.
The event also affected roads, bridges and other infrastructure along an important transport corridor between Nepal and China.

The disaster showed that the risk from a landslide does not end at the location where the slope fails, rather it starts when a landslide blocks a river, the river itself becomes part of the hazard process.
The 2021 Melamchi disaster provided another example of how several processes can interact.

An assessment by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) found that the disaster involved several processes operating at different locations, including rainfall, high-altitude processes, landslides, river damming, outburst flooding, erosion and debris deposition.
The different processes interacted and increased the impact downstream.
ICIMOD highlighted the need for a more integrated approach to multi-hazard risk management rather than assessing individual hazards separately.
These events show that cascading hazards are not new in the Himalaya.

A sharp contrast The 2025 and 2026 floods in the Lhende river system provide a particularly important example because they involved different cryospheric processes within the same broader mountain environment.
On July 8, 2025, about 35 kilometres upstream from the Nepal-China border, a supraglacial lake on Tibet’s Purepu Glacier rapidly drained, causing a flash flood.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) of the Government of Nepal reports that the flood caused significant damage downstream as it moved along the Lhende river, also referred to as the Bhotekoshi river in Nepal.
Roads, bridges, hydroelectric plants, and the Rasuwagadhi dry port were all impacted by the catastrophe.
The NDRRMA report also used satellite observations to investigate the source of the flood.
Sentinel-2 imagery showed that supraglacial ponds began forming on the Purepu Glacier in March 2025 and expanded during the following months.
By July 7, the combined lake area had reached approximately 0.75 square kilometres.
On July 8, the lake area had decreased sharply and drainage features were visible on the glacier surface.
These observations supported the conclusion that rapid drainage of the supraglacial lake contributed to the downstream flood.

The death toll from the devastating flash floods in Nepal rose to 1,344 on Saturday as more bodies were recovered from the affected districts, police said.
Rescue teams continued to search for around 4,900 people who remain missing.

Of the total bodies recovered so far, 758 were adults, 85 were children and 501 were recovered with body parts missing, officials said, attributing the condition of the bodies to prolonged exposure to water and the weight of debris.
The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.
The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.
The disaster also killed at least 21 people on the Chinese side, while more than 500 people remain missing in Tibet, according to Chinese media reports.
In Nepal, around 360 bodies have been recovered in Chitwan district alone -- the highest among all districts.
Other districts from which bodies were recovered include Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Tanahun, Nawalparasi East and Nawalparasi West.
So far, 1,030 bodies have been temporarily buried after required procedures, including DNA collection, were completed.

Authorities continued to monitor water levels in several rivers, including the Koshi, Narayani, Bagmati, Karnali, Mahakali, Kankai, Kamal, Kamala, Babai, Eastern Rapti and Western Rapti, while joint rescue teams led by the Nepal Army continued search and rescue operations for the eleventh day.
The number of missing people was estimated at 4,898.
The missing include more than 600 children in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, officials said.
More than 13,000 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Major rescue operations were underway at hydropower projects in flood-affected districts, where hundreds of men are believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Teams of experts from India and China were assisting their Nepali counterparts in the operations.
On Friday, two men were rescued alive from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project.
They were identified as Kabir Maharjan, 45, a mechanical supervisor on the project, and Sanjay Sah, 30, a foreman, according to the Public Relations Directorate of the Nepal Army.

Nepali engineer Rabindra Hamal has recalled the terrifying moments he and his colleagues outran an oncoming torrent of water and mud to clamber to safety.
Hamal had been stationed at the hydropower plant by the Upper Trishuli river in Nepal's Rasuwa region on 26 August when colleagues working upstream sent them a dire warning.

The 46-year-old told the ABC that about 8:30am a colleague on the dam side of the river, about 10 kilometres upstream, relayed a message over the radio informing his team that disaster was heading their way.
"We immediately informed all our colleagues who were working with us in our office and rushed outside.

"Once we got outside, there was lots of confusion and panic around us." A video shared among his colleagues shows the moment a large wave engulfed the dam as workers fled for their lives, closer to the Tibet border.
Hamal said he and six others jumped in a vehicle and quickly started driving downstream to get as far away as possible.
He said they had only travelled 700 metres from their camp before they noticed a "large muddy wave" right behind them.
"It just looked like [something from a] Hollywood movie … I cannot even describe [it]," he said.
"We abandoned the vehicle … and started running towards higher ground.
"Fortunately, it was not the main flood wave because that gave [some of] us enough time to reach … safe ground.

"But unfortunately, we lost our two friends." He said the flood wave hit them but because of a small boulder in front of them, they were able to avoid the full impact of the wave and travel just five metres more to escape danger.
The engineer said two from his group of seven, a driver and cook, were not as lucky and were swept away in the floodwaters before they could reach higher ground.
A verified video circulating online shows the base camp with red coloured rooftops, where Hamal said his team were stationed, being destroyed by the flash flood just minutes after they escaped.

Violent shaking before second wave He said his group thought they were safe standing on a large boulder before the ground beneath their feet started "shaking violently" as a second, even larger floodwave approached.

"We were afraid that the rocks around us might fall … fortunately no rock fell and we were able to survive and stay their safely." Four hours later, the surviving group of five heard a helicopter in the distance but they could not wave it down.
Hamal said they spent the night covered in mud, on a boulder in the middle of the jungle.
"It was a very difficult and frightening night we experienced," he said.
"The next day, fortunately, we were rescued by helicopter, finally reached at home safely.
Rabindra said the flash flood looked like something from a Hollywood movie.

UN aims to raise nearly $50 million for Nepal flood response 4 September 2026 - The UN and its humanitarian partners launched a $49.6 million flash appeal on Friday to deliver emergency assistance to more than 84,000 people affected by last week's catastrophic floods in Nepal.

On 26 August, a glacier on the border between Nepal and the Tibet autonomous region of China collapsed, triggering floods that have now claimed more than 1,250 lives and left thousands missing, according to the UN's office in Nepal.
The UN's local humanitarian team estimate that 84,270 Nepalis - or 19,284 households - were affected by the floods.

Devastating toll Across the Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading regions of northern Nepal, critical infrastructure such as roads, schools, power grids and water systems have been damaged or destroyed, while many survivors have lost their homes and family members.

Working with Nepali emergency operations, the UN aims to help families buy essential goods, revitalise local economies, restore power, prevent disease outbreaks and help prepare residents for the upcoming winter.

Humanitarian workers will deliver direct cash assistance, cold-weather shelter materials, portable solar power units, water purification systems and food aid, while emergency mobile clinics will provide medical treatment and nutritional support.
"Families have lost everything: their loved ones, their homes, their livelihoods, swept away in minutes," said Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN's Resident Coordinator in Nepal.

"Working under the Government's leadership, this appeal will get cash, shelter, healthcare, clean water and protection to the hardest-to-reach communities before winter closes in." In a country where agriculture makes up 24 per cent of gross domestic product, half of which comes from livestock, according to the World Bank, aid teams will even help locals keep surviving animals alive and safe.
UNICEF aid influx But the UN Children's Fund (UNICEF) isn't waiting, and neither are other UN agencies, as they support rescuers still racing to find survivors.
On Friday, a flight supported by UNICEF and the European Union carrying 84 metric tonnes of humanitarian supplies landed in the capital Kathmandu.
