But in Chilime and across the flood-ravaged districts, mourning remains suspended between identification and hope.
Thousands of families still do not know whether they are waiting for a survivor or a body.
What Is Happening Inside the Chilime Tunnel?
Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava said the joint technical team was making steady progress despite challenging conditions.
“Safety rope connectivity to induct the team into the tunnel was successfully achieved,” he said in a social-media update.

“A large mud pump and a generator were brought in to clear slush and mud from the tunnel.” Rescuers are also constructing an approach road through controlled blasting, enabling larger equipment to reach the site.
The safety rope is crucial because the flooded tunnel presents several simultaneous risks.
Rescuers must move through mud and debris with limited visibility while guarding against unstable surfaces, water accumulation, falling material and further movement in the surrounding landscape.
The authorities have not disclosed how many people may be trapped inside the tunnel or how far rescue teams have penetrated.
The operation should therefore not be interpreted as confirmation that survivors or bodies have been located.
At this stage, progress means access.
Every metre cleared gives the teams another place to search.
Why Has the Rescue Become So Difficult?
The floods did not create a single, clearly defined disaster site.
They damaged roads, bridges, settlements, hydropower installations and other infrastructure across several districts.
Search teams are operating along river systems, inside tunnels and beneath enormous deposits of mud and debris.

Australian tunnelling expert Arnold Dix, who helped advise rescuers during the 2023 Silkyara tunnel operation in Uttarakhand, described the Nepal emergency as unlike anything he had previously encountered.

“Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved,” Dix wrote from the field.
The Silkyara operation involved 41 workers trapped inside a defined tunnel space.
Nepal’s rescuers are confronting multiple possible entrapment zones across a landscape altered by water, landslides and destroyed access routes.
The location of the missing may itself be uncertain.
Where Have the Bodies Been Recovered?
The official district-wise toll places Chitwan at the centre of the recovery operation, with 363 bodies found there.
Nawalparasi East has reported 223 bodies, followed by Nawalparasi West with 221, Nuwakot with 197 and Rasuwa with 169.
Gorkha has reported 75 deaths, Dhading 70 and Tanahun 38.
Together, these figures account for the official toll of 1,356.
The recovery geography also demonstrates how far the disaster travelled.
The Bhotekoshi flood devastated parts of Rasuwa before the impact spread into downstream areas along the Trishuli river system, including Nuwakot and Dhading.
Homes and roads were destroyed, communities were displaced and electricity, water supply and transport links were disrupted.
The largest concentrations of missing people have been reported in Nuwakot and Rasuwa.
Around 2,340 people remain unaccounted for in Nuwakot and approximately 1,967 in Rasuwa.
How Many People Have Been Rescued?
Nepal’s disaster authority said 13,396 people had been rescued by Monday.
More than 21,400 security personnel have been deployed across the affected areas, including 7,912 Nepal Police personnel, 9,287 soldiers and 4,203 members of the Armed Police Force.
The official update said treatment had been provided to 6,676 injured people through hospitals and medical teams operated by the Nepali Army and Armed Police Force.
Another 3,533 people are staying at 39 holding centres.
Nuwakot accounts for 2,651 of them, while 669 are in Rasuwa and 213 in Dhading.
The government has released emergency cash support to the most severely affected districts and local administrations.
Search operations, relief distribution and restoration work are proceeding simultaneously, stretching personnel and equipment across a wide disaster zone.
Why Has DNA Become Central to the Operation?
Floodwater, mud and prolonged exposure can make visual identification difficult or impossible.
Nepal’s disaster authority said the recovered remains include unidentified bodies and human remains.
Only 98 bodies had been handed over to families at the time of its update.

An Indian forensic team working at two Kathmandu laboratories has processed more than 1,200 DNA samples and generated approximately 292 DNA profiles, according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs.
Processing a sample and producing a usable profile are different stages.
A sample may be damaged, incomplete or require repeated laboratory work before forensic scientists can extract sufficient genetic information for comparison.
Families searching for missing relatives have been asked to provide DNA samples, photographs and documents establishing kinship through the relevant district police offices.
The profiles obtained from relatives can then be compared with those generated from unidentified remains.
For thousands of families, rescue has therefore entered its most painful phase: proving identity when recognition is no longer possible.
What About Indians Missing in China?
A parallel identification effort is under way across the border.
The Indian Embassy in Beijing has asked relatives of Indian nationals missing in China following the August 26 mudslide and flash flood to submit DNA data.
This is connected to the same wider Himalayan weather disaster but is distinct from the forensic operation taking place in Kathmandu.
Chinese authorities have agreed to receive DNA information relating to the missing Indians.
Families have been asked to submit the data in the internationally recognised Combined DNA Index System, or CODIS, format to the Indian Embassy, which will forward it for comparison.
The request indicates that the search is no longer confined to national boundaries.

Floods and mudslides across the Himalayan region affected Nepal as well as adjoining territory controlled by China, leaving foreign workers, travellers and local communities caught across different jurisdictions.
Why Is Nepal Observing National Mourning?
Nepal’s Cabinet declared Monday a day of national mourning for those killed in the floods.
The national flag was flown at half-mast at government institutions, embassies and diplomatic missions around the world.
The observance came as the country struggled to establish the disaster’s final human cost.
With 4,994 people still missing, the confirmed toll is likely to remain provisional.
The large number of unidentified victims also means many families have been denied the rituals that ordinarily follow death.
Nepal is mourning 1,356 confirmed lives.
Thousands more remain suspended in official records under one word: missing.
The immediate priorities are gaining deeper access to the Chilime tunnel, reaching isolated communities, clearing transport routes and identifying the recovered bodies.

The tunnel operation will depend on whether pumps can remove mud and water faster than they re-enter, whether the access road can support heavy equipment and whether the internal structure remains safe for rescuers.
Across the wider disaster zone, authorities must continue matching DNA, supporting displaced residents and restoring roads, power and drinking-water supplies.
The number rescued—13,396—demonstrates the scale of the mobilisation.
The number missing—4,994—defines everything still unfinished.
In Chilime, a rope now extends into the darkness.
Behind it will come rescuers, pumps and machinery.
For the families waiting outside, it carries something far more fragile.
A route towards an answer.

Nepal has fallen silent for a national day of mourning as families mark 13 days since catastrophic floods tore through the Himalayas, killing more than 1300 people and leaving thousands more missing.
Flags were lowered to half-mast at government offices on Monday as families completed traditional Hindu mourning rituals for those killed in the August 26 disaster.
But for thousands of families, there is still no body to farewell.

About 5000 people remain missing across Nepal and Tibet, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency, as increasingly desperate relatives demand more be done to find their loved ones.
Several families performed symbolic funerals on Monday despite their relatives remaining missing, allowing them to complete important final rites without their bodies.
In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning traditionally lasts 13 days, with rituals performed on the final day to pray for the souls of the dead.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said.

“The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.” Authorities say rescue operations are focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.
Teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States are searching debris, damaged buildings and tunnels, with glimmers of hope emerging in recent days.
Two Nepalese workers were pulled alive from a hydropower tunnel on Friday, while a Chinese man was rescued on Saturday.
Among those still desperately waiting for news are Australian families.

He has chartered a helicopter, tracked her last phone signal and repeatedly approached authorities for information.

“Our government is trying, but it’s not enough.” A group of Australian families has also called for greater transparency from tour operators and authorities as 36 Australians remain among the missing.
Australia has deployed a disaster assistance response team and specialist resources to Kathmandu and committed $11 million to the response.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged the agonising wait facing families on Monday.
“This is now very much a race against time,” Mr Albanese told Parliament.

Two weeks after a glacier collapse on the flank of Langtang Lirung sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli valleys, Nepal's government has begun the arithmetic of rebuilding — and the numbers are outrunning the country's ability to pay for them.

Officials in Kathmandu now expect a formal Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, due within five weeks, to put losses at least 30% above the initial estimate of 400 billion rupees, implying a reconstruction bill of $4 billion to $5 billion for a country whose debt has already swelled since the 2015 earthquake.

The official toll on the Nepali side stands at 1,377 confirmed dead, 5,326 missing and 6,827 injured, with no new survivors reported since the weekend rescues that briefly turned recovery back into rescue.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Kathmandu Post that the government prefers grants and aid over loans, and on Tuesday instructed senior diplomats to press that preference with foreign governments and institutions.

"Given the way the loan portion is ballooning compared to our GDP, if we are able to generate grants and aid in a considerable amount, it would be easier for us," he said, while acknowledging that declining loans is "not a declared policy." Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said grants were always preferred but could not meet all of Nepal's needs.

Govinda Raj Pokharel, who oversaw the needs assessment after the 2015 earthquake, was blunter: in the current financial architecture, he said, "it is almost impossible to receive sufficient grants," and Nepal should reach out to wealthy individuals and philanthropies while also considering soft loans.

The National Planning Commission's assessment will form the basis for a donor conference; the government also plans to file a claim with the global Loss and Damage Fund, arguing that climate change contributed to the flood's severity.
A senior official said the sum sought there might be symbolic but could "open more avenues for us to claim compensation." The scale of the damage explains the gap.
Initial assessments count 7,570 houses destroyed or damaged and 32,933 people directly affected across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts.

The Nepal Electricity Authority says 13 hydropower projects were hit, removing an estimated 431 megawatts from the grid and damaging projects under construction with a further 470 megawatts of capacity; the Independent Power Producers' Association puts losses at a dozen plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot alone at 25 to 30 billion rupees, a figure it says is provisional because its members are still occupied with searches.

Along the Trishuli, whole commercial strips such as Trishuli Bazar stand as gutted concrete frames, the ground floors sheared away or buried under gray sludge, and rescuers say the riverbed rose 30 to 50 feet in places, shifting the river's course over what were once tunnel entrances.

The needs assessment is expected to recommend changes to settlement patterns, river-basin planning and the relocation of people from high-risk areas — recommendations that would require funding beyond reconstruction itself.
The search has not formally ended.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah declared a shift toward rehabilitation last week after teams entered the last of the hydropower sites where active operations were under way and found no one; the weekend rescues of two hydropower workers from the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a Chinese worker from a flooded tunnel in Rasuwa, and a 60-year-old woman from a collapsed building in Nuwakot forced crews to keep listening at tunnel mouths.

At least 557 workers remain missing from Trishuli 3A, about 115 of them believed to have been in the main tunnel when the water hit, and roughly 900 hydropower workers across a dozen projects are still out of contact.
One of the rescued men told rescuers that more people remained alive in the tunnel; no further survivors have been reported.

The Electricity Authority has asked relatives of missing workers to submit DNA samples, and mass burials with forensic documentation continue in the Devghat forest in Chitwan, nearly 200 kilometers downstream, where the river continues to return bodies.

The missing include, by the government's count, 147 officials — police, soldiers, customs and immigration staff, teachers and local representatives — as well as some 622 students and roughly 300 trade and transport workers who were at the Gyirong border crossing when the surge struck within minutes of the collapse.
Hundreds of foreign nationals remain listed as unaccounted for on the Nepali side, among them dozens of Americans the U.S.
State Department has said it continues to track, along with citizens of Ukraine, Malaysia, Britain and Canada.

On the Chinese side, where 16 deaths and 546 missing were reported, Reuters described search teams picking through the ruins of the Gyirong port, once the busiest land crossing between the two countries; Chinese state media say more than 2,500 rescuers have been deployed there and the road to the border has been largely reopened along a route cut into the riverbank.
Nepal's handling of foreign assistance has been selective by design.

The government initially declined offers of foreign search-and-rescue teams, citing the coordination problems of the 2015 earthquake response, before admitting specialists from India, China, Australia and South Korea for tunnel rescues, DNA testing and forensic work.

More than 9,300 Nepali soldiers remain deployed for medical care, road clearance and patrols, and army engineers have been erecting temporary iron bridges to reconnect communities cut off since the flood destroyed their crossings.

The Kathmandu Post reported Tuesday that the collapse of the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir, the main road west from the capital, has engineers urging urgent stabilization and a permanent tunnel or bridge, and that tourist hubs across the country have emptied in what should be peak trekking season — a second economic blow for a country where tourism is a principal source of foreign exchange.
The danger upstream has not passed.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology has kept the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli under high flash-flood warnings with rain continuing in the upper catchment, and the debris-dammed lake that formed above Gyirong after the collapse remains under watch; Chinese authorities say the risk has been reduced but not removed.

A rapid assessment by an international scientific consortium found that pre-event satellite imagery showed visible signs of instability — meltwater discharge and cracks in surrounding bedrock — in the days before the collapse, findings that have renewed calls for early-warning systems and cross-border data sharing.
The same corridor flooded fourteen months earlier, killing nine and destroying the friendship bridge at the border.
That history is the subtext of the financing debate.

Nepal borrowed heavily to rebuild after 2015 and is now being asked to borrow again for a disaster its officials describe as climate-driven, in a valley where the last flood was still being repaired when this one arrived.

Whether donors treat the Bhotekoshi flood as a one-time catastrophe to be funded with grants, or as the first installment of a recurring bill to be met with loans, will be decided at the donor conference the needs assessment is meant to prepare — and it will shape not only what Nepal rebuilds but where, and whether the settlements along the Trishuli are rebuilt at all.

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug.
26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.
Monday was the 13th day since the flooding which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.
In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects.
Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.
Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals.
Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.
The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.
Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.

In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.
Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.
Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood.
The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.
“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said.

“The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.” Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site.

He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.” Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.
Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.
Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.
Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

“Today is the ninth day, still family members are waiting, maybe.
They hope that they will be back,” Sapkota said.
Sapkota is waiting for an update on a childhood friend and his middle school teacher.
No one has heard from them since the floods.
Flooding described as sudden The U.S.
Geological Society said the speed of the water combined with 30-foot waves washed out towns within minutes.
Subash Baniya, healthcare coordinator with the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said the flooding caught people off guard.
“That wasn’t something that people were anticipating or like anything like that, because it happened out of nowhere,” Baniya said.
UNL student reflects on nearby hometown Sandeep Sharma, a Ph.D.
student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and president of the Nepalese Student Association at UNL, was born in Nuwakot, nine miles from the flood site.
“You really can’t not look at all of those, like, videos or not feel for the families that have had their family members missing or look at their stories and see how difficult it is,” Sharma said.
Society organizes relief efforts The Nebraska Nepalese Society has created GoFundMe pages, reposted flyers for missing people and spread awareness about Nepal this week.

“I think one of the biggest things that we have seen in a crisis like this is how different communities and people from all over the world have really come together to help people in need of this crisis,” Sharma said.

“It has been a really humbling experience for all of us because there are different communities, different people really trying their best in order to help and support these victims and the families impacted,” Sharma said.

NUWAKOT, Nepal: A delirious Kabir Maharjan drifted in and out of consciousness in a pool of muddy water in complete darkness, trapped for nine days in a tunnel beneath the wreckage of Nepal's worst flood disaster in decades.
When he finally awoke at a hospital after a miracle rescue, he did not recognise his wife.
Confused, he asked her why she had not given him a bed sooner.

Maharjan was one of hundreds of hydropower workers believed to have been buried when a glacier collapsed above Nepal's Trishuli valley on Aug 26, unleashing a wall of mud and water that killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands missing across Nepal and neighbouring Tibet.
He and mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah survived in an air-filled chamber, said lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane, a veteran tunnel engineer who helped lead the rescue effort.

Their rescue against the odds has given hope to search teams working at the sites along the devastated valley that some of the 121 workers still believed to be trapped in tunnels as of Monday (Sep 7) are still alive.

Reuters has reconstructed the full story of the men's survival and the frantic effort to save them through exclusive interviews with a dozen people, including the previously unreported accounts shared by relatives, engineers, government officials and rescuers directly involved in the operation and a review of site documents, maps, and internal conversations between rescuers.
THE MORNING At 7.30am local time on the day of the disaster, Maharjan called his wife before his shift at the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project.
“I have to go inside the tunnel,” he told her.

“There won’t be any network inside.” Around 60 minutes later, a glacier collapsed at the Langtang Lirung mountain some 25 miles upstream, causing a landslide so powerful that it formed a wall of water that flattened villages and submerged a network of 12 hydropower projects with nearly 900 workers inside.
In the capital Kathmandu, electricity department officials were monitoring the projects' power supplies on their screens.
Then the fields started going blank — one after another, stations disappearing from the control panels, falling like dominoes.
Suraj Dahal, an engineer at the Nepal Electricity Authority who led parts of the rescue effort, said he was not immediately alarmed because "floods are normal" in Nepal.
Because the 3A station manager was abroad, it took officials two extra minutes to reach out on call to the roughly 40 workers estimated to be inside.
By then, at least two hydropower projects upriver had already been hit.

— two minutes after Maharjan's wife, Hira Shova Maharjan, had tried and failed to reach him —officials gave the final order to 3A:"Evacuate!" Sah, who worked in the power house's control room, sped from floor to floor, warning colleagues individually, he later told rescuers.
Outside the tunnels, evacuating workers tried to run away from the flood, but were not fast enough.
Officials pointed to footage showing a group of roughly 30 workers swept away by a wave many times their height.
Rescuers later identified an escape ladder which, had workers known of it, could have saved as many as two-thirds of those inside,said Dahal.
But they "didn't know where to go," he said.

Of the tunnel's four access routes, engineering drawings seen by Reuters showed one ran more than 180 meters to the underground powerhouse — but rescuers believed it was fully flooded, offering no hope of survivors.
Neupane instead turned his attention to a shorter cable-duct tunnel that sloped upward and was less exposed to the floodwaters.
It was there that Maharjan and Sah had taken shelter, just 160 meters from the exit — "at the corner, at the edge of the tunnel," as Maharjan would later describe it to his wife.
FEAR OF THE WORST For the next nine days, the air pocket that had saved their lives became their prison.
Sah said he recited Hindu prayers to keep his courage.
Maharjan sipped the same muddy water he slept in to stay alive,his wife said.
When Hira Shova first heard about the flood, she assumed the powerhouse would be safe.
She tried calling her husband, colleagues, anyone who might know something.
When officials later showed her photographs of where the site entrance once stood — now a bare riverbank — she told herself, "he couldn't possibly be alive".
"Deep down in my heart, a terrible hopelessness was setting in," she recalled, but to her sons, 15 and 10, she kept up a brave front.
RACE AGAINST THE MOUNTAIN Officials believed that oxygen pockets scattered through the wreckage might help some workers survive.

With more than 7,500 houses destroyed across the valley, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, rescuers had to make brutal triage decisions about where to dig first.
But 3A ranked near the top of the list because officials hoped its multi-story structure of turbines and ventilation floors might have trapped pockets of air.
Lawmaker and engineer Sagar Dhakal, along with Neupane, reached the site by army helicopterthe day after the disaster.
They found heavy machinery couldn't move in immediately; the debris was too saturated.
"Everything you drop on that place just goes under," said Prakash Pokhrel, a geologist with Nepal's disaster management authority.
Crews first had to build a stable platform before any excavation could begin.
Serious digging didn't start until three days after the disaster.
All four tunnels were blocked — mud, rock, timber and debris, some of it buried under 15 to 30 meters (49 to 98 feet) of landslide material.
Rescuers turned to drilling, controlled blasting and heavy equipment to inch a path forward.
A breakthrough came when a 5-inch borehole drilled from above finally confirmed the tunnel's true alignment, giving crews a fixed point to dig toward.
Several nights, downpours refilled the excavated shaft with fresh water and debris, undoing hours of work in minutes.
It took rescuers nearly six days just to reach the tunnel's buried entrance, said Amshu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal Electricity Authority.
When they called out for survivors, nobody answered.
THE BREAKTHROUGH The night before the survivors were found, rescuers hit a wall of mud-clogged debris they couldn't move.
Dhakal's crew improvised, tapping a natural channel some 15 meters above the tunnel and forcing water through it with a high-pressure jet that cleared 4 to 5 meters in minutes during testing.
Then the rain came again, triggering a partial collapse that briefly trapped several rescuers themselves.
The operation stalled for hours before colleagues talked them back inside, and crews reinforced the passage with metal sheeting and gabion wire.
on the 10th day, Dahal got a call from a heavy equipment operator: the rescuers had heard something.
Maybe just an echo of the rescuers' own voices calling into the dark.
On the ground, Ganga Baral, who led the rescue team, said they began to hear noises as they drilled into the tunnel.
Again and again, they cut their machines' engines to listen.
"We would call out, 'Where are you?
"Sometimes it felt like there was a person alive trying to communicate with us." They still couldn't make out words — but they now estimated the source was just 15 to 20 meters away.
Then, in the beam of a light, they saw a hand.
Another 5 to 10 meters of mud-choked passage stood between them and the survivor.
By 7 a.m., soldiers broke open a small hole.
From inside came a single word:"hunuhuncha", which loosely translates to "we are here".
INTO THE LIGHT Neither man could stand when rescuers finally pulled them from the tunnel.
Sah, his face caked in mud, had to be carried out on a rescuer's back.
He managed to lift one hand toward a camera.
Maharjan, with more severe injuries, went out on a stretcher.
"Mummy, Papa is back!"his sons shouted when they heard.
Dhakal, who ran the operation from outside but never entered the tunnel himself, wept when the two men emerged.
"I couldn't hold my tears," he said.
The following day Chinese national LuHaitao wasfound in the tunnel of a separate station, the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project.
At the hospital, doctors operated on a deep, infected wound on Maharjan's leg, his wife said.
When Hira Shova walked into the hospital room, he did not recognise her.
“Where am I?” he asked her.
But she was just thrilled to get him back alive.

NUWAKOT/KATHMANDU/UPPER TRISHULI 3A HYDROPOWER STATION - A delirious Kabir Maharjan drifted in and out of consciousness in a pool of muddy water in complete darkness, trapped for nine days in a tunnel beneath the wreckage of Nepal’s worst flood disaster in decades.
When he finally awoke at a hospital after a miracle rescue, he did not recognise his wife.
Confused, he asked her why she had not given him a bed sooner.

Maharjan was one of hundreds of hydropower workers believed to have been buried when a glacier collapsed above Nepal’s Trishuli valley on Aug 26, unleashing a wall of mud and water that killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands missing across Nepal and neighbouring Tibet.
He and mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah survived in an air-filled chamber, said lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane, a veteran tunnel engineer who helped lead the rescue effort.

Their rescue against the odds has given hope to search teams working at the sites along the devastated valley that some of the 121 workers still believed to be trapped in tunnels as of Sept 7 are still alive.

Reuters has reconstructed the full story of the men’s survival and the frantic effort to save them through exclusive interviews with a dozen people, including the previously unreported accounts shared by relatives, engineers, government officials and rescuers directly involved in the operation and a review of site documents, maps, and internal conversations between rescuers.
The morning At 7.30am on the day of the disaster, Maharjan called his wife before his shift at the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project.
“I have to go inside the tunnel,” he told her.

“There won’t be any network inside.” Around 60 minutes later, a glacier collapsed at the Langtang Lirung mountain some 40km upstream, causing a landslide so powerful that it formed a wall of water that flattened villages and submerged a network of 12 hydropower projects with nearly 900 workers inside.
In the capital Kathmandu, electricity department officials were monitoring the projects’ power supplies on their screens.
Then the fields started going blank – one after another, stations disappearing from the control panels, falling like dominoes.
Suraj Dahal, an engineer at the Nepal Electricity Authority who led parts of the rescue effort, said he was not immediately alarmed because “floods are normal” in Nepal.
Because the 3A station manager was abroad, it took officials two extra minutes to reach out on call to the roughly 40 workers estimated to be inside.
By then, at least two hydropower projects upriver had already been hit.

At 9.15am – two minutes after Maharjan’s wife, Hira Shova Maharjan, had tried and failed to reach him – officials gave the final order to 3A: “Evacuate!” Sah, who worked in the power house’s control room, sped from floor to floor, warning colleagues individually, he later told rescuers.
Mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah is rescued alive from a tunnel at the Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project.
PHOTO: REUTERS Outside the tunnels, evacuating workers tried to run away from the flood, but were not fast enough.
Officials pointed to footage showing a group of roughly 30 workers swept away by a wave many times their height.
Rescuers later identified an escape ladder which, had workers known of it, could have saved as many as two-thirds of those inside, said Dahal.
But they “didn’t know where to go,” he said.

Of the tunnel’s four access routes, engineering drawings seen by Reuters showed one ran more than 180m to the underground powerhouse – but rescuers believed it was fully flooded, offering no hope of survivors.
Neupane instead turned his attention to a shorter cable-duct tunnel that sloped upward and was less exposed to the floodwaters.
It was there that Maharjan and Sah had taken shelter, just 160m from the exit – “at the corner, at the edge of the tunnel,” as Maharjan would later describe it to his wife.

Sah said he recited Hindu prayers to keep his courage.
Maharjan sipped the same muddy water he slept in to stay alive, his wife said.
When Hira Shova first heard about the flood, she assumed the powerhouse would be safe.
She tried calling her husband, colleagues, anyone who might know something.
When officials later showed her photographs of where the site entrance once stood – now a bare riverbank – she told herself, “he couldn’t possibly be alive”.
“Deep down in my heart, a terrible hopelessness was setting in,” she recalled, but to her sons, 15 and 10, she kept up a brave front.

With more than 7,500 houses destroyed across the valley, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, rescuers had to make brutal triage decisions about where to dig first.
But 3A ranked near the top of the list because officials hoped its multi-storey structure of turbines and ventilation floors might have trapped pockets of air.
Lawmaker and engineer Sagar Dhakal, along with Neupane, reached the site by army helicopter the day after the disaster.
They found heavy machinery couldn’t move in immediately; the debris was too saturated.
“Everything you drop on that place just goes under,” said Prakash Pokhrel, a geologist with Nepal’s disaster management authority.
Crews first had to build a stable platform before any excavation could begin.
Serious digging didn’t start until three days after the disaster.
All four tunnels were blocked – mud, rock, timber and debris, some of it buried under 15m to 30m of landslide material.
Rescuers turned to drilling, controlled blasting and heavy equipment to inch a path forward.
A breakthrough came when a 12.7cm borehole drilled from above finally confirmed the tunnel’s true alignment, giving crews a fixed point to dig toward.
Several nights, downpours refilled the excavated shaft with fresh water and debris, undoing hours of work in minutes.
It took rescuers nearly six days just to reach the tunnel’s buried entrance, said Amshu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal Electricity Authority.
When they called out for survivors, nobody answered.

Dhakal’s crew improvised, tapping a natural channel some 15m above the tunnel and forcing water through it with a high-pressure jet that cleared 4m to 5m in minutes during testing.
Then the rain came again, triggering a partial collapse that briefly trapped several rescuers themselves.
The operation stalled for hours before colleagues talked them back inside, and crews reinforced the passage with metal sheeting and gabion wire.
At 4am on the 10th day, Dahal got a call from a heavy equipment operator: the rescuers had heard something.
Maybe just an echo of the rescuers’ own voices calling into the dark.
On the ground, Ganga Baral, who led the rescue team, said they began to hear noises as they drilled into the tunnel.
Again and again, they cut their machines’ engines to listen.
“We would call out, ‘Where are you?

Another 5m to 10m of mud-choked passage stood between them and the survivor.
By 7am, soldiers broke open a small hole.
From inside came a single word: “hunuhuncha”, which loosely translates to “we are here”.

Sah, his face caked in mud, had to be carried out on a rescuer’s back.

Maharjan, with more severe injuries, went out on a stretcher.

Tsering Phuntsok watched news of the Nepal-Tibet flood unfold from thousands of miles away in southern India.
The 46-year-old Tibetan in exile has missing family members on both sides of the border; those in Nepal are named in official government lists, but in Tibet he has received no information.
“I have started praying for the lost ones now.

I have to accept they will not return [because] … I’m not getting any information.” The flooding disaster is an example of the increasing use by Chinese authorities of “Clean Internet 2026”, the latest version of a long-running campaign by the Ministry of Public Security that criminalises anything officials regard as false information, which includes unofficial accounts of the floods.

It follows a well-established playbook in which authorities promote official narratives, suppress independent accounts, discourage efforts to look back at the causes of a disaster and punish those who post claims that differ from the government-approved narrative.

While earlier versions of the campaign focused on cybercrime and hacking, it is increasingly being used to target what the authorities call “rumours” which include unofficial information about the disaster.
“The campaign serves a dual purpose.

Tackling genuine problems like fraud and misinformation while tightening control over public narratives,” says Tencho Gyatso from the International Campaign for Tibet, a US based Tibetan advocacy group.
“That dual purpose is what makes it more nuanced and challenging to criticise.” In the hours after the floods, researchers say they saw a huge surge in interest across Chinese social media.
The topic was trending, but then fell away as comments were removed in real time.

Photograph: Tingshu Wang/Pool Reuters/AP Screenshots seen by the Guardian show the Chinese app WeChat restricting posts about the floods.
In one case, a user was notified by WeChat that a post about the flooding had been reported and then deleted for containing “politically sensitive content”.
Another was stopped from being shared.
It was said to be “unavailable due to policy violation” and that it contained “prohibited content”.
“[The trend] was constantly shifting and being manipulated because there was real interest,” says David Bandurski, director of the China Media Project, a research group that monitors Chinese media.
“A ‘crackdown’ is not the right word, because they don’t crack down.

It’s a consistent, persistent, everyday application of a policy of public-opinion guidance.” On 30 August, four days after the disaster, police in Tibet reported 10 cases under the Clean Internet 2026 campaign relating to “rumours” about the disaster.
In the majority of cases there were claims that more than 1,000 people had been swept away in the floods.
So far, Chinese authorities have released a death toll of 43.
Human rights and Tibetan advocacy groups have accused the Chinese government of concealing the true scale of the death toll.
The police notice said that spreading of “rumours” “misleads the public and disrupts online order” and it intended to “ensure that disaster relief work proceeds smoothly”.
A user from Jiangxi, a province 3,000km away from the disaster, posted on a video platform claiming “the number of missing people had risen to 826”.
According to the police report the user faced “administrative punishment” without specifying what that involved.

‘Proving that the state is working hard’ One former Chinese state media journalist, who agreed to speak on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals, says control in times of crisis also works through simple omission of information as much as suppression: “Official news coverage devotes enormous space to proving that the state is working hard, but gives very little information answering the most basic questions: who is missing?
Where were they last seen?
Which buildings have been searched?
“Controls have become much stricter, especially regarding the internet, though there are nuances, as there are still ways to bypass restrictions.
For instance, by posting quickly or using veiled language to get content through,” they say.

But allowing some reporting can serve the interests of central authorities, says one former CGTN editor who worked at the broadcaster during the Covid pandemic and who also asked not to be named for fear of reprisals.

“But if journalists are given completely free rein to uncover and publish those truths, they may expose things that are politically uncomfortable or challenge the interests of the state.” Bandurski says: “The [Communist] party sees itself in a global public-opinion struggle.
It is wrestling with the world fighting to get its view out.
This is how China sees information globally, in a very, very oppositional framework.” Phuntsok hopes his family on the Nepal side could still be alive.

On the Tibet side he is unwilling to share the names of his missing relatives with the Guardian for security reasons.

"We must look beyond offering food grains for Rs 2 per kg to flood victims", the witty leader can be heard saying in his trademark style.
Prasad also claimed, "Bihar is reeling under the worst floods in a decade.

Notably, the RJD president's son and heir apparent Tejashwi Yadav, who is the leader of the opposition in the state assembly, had recently written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, seeking financial assistance to Bihar and declaration of the floods as a "national disaster".

Earthquake seismograph NEW DELHI: An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck Nepal at 9.38 pm on Tuesday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, as the region continues to grapple with the aftermath of devastating flash floods that have killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal.The tremor was reported hours after a magnitude 5.3 earthquake struck Tibet, according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC).

The Tibet quake occurred at a depth of 35 km.The latest tremors come days after another earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck Tibet on Thursday last week, according to data from the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ).

That earthquake was recorded at a depth of 10 km.The earthquakes come as the Tibet-Nepal region continues to reel from devastating flash floods that struck on August 26.The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, sending a massive surge of water and debris downstream through the Bhotekoshi River.

The disaster devastated settlements across northern and central Nepal and damaged several hydropower projects.Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the death toll from the floods had risen to 1,357 as of Tuesday, with rescue teams continuing searches for 5,326 people.A total of 13,583 people had been rescued.Security forces recovered hundreds of bodies from affected districts including Chitawan, Nawalparasi East and West, Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Gorkha, Dhading and Tanahu.

Authorities said 102 bodies had been handed over to families after identification and completion of legal formalities.At least 43 people were also killed on the Chinese side, while more than 500 remained missing in Tibet, according to Chinese media reports.The floods washed away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaged hydropower infrastructure.

Rescue operations were also underway at hydropower projects where 121 people were believed to be trapped in underground tunnels.The disaster has also raised concerns over the fragile environment of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, with Chinese climate experts pointing to rising temperatures, accelerated glacier melt, local geological and geomorphological conditions and broader climatic influences as possible contributing factors.Sun Xiaoguang, head of the Meteorological Observatory of the Tibet Autonomous Region, said: “According to our monitoring, we can see the short-time rain days, or the imbalance of the rain pattern and the rising of the temperature in Tibet.”He said the region could be affected by the climate change crisis and that extreme weather events in China could become more frequent.Chinese officials said Tibet has about 33,000 glaciers, including 187 classified as high-risk and requiring round-the-clock satellite monitoring to predict possible collapses, according to PTI.Kang Shichang, director and researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said glaciers across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau had shrunk by about 24% in area over the past six decades.In the southern part of the plateau, including the Himalayas, glacier coverage had fallen by about 40% over the same period, Kang told Chinese daily The Paper, attributing the retreat primarily to global warming.The scale of the disaster has also renewed scrutiny of hydropower projects in Tibet, including China's planned mega dam on the Brahmaputra River.The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau is the source of around 10 transboundary rivers, including the Brahmaputra, making changes to its glaciers, rivers and extreme weather patterns significant for downstream regions.Chinese researchers have linked the growing risks in the region to glacier retreat and climate change as authorities continue rescue and recovery operations following the August 26 floods.

Rethink development models in fragile mountain areas By Raghu The sudden and catastrophic flash flood that hit Nepal near its border with Tibet-China on 26 August has claimed at least 1200 lives at the time of writing, with an estimated 3900-4800 people still unaccounted for.
Indians form the largest national cohort of victims, chiefly due to the on-going pilgrimage to Kailash-Mansarovar in Tibet.

Horrifying videos of the floods hitting what appears to be a large and sturdy border post at Gyirong on the Chinese side of the border with Nepal, and from a little further downstream, show a massive and fast-moving volume of muddy waters rushing past, sweeping aside everything in its path including multi-storied buildings, steel bridges, roads, vehicles and, unfortunately, people.

Given the remoteness of the area and the total destruction of infrastructure, it took several days for rescue and relief teams to even reach the disaster hit locations, and begin the arduous task of reaching and rescuing survivors, locating the missing, and the grim task of recovering bodies of the dead, all of which are continuing.
It took several days for international rescue teams to reach the disaster zone after roads were at least partially cleared, and authorities in Nepal organized coordination of these efforts.

Major rescue operations are currently underway to try to locate, and then rescue, around 900 missing hydro-electric power project workers who might still be alive and trapped in project tunnels now buried under rocks and mud.

Latest reports suggest that the Nepalese government is preparing to shift much of its efforts to rehabilitation, even while most rescue efforts wind down and relief continues to be provided to the thousands displaced from their homes and work.

The disaster raises very disturbing questions and poses major challenges for governments, policy makers, academic and research institutions, think tanks and civil society in Tibet-China and South Asian countries around the Hindukush-Himalaya all the way from Afghanistan and Pakistan in the west to Nepal, Bhutan and India and its North-Eastern regions with impacts in Bangladesh and Myanmar.

This disaster in Nepal, believed to be the worst flooding event in over a generation, albeit dwarfed by the magnitude of the 2015 earthquake that took over 9,000 lives, may indeed be unprecedented in scale but lists among an increasing number and rising frequency of similar events in the region.
What caused this particular event?
To what extent do these events and their rising frequency result from climate change, and what do answers to that question tell us about future actions and response?
Could the Nepal disaster have been predicted?
More generally, to what extent can early warning systems assist in saving lives and minimizing damage, as has been put in place or attempted in other types of disasters?
What are the potentialities and limitations?
And finally, what can we learn about reducing the risks and damage caused to life, livelihoods, habitats, infrastructure and the economy as a whole?
Compilation of all relevant data and analysis by scientists and experts, as well as peer review, leading to definitive pronouncement of causes would take more time.
As of now, some preliminary conclusions may be arrived at based on available information.

Preliminary assessment by most geologists is that the floods were caused by a dual high-altitude glacier and rock failure, and fall of the massive ice and rock chunks over several thousand feet to the river below.
The collapse occurred on the north face of Langtang Lirung on the Nepal-Tibet border at around 5200 metres.
As of now, it may not be possible to state unambiguously whether the glacier collapsed and took a big chunk of the bedrock with it or the other way around.

With rising temperatures, glacier melts have become quite common in the Himalayas and can cause large pieces to breakaway, or alternatively melting of ice in the permafrost can weaken the hold of the bedrock leading to its break-up under stress taking pieces of the glacier with it.

Either way, a study in Nepal is reported to have concluded that huge masses of ice, rocks and debris fell from 5200 metres down to the Lhende river at around 3000 metres and then traveled down through the Bhotekoshi and then the Trishuli rivers making a massive and debris-laden flood moving rapidly downstream.
Satellite imagery seems to show geographical changes over around 10 sq.km at the peak, and that about 0.56 sq.km or 50 hectares of glacier and rock had broken away.
Time stamped flood sensors and other indicators show that the flood wave traveled extremely fast.

It covered around 22 km to Rasuwagadhi in about 7 minutes at an estimated average speed of 167 kmph, dropping to about 22kmph further downstream but still carrying massive quantities of rock, ice and mud.
Satellite images do not show any new glacial lake formation in the upper reaches, ruling out that early speculation.
Seismic records showing tremors of 5.2 on the Richter scale also do not appear an earthquake but rather reflect the rock-glacier failute and collapse, putting to rest another plausible explanation.

However, river flow readings before Rasuwa show levels dropping several hours before the flood wave arrived, indicating a possible damning of the river upstream by falling boulders from above, presaging the glacier-rock collapse to follow.

These conclusions should surprise no one since such glacier-rock collapses have become common in the era of climate change, not only in the Himalayas but also in Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and other places in Europe, in Chile, Alaska, new Zealand and elsewhere.
Are all such disasters caused by climate change?
Science is all about what can be said with certainty, or can be said with a specified probability or degree of certainty.
So it is not possible to state definitively that an individual instance of extreme rainfall or glacier melt is caused by climate change, there is a very high probability that it is.
It is well established that global average temperatures are continuing to rise as predicted by climate science.

It is also well established, including by compilation of peer-reviewed scientific findings in the IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate ( IPCC/SROCC), that ice in the poles and in high mountain regions especially the Himalayas, is melting rapidly.
The Hindukush-Himalayas holds the largest volume of ice outside the polar region, and is hence often called ‘the third pole,’ and feeds 10 major Asian river systems.
it is melting faster than the global average.
The prognosis is therefore not good.
IPCC/SROCC says that polar ice and glaciers will continue to melt till 2050 given the current level of global emissions.
Even after that, and only if accelerated emissions reduction are achieved, there is some prospect of checking that trend by the end of this century.
Regrettably, this means that humanity and countries will have to live with glacier melts and its consequences as witnessed in Nepal and elsewhere, including in India.
The urgent need, therefore, is to reduce the risks and extent of damage that is likely to result from glacier-rock failures, glacier lake outbursts and similar catastrophic events.
The first line of defence is early warning.
Some limited early warning systems have been developed and put in place mostly for glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF) in the form of satellite-based surveillance and ground-based sensors.

But the difficulty may well be imagined from the fact that India itself has over 7,000 glacial lakes which are caused by glacier melt, blocking of water flow by rockslides or re-frozen ice, with risk of flash floods by sudden collapse of these temporary dams.
These locations are remote and at high altitude making installation and maintenance of ground-based sensors extremely difficult.
The trans-boundary nature of these glaciers, lakes and water flows pose further difficulties.
Early warning for disasters like the glacier-rock failure in Nepal poses even more difficulties.
Not only must satellite surveillance by intensified over vast areas, ground sensors must also be installed, monitored and maintained in remote, high altitude, often trans-boundary locations.
It is also difficult to predict a glacier or permafrost rock failure or its precise time, without which an early warning system would not serve its purpose.
Further, as the unfolding events in the Nepal tragedy showed, even if warning had been sounded, it may leave little time to evacuate the likely affected population.
Ultimately however, the very path of development currently being adopted, certainly in India and South Asia, is increasing rather than reducing the risks.
It has been reported, based on official data from Nepal, that the population in the districts most affected by the present Nepal disaster has increased by about 1 million in the past few decades.
Increasing settlements and related infrastructure, mostly on or near the narrow floodplains, vastly increase the risks to life, livelihoods and property.
The videos of the floods in Nepal showed buildings, roads, bridges etc crumbling in the face of the flood fury.
Over 14 hydro-power projects have effectively been buried.
Economic losses have been estimated at close to 10% of Nepal’s GDP.

In India too, similar destruction was witnessed in 2021 when a part of the Nanda Devi glacier collapsed and caused flooding in several rivers downstream in Chamoli District, destroying the Tapovan-Vishnugarh hydro-power projects.
The 2013 Uttarakhand floods caused immense damage to settlements along river floodplains.
The trajectory set by climate change, and the likelihood of extreme weather events and related or other glacier-related disasters, are now clear.
Business as usual is no longer possible.
A major re-think of development patterns in these fragile mountain areas is clearly required, certainly in India.

New Delhi [India], September 9 (ANI): India has delivered 95 tonnes of emergency relief materials on board seven aircraft to support Nepal during its ongoing flash flood catastrophe, the Ministry of External Affairs announced on Tuesday, expressing deep solidarity and sympathy with the people and government of the neighbouring country.

Speaking during a weekly press briefing, MEA Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal affirmed that India, as a close neighbour, responded promptly and will continue to back long-term relief, rescue, and reconstruction efforts.
Beyond material aid, Jaiswail noted that specialised Indian teams are providing critical operational support on the ground.
An Indian forensic team is currently stationed in Kathmandu to process DNA samples aimed at identifying victims.
Simultaneously, an Indian tunnel rescue team remains deployed in affected zones.
'We have expressed solidarity and sympathy with the people and government of Nepal, and we are doing our best to help them in this particular disaster.
As a close friend and neighbour, India has responded promptly and will continue to support Nepal's relief, rescue, and reconstruction efforts,' he said.
'We have sent 95 tonnes of relief material on board seven aircraft, and some more material shall be sent there soon.
Our forensic team and our tunnel rescue team, both the teams, are operating on the ground.
They are giving a helping hand in the rescue and relief efforts.
The forensic team is currently working in two laboratories in Kathmandu, where they are working on 1,200 DNA samples in these two laboratories.
We will continue to support Nepal as per their requirement,' he added.
Reiterating that India remains committed to extending assistance tailored to Nepal's specific requirements, the spokesperson also provided an update on Indian citizens affected by the crisis.

Out of 275 Indian nationals currently listed as missing, a figure that includes 49 individuals who disappeared on the Chinese side of the border, 169 Indian nationals have been successfully rescued to date.
'As I told you last time, 275 Indian nationals are missing in this disaster.
169 Indian nationals have been rescued so far.
And these 275 Indian nationals who are missing, as I mentioned, also include 49 people who went missing on the Chinese side,' he said.
Meanwhile, according to the data compiled up to 8 PM, Nepal Police informed that 1,366 casualties have been reported, while 4,077 individuals remain unaccounted for across the disaster zone.
The official breakdown of recovered victims includes 533 men, 339 women, and 502 partial human remains.
Out of the total recoveries made so far, police authorities have successfully verified and handed over 102 bodies to their families for final rites.
To preserve unidentified remains safely, 1,147 bodies have been buried underground under strict forensic guidelines.
The Police highlighted a staggering missing person count of 4,077 individuals, comprising both domestic residents and foreign visitors.
Missing Nepalese citizens account for 3,469 people, broken down into 2,907 men and 562 women.
Foreign nationals account for 598 missing individuals, which includes 269 men and 329 women.
Rescue and medical response efforts led by Nepal Police personnel have accounted for 9,254 rescued or injured individuals, including 6,380 men, 2,824 women, and 50 unidentified cases.
In addition, 3,030 displaced people are receiving shelter across designated holding centres managed by authorities.

To support victim identification, specialised teams have collected 2,698 DNA samples, comprising 1,286 samples from deceased victims and 1,412 samples from relatives searching for their missing family members.
Profiles and photographs of 1,310 unidentified victims have also been uploaded to the official website to assist the public in matching missing relatives.
The operations have required massive logistical deployment, with 7,975 Nepal Police personnel actively mobilised on the ground.
During the disaster response, 65 police personnel were directly affected, and 25 officers remain out of contact.
Parallel to rescue duties, police teams have conducted 158 community awareness and disaster guidance programs, reaching 43,943 local participants.

Meanwhile, India has asked families of Indian nationals who remain missing in China following the 'devastating' mudslide and flash flood on August 26 to submit DNA samples to assist in the identification process.

SINGAPORE – Five people, aged between 29 and 66, have been identified and interviewed by the police over certain comments made online on the recent Nepal flood disaster and discussions surrounding Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) investment in Air India.
The police said in a statement on Sept 9 that they would continue to investigate and identify those responsible for the online comments.
They added that they were unable to comment further on the details of the individual cases, as investigations were ongoing.
“The police take a serious view of conduct that may wound racial feelings or incite hostility and ill will between different racial groups,” they said.
The police statement comes after Senior Minister K.
Shanmugam on Sept 5 said that the authorities were looking into racist and xenophobic comments relating to the Nepal floods and Singapore Airlines’ investment in Air India.
The online comments on the issues – which make references to snakes, curry, prata, black magic and other racist stereotypes – have been “shameful, nasty and totally unacceptable”, said Shanmugam.
Addressing the anti-Indian comments, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said in a Facebook post on Sept 6 that Singapore must never allow prejudice against any community to become accepted or normalised.
He noted that there will always be people who seek to exploit Singapore’s differences, but how the country responds is up to Singaporeans.
While not every hateful comment online can be stopped, “we can reject such views, and refuse to give them more space or legitimacy”, he added.

In a Facebook post on Sept 6, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong called on Singaporeans to “reject hatred”, and said it was deeply troubling to see racist comments and hateful remarks directed at the Indian community in the wake of the Nepal flood tragedy.
The response at times like these should be compassion and solidarity, he said, adding that Singaporeans should stand by one another regardless of race, language or religion.

“When incidents like this happen, leaders must speak up with force and conviction to call out what is happening, condemn the manipulation of base emotions, and call on all Singaporeans to stand together,” he said.
Singaporeans missing after Nepal-Tibet floods Nine Singaporeans have been reported missing since the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods on Aug 26.
On Aug 31, Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC MP Alex Yam said in a post on Facebook that he noticed comments that questioned whether the nine missing were “really Singaporeans”.

“While families wait desperately for news of their loved ones, a loud minority of people apparently looked at the names and faces of those missing and decided that this was the moment to ask whether they were really Singaporean,” he said.
Yam added that some of these comments wished harm on those missing, while others questioned why the authorities should help these Singapore citizens.
Some of the comments were not just racist, but also downright heartless, he said.
“May we remember that before race, nationality or politics, there are frightened families hoping that someone they love comes home.
And I pray we never become so angry with one another that we lose the ability to simply be human.” Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth Dinesh Vasu Dash echoed Yam’s sentiments.
“At a moment like this, our first response must be humanity.
Every missing person is someone’s parent, spouse, child, sibling or friend,” Dinesh told The Straits Times.
“Let us be clear: Using a person’s name, race or appearance to question whether that person is truly Singaporean is racism.

It is wrong, and it must be called out.” Temasek CEO attacked online after news of SIA-Air India deal Shanmugam on Sept 5 also drew attention to the way Temasek’s chief executive, Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara, and the investment giant’s senior management were attacked online after it was reported that Air India was seeking about US$1.5 billion (S$1.9 billion) of investment from its shareholders, which include SIA.
He said the attacks, which included comments claiming that the Temasek chief would favour Air India due to his Indian ethnicity, were “vile”.
Temasek has a majority stake in Singapore’s flag carrier.

With regard to the SIA-Air India deal, Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said on Sept 8 that the national carrier’s investment in Air India has no adverse impact on its ability to operate and serve Singaporeans.
While SIA has a 25.1 per cent stake in Air India, the latter’s finances are not SIA’s, so its losses do not automatically become the Singapore carrier’s liabilities, he added.

Siow was replying to a parliamentary question submitted by Workers’ Party MP Kenneth Tiong (Aljunied GRC) on whether SIA’s losses from its foreign investments have been assessed against its capacity to provide essential transport services.

KATHMANDU, Nepal: Rescue teams in Nepal are concentrating their efforts on three hydropower project tunnels where dozens of workers are believed to be trapped, authorities said this week.
The search comes two weeks after a massive flood and mudslide struck the Himalayan country, killing hundreds of people and leaving thousands missing in Nepal and neighboring Tibet in China.
The disaster happened on August 26, when a glacier collapsed into a river along the Nepal-China border.
The sudden rush of ice, rocks, mud and water swept through the area and badly damaged at least 11 hydropower projects.
Debris buried the entrances to several tunnels, cutting off workers who may have been inside.
Dharma Raj Upreti, head of Nepal's disaster management authority, said rescuers were continuing to search for survivors, with tunnels now among their main targets.
"Our search operation is focused on finding survivors, including in tunnels.
Our bigger focus is on the Chilime hydroelectric project, where we believe people are trapped, because there was a canteen, residency and arrangements for food," Upreti told Reuters.
Rescue teams are also concentrating on the tunnels of the Upper Trishuli 3A and 3B hydropower projects.
The two projects are connected through an underground tunnel system, making the search particularly important.
Upreti said rescuers pumped oxygen into the tunnels through pipes to keep anyone trapped inside alive.
Teams have also brought in new equipment that could help them clear debris and create an opening into the blocked tunnels.
In recent days, rescue workers have saved four people from different locations.
A Chinese national was pulled alive from a tunnel on September 5.
Rescuers rescued two hydropower workers from another tunnel a day earlier.
A Nepali woman was also found alive after rescuers pulled her from the remains of her buried home the following day.
Despite these rescues, the disaster's scale remains enormous.
At least 1,399 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal and Tibet, while more than 5,400 people are still missing.
The disaster has also caused heavy losses on the Chinese side of the border.
As of September 5, at least 43 people had died in Tibet, and another 519 were reported missing.
China's state news agency Xinhua reported that none of the bodies recovered in Tibet so far belonged to foreign nationals.
Among those desperately searching for missing relatives is Australian medical student Sarada Viswanathan, 23.
Her boyfriend, Rishab Iyer, and members of his family disappeared near the Nepal-China border after the glacier collapse triggered the massive flood of water and debris.
Viswanathan appealed to technology and telecommunications companies to share location and tracking information that could help rescue teams reduce the areas they need to search.
Viswanathan said Apple and Australian telecommunications company Optus had refused her requests for location data that might have helped establish the family's last known movements.
Optus said it could not comment on individual customers, while Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
An earlier report said Life360 had also declined to discuss the specific case, but later clarified it had not.
